## What it says
Let $\tau$ be any $R$-linear map from the infinite type-$A$ Hecke algebra to $R$. For braids $b,c$ on $n+1$ strands and an elementary braid $\sigma_i$, $i<n$,
$$\tau(\gamma(b\,\sigma_i\,c))-\tau(\gamma(b\,\sigma_i^{-1}\,c))=(q-q^{-1})\,\tau(\gamma(b\,c)),$$
where $\gamma$ is the braid homomorphism `braidHom R q (n + 1)`. It follows from $T_i-T_i^{-1}=q-q^{-1}$ by linearity, with no trace hypothesis on $\tau$. This is the Hecke skein relation in an arbitrary braid context, with the sign the roadmap prescribes for this convention.

## References and tests
- [TauCetiRoadmap, TypeAHeckeAlgebras, H2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/3b51055b32da85f548435c4abb76e29881106131/TauCetiRoadmap/TypeAHeckeAlgebras/README.md#L156): the braid representation $\gamma_n\colon B_n\to H_n$ and the trace of braids.
- [TauCetiRoadmap, TypeAHeckeAlgebras, H2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/3b51055b32da85f548435c4abb76e29881106131/TauCetiRoadmap/TypeAHeckeAlgebras/README.md#L162-L163): under $T^2=(q-q^{-1})T+1$ the skein sign is dictated by $T-T^{-1}=q-q^{-1}$.
- `TauCeti.InfiniteTypeAHeckeAlgebra.T_sub_val_inv_unitT` — the element identity it rests on.

## Lean subtleties
- `q : Rˣ` is a unit of the commutative ring $R$, and `↑q⁻¹` is its inverse coerced into $R$ (`↑` is the coercion). Because $q$ is a unit there is no junk value for $q^{-1}$, but $q=0$, and with it the $0$-Hecke algebra, is outside this normalisation.
- It is stated in the namespace `LinearMap` (written `_root_.LinearMap.map_braidHom_skein` in the source) so that it can be called as `τ.map_braidHom_skein`.
- `BraidGroup (n + 1)` has $n$ elementary braids, indexed by `i : Fin n`; the statement covers every braid group with at least one strand.

## What it says
For a commutative ring $R$ (`R : Type*`, `[CommRing R]`) and a unit $q$ of $R$, `InfiniteTypeAHeckeAlgebra R q` is the quotient of the free $R$-algebra on generators $T_0,T_1,\dots$ by the relations of `TauCeti.InfiniteTypeAHeckeAlgebra.Rel`:
$$T_i^2=(q-q^{-1})T_i+1,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\ (|i-j|\ge2).$$
It is the type-$A$ Iwahori–Hecke algebra on infinitely many strands, the union of the Hecke algebras $H_n(q)$ of the symmetric groups, in the normalisation where every generator has eigenvalues $q$ and $-q^{-1}$. In the more common normalisation $(T-Q)(T+1)=0$ this is the algebra with parameter $Q=q^2$, with generators rescaled by $q^{-1}$. At $q=\pm1$ the quadratic relation reads $T_i^2=1$, and the algebra is the group algebra of the finitary symmetric group. Its ring and $R$-algebra structures are the instances declared right after it.

## References and tests
- [TauCetiRoadmap, TypeAHeckeAlgebras, Scope and conventions](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/3b51055b32da85f548435c4abb76e29881106131/TauCetiRoadmap/TypeAHeckeAlgebras/README.md#L9-L14): the type-$A$ Hecke algebra over a commutative ring with a chosen unit $q$, with $(T_i-q)(T_i+q^{-1})=0$, equivalently $T_i^2=(q-q^{-1})T_i+1$, and the braid and distant-commutation relations.
- [TauCetiRoadmap, TypeAHeckeAlgebras, Scope and conventions](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/3b51055b32da85f548435c4abb76e29881106131/TauCetiRoadmap/TypeAHeckeAlgebras/README.md#L16-L21): $H_\infty(q)$ is the `RingQuot` of `FreeAlgebra R ℕ` by these relations, and its stage $S_n$ is `Algebra.adjoin R (range (i : Fin (n−1) ↦ T_i))`, the image of the Hecke algebra on $n$ strands.

## What it says
`Rel R q` is a relation on `FreeAlgebra R ℕ`, the free associative $R$-algebra on generators $\iota(0),\iota(1),\dots$, for a commutative ring $R$ and a unit $q$ of $R$. It relates exactly these pairs:

- `mul_self i`: $\iota(i)\iota(i)$ and $(q-q^{-1})\,\iota(i)+1$, the quadratic relation;
- `braid i`: $\iota(i)\iota(i+1)\iota(i)$ and $\iota(i+1)\iota(i)\iota(i+1)$, the braid relation of adjacent generators;
- `distant h`: $\iota(i)\iota(j)$ and $\iota(j)\iota(i)$ when $i+2\le j$.

These are the defining relations of the type-$A$ Iwahori–Hecke algebra on infinitely many strands: the Coxeter relations of type $A_\infty$ with the quadratic relation in the normalisation $(T_i-q)(T_i+q^{-1})=0$, to which it is equivalent. Distant commutation is imposed for one order of each pair; the ring congruence generated is symmetric, so nothing is lost.

## What it says

- `hself`: $f(i)^2=(q-q^{-1})\,f(i)+1$ for all $i$;
- `hbraid`: $f(i)f(i+1)f(i)=f(i+1)f(i)f(i+1)$ for all $i$;
- `hdist`: $f(i)f(j)=f(j)f(i)$ whenever $i+2\le j$.

Then `lift f hself hbraid hdist` is the $R$-algebra homomorphism from the infinite type-$A$ Hecke algebra to $A$ sending $T_i$ to $f(i)$. It is the map a presentation by generators and relations induces, built from `FreeAlgebra.lift` and `RingQuot.liftAlgHom`.

## What it says
For $n\le1$, the stage $H_n$ is `⊥`, the smallest subalgebra, which consists of the scalars $r\cdot1$, $r\in R$. On at most one strand there are no generators, and the Hecke algebra on $0$ or $1$ strand is $R$.

## What it says
Throughout, $n \ge 4$ and the $2n$ coordinates are indexed by `Fin n ⊕ Fin n`: `inl j` is the basis vector $e_j$ and `inr j` its hyperbolic partner $e_{\bar j}$ ($j = 0, \dots, n-1$). Mathlib's `LieAlgebra.Orthogonal.typeD (Fin n) K` is the Lie algebra of $2n \times 2n$ matrices $X$ over $K$ with $X^{T} J = -J X$, where $J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I \\ I & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is the split (hyperbolic) form.

`cartanGenerator n hn i` is the diagonal matrix $h_i = \mathrm{diag}(\alpha_i, -\alpha_i)$, where $\alpha_i \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ is the $i$-th simple root in the coordinates $\varepsilon_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}$ (`DynkinType.typeDSimpleRoot n hn i`), cast to $K$: the coroot of $\alpha_i$, which for this simply laced system has the same coordinates as $\alpha_i$.

So $h_0, \dots, h_{n-1}$ are the simple coroots $H_{\alpha_i}$ in the diagonal Cartan subalgebra: on the chain
$h_i = E_{ii} - E_{i+1,i+1} - E_{\bar i\bar i} + E_{\overline{i+1}\,\overline{i+1}}$, and at the fork
$h_{n-1} = E_{n-2,n-2} + E_{n-1,n-1} - E_{\overline{n-2}\,\overline{n-2}} - E_{\overline{n-1}\,\overline{n-1}}$.

- `hn : 4 ≤ n` is an explicit proof argument: the statement is made only for $n \ge 4$, the range in which the project's type $D_n$ is defined (`DynkinType.D n` is valid exactly when $4 \le n$). The same matrices would describe $D_2 = A_1 \times A_1$ and $D_3 = A_3$, which are left out; at $n = 1$ the two fork coordinates would coincide.
- Indexing is zero-based: `i : Fin n` is Bourbaki's node $i + 1$ and the coordinates are $\varepsilon_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}$. The chain nodes are $i = 0, \dots, n-2$ (root $\varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_{i+1}$) and the last node $i = n - 1$ carries the fork root $\varepsilon_{n-2} + \varepsilon_{n-1}$, Bourbaki's $\alpha_n = \varepsilon_{n-1} + \varepsilon_n$.
- `[CommRing K]`: $K$ is any commutative ring, the zero ring and characteristic $2$ included. In characteristic $2$ Mathlib's `typeD` (skew-adjoint matrices for a symmetric form) is larger than the Lie algebra of $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$; the matrices here have skew blocks with zero diagonal and lie in the smaller algebra too.
- The integer vector $\alpha_i$ is cast into $K$ (the arrow `↑`); in characteristic $2$ the fork coroot is still
  nonzero, its entries being $\pm 1$.

- `[Finite G] [IsCyclic G]`: $G$ is finite and cyclic.
- `FixedPoints.subfield G F` is $F^G$; `F ≃ₐ[FixedPoints.subfield G F] F` is $\mathrm{Aut}(F/F^G)$.

There is no hypothesis relating $j$ and $r$; the $\min$ in the upper limits is what makes it hold for all of them. As the docstring says, it is the identity the Fourier coefficients of Hecke operators at a prime power satisfy, with $a(t)$ the coefficient at $p^t m$ and $c = \chi(p) p^{k-1}$. A double sum over the blocks of a word, split at one position.

## What it says
Let $\mu$ be a nonzero measure on $\mathbb R$ and $t$ a real with $bt$ in the exponential-integrability domain of
$\mu$. Then the cumulant-generating function of the image of $\mu$ under $x \mapsto a + bx$ at $t$ is
$at + K_\mu(bt)$: $K_{a+bX}(t) = at + K_X(bt)$.

- `[NeZero μ]`: $\mu \ne 0$ (a typeclass hypothesis); no finiteness is assumed.
- `ht : b * t ∈ integrableExpSet id μ`: $x \mapsto e^{btx}$ is $\mu$-integrable.
- `cgf id ν t` is $\log \int e^{tx}\,d\nu$.

This is the roadmap's $K_{a+bX}(t) = at + K_X(bt)$ for $t \in D$, with $D$ the domain of the transformed law, which
by `TauCeti.Probability.integrableExpSet_id_map_affine` is the condition `ht`.

## What it says

under $x \mapsto a + bx$ at $t$ is $e^{iat} \varphi_\mu(bt)$: $\varphi_{a+bX}(t) = e^{iat}\varphi_X(bt)$.

This is the characteristic-function transport of the roadmap.

## What it says
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ (any measure: no finiteness is assumed) and real numbers $a, b, c, d$:
pushing $\mu$ forward by $x \mapsto a + bx$ and then by $y \mapsto c + dy$ gives the same measure as pushing it
forward once by $x \mapsto (c + da) + (db)x$.

- `μ` is an implicit measure on `ℝ`; `a b c d : ℝ` are the two intercepts and slopes.
- The conclusion is an equality of measures on $\mathbb R$.

This is functoriality of the image measure, $(g \circ f)_*\mu = g_*(f_*\mu)$, together with the composition
law of affine maps $c + d(a + bx) = (c + da) + (db)x$. It is the composition law asked for in the roadmap.

## What it says
The map sending a triple $(\mu, a, b)$, with $\mu$ a probability measure on $\mathbb R$ and $a, b$ real, to the
image measure of $\mu$ under $x \mapsto a + bx$ is measurable.

- The domain is `ProbabilityMeasure ℝ × ℝ × ℝ`: probability measures on $\mathbb R$, with the intercept $a$ and
  the slope $b$. Measurability on `ProbabilityMeasure ℝ` and `Measure ℝ` refers to the Giry σ-algebra, the
  smallest one making every evaluation $\mu \mapsto \mu(B)$, $B$ Borel, measurable; on $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R$ it
  is the Borel σ-algebra.

This is the joint measurability in $(\mu, a, b)$ that the roadmap asks of affine transport, which lets a
location–scale family built by pushing forward a measurably parametrised law be measurable in its parameters.

## What it says
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$ and $0 < u < 1$. For all reals $a, b$, the lower quantile at level
$u$ of the image of $\mu$ under $x \mapsto a + bx$ is
$a + bQ_\mu(u)$ if $b > 0$, $a$ if $b = 0$, and $a + bQ^+_\mu(1 - u)$ if $b < 0$.

- `[IsProbabilityMeasure μ]`: $\mu$ is a probability measure (a typeclass hypothesis).
- `h0 : 0 < u`, `h1 : u < 1`: the level is interior.
- `μ.quantile u` is the lower quantile $Q_\mu(u) = \inf\{{x : u \le F_\mu(x)\}}$ and `μ.upperQuantile u` the upper quantile $Q^+_\mu(u) = \inf\{{x : u < F_\mu(x)\}}$, both written with `sInf`, the infimum of a set of reals.

This is exactly the transport formula of the roadmap. At a negative slope the order reverses and the lower
quantile becomes a reflected upper quantile; the two differ when the distribution function of $\mu$ is flat at
level $1 - u$.

Let $\mu$ be an s-finite measure on $\mathbb R$ and $b \ne 0$. The Radon–Nikodym derivative of the image of $\mu$
under $x \mapsto a + bx$ with respect to Lebesgue measure equals, Lebesgue-almost everywhere,
$y \mapsto |b|^{-1} \, \frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}((y - a)/b)$.

- `[SFinite μ]`: $\mu$ is a countable sum of finite measures (a hypothesis carried as a typeclass).
- `hb : b ≠ 0`.
- `=ᵐ[volume]`: equality outside a Lebesgue-null set.

For an absolutely continuous $\mu$ this is the density transport of the roadmap. For a general $\mu$,
`rnDeriv` is the density of the absolutely continuous part in the Lebesgue decomposition, and the image of the
singular part stays singular, so the formula holds as stated.

## What it says
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$ and $0 < u < 1$. For all reals $a, b$, the upper quantile at level
$u$ of the image of $\mu$ under $x \mapsto a + bx$ is
$a + bQ^+_\mu(u)$ if $b > 0$, $a$ if $b = 0$, and $a + bQ_\mu(1 - u)$ if $b < 0$.

- `[IsProbabilityMeasure μ]`: $\mu$ is a probability measure (a typeclass hypothesis).
- `h0 : 0 < u`, `h1 : u < 1`.
- `μ.quantile u` is the lower quantile $Q_\mu(u) = \inf\{{x : u \le F_\mu(x)\}}$ and `μ.upperQuantile u` the upper quantile $Q^+_\mu(u) = \inf\{{x : u < F_\mu(x)\}}$, both written with `sInf`, the infimum of a set of reals.

These are the "upper versions" of the roadmap's quantile transport: at a negative slope the upper quantile becomes
a reflected lower quantile.

## What it says
If a subgroup $\Gamma \le \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ contains the principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$, then for every $\gamma \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ the conjugate $\gamma^{-1}\Gamma\gamma$ contains $u(x) = \begin{pmatrix}1 & x\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ at $x = N$: $N$ is a strict period of $\Gamma$ at the cusp $\gamma\infty$.

- `{Γ : Subgroup (GL (Fin 2) ℝ)} {N : ℕ}`: a subgroup $\Gamma$ and a level $N$, inferred by Lean.

- `(γ : SL(2, ℤ))`: any element of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
- The conclusion: `↑N ∈ (ConjAct.toConjAct (mapGL ℝ γ)⁻¹ • Γ).strictPeriods`. `ConjAct.toConjAct g • Γ` is $g\Gamma g^{-1}$, so with $g = \gamma^{-1}$ this is $\gamma^{-1}\Gamma\gamma$, whose behaviour at $\infty$ is that of $\Gamma$ at $\gamma\infty$.

The reason: $T^N \in \Gamma(N)$, and $\Gamma(N)$ is normal in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, so $\gamma T^N\gamma^{-1} \in \Gamma(N) \le \Gamma$. As $\gamma$ ranges over $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, $\gamma\infty$ ranges over all of $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{Q})$.

## What it says

## What it says
For a real number $c$, the map $z \mapsto c - 1/z$ of $\mathbb C$ restricts to a bijection of the open upper half-plane $\mathbb H = \{z \in \mathbb C : \operatorname{Im} z > 0\}$ onto itself. `BijOn f s t` means three things: $f$ maps $s$ into $t$, $f$ is injective on $s$, and every point of $t$ is the image of a point of $s$. ## What it says
Two retracts of $X$ whose idempotents add up to the identity exhibit $X$ as their biproduct: the isomorphism $X \cong Y \oplus Z$.

- `{C : Type u}` with `[Category.{v} C] [Preadditive C]`: a category whose hom-sets are abelian groups with bilinear composition; `[HasBinaryBiproducts C]`: chosen binary biproducts.
- `{X Y Z : C}` and maps `i₁ : Y ⟶ X`, `r₁ : X ⟶ Y`, `i₂ : Z ⟶ X`, `r₂ : X ⟶ Z`.
- `(h₁ : i₁ ≫ r₁ = 𝟙 Y)`, `(h₂ : i₂ ≫ r₂ = 𝟙 Z)`: $r_1 i_1 = \mathrm{id}_Y$ and $r_2 i_2 = \mathrm{id}_Z$, so $Y$ and $Z$ are retracts of $X$.
- `(h : r₁ ≫ i₁ + r₂ ≫ i₂ = 𝟙 X)`: $i_1 r_1 + i_2 r_2 = \mathrm{id}_X$.

Its value is the isomorphism whose forward map is `biprod.lift r₁ r₂`, the map $(r_1, r_2) : X \to Y \oplus Z$, and whose inverse is `biprod.desc i₁ i₂`, the map $[i_1, i_2] : Y \oplus Z \to X$ (`TauCeti.isoBiprodOfRetracts_hom`, `TauCeti.isoBiprodOfRetracts_inv`). The orthogonality relations $r_2 i_1 = 0$ and $r_1 i_2 = 0$ are not asked for: they follow, since $i_1 = (i_1 r_1 + i_2 r_2) i_1 = i_1 + i_2 r_2 i_1$ and $i_2$ is a split monomorphism. This is the usual recognition of a direct sum by its "total" identity; Mathlib's `isBinaryBilimitOfTotal` does the same for a bicone, which already carries the orthogonality relations.

## What it says
If a module $M$ is the internal direct sum of a sequence of submodules $N_0, N_1, N_2, \dots$ indexed by the natural numbers, then it is also the internal direct sum of the sequence $0, N_0, N_1, N_2, \dots$ obtained by putting the zero submodule in front and shifting the rest by one place.

## What it says

## What it says

## What it says
Let `R` be a commutative semiring mapping to a field `M` which is an algebraic extension of the field `E`. If the image of `R` generates `M` over `E` as a field, then the image of `R` spans `M` as an `E`-vector space: every element of `M` is an `E`-linear combination of images of elements of `R`. The point is that, for an algebraic extension, the algebra generated by a subring is already a field, so field generation and algebra generation coincide, and a multiplicatively closed set spans the algebra it generates. Algebraicity is essential: for `R = E[X]` and `M = E(X)` the hypothesis holds but the span is a proper subspace.

None.

## What it says
A finite-type commutative Hopf algebra `H` over a field `k` (an affine algebraic group over `k`) is reductive when (1) `H` is smooth over `k`, (2) `H` is geometrically connected, i.e. its spectrum stays connected after every field extension, and (3) every closed subgroup of the geometric fibre that is normal, connected and smooth-unipotent is trivial. This is the standard geometric definition: a smooth connected affine group whose geometric unipotent radical is trivial. It is built as the instance of `geometricNormalSubgroupFreeCommHopfAlgProperty` with candidate property `smoothUnipotentCommHopfAlgProperty (AlgebraicClosure k)`. The statement compares with the textbook notion without dropping smoothness, connectedness or the passage to the algebraic closure; the unipotent radical is replaced by the equivalent statement about all smooth connected unipotent normal subgroups.

Here `k` is a field, `AlgebraicClosure k` is a fixed algebraic closure (chosen classically), and the geometric fibre of `H` is the Hopf algebra `H` tensored up to that closure (`FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.baseChange`). A closed subgroup of the geometric fibre is the quotient by a Hopf ideal `I`; it is trivial exactly when `I` is the augmentation ideal (the kernel of the counit), not the zero ideal, because the correspondence between subgroups and ideals reverses inclusion.

- `[ContinuousSMul K A]`: scalar multiplication is jointly continuous.
- `hc : ‖c‖ ≤ 1`: the scalar has norm at most one.
- Conclusion: `IsPowerBounded (algebraMap K A c)`.

The argument: continuity gives a neighbourhood $V$ and a radius $\varepsilon$ with $tV \subseteq U$ for $\|t\|<\varepsilon$; choosing $d$ of small nonzero norm, $dV$ is a neighbourhood of $0$ and $(dv)c^n = (c^n d)v \in U$ since $\|c^n d\| \le \|d\|$.

- `[Module.Flat R C]`: $C$ is flat over $R$, so $P$ carries the inherited comodule structure and the inclusion `Subcomodule.subtype P` is a comodule morphism.
- `(f : Hom R C M N)`, `(P : Subcomodule R C N)`, `(h : ∀ m, f m ∈ P)`: as above.
- The conclusion is an equality of comodule morphisms $M \to N$; `Comodule.Hom.comp g f` applies `f` first, then `g`.

This is the universal property of corestriction in the form that the factorisation of $f$ through $P$ exists.

## What it says
Let $p : E\to B$ be a local homeomorphism of Hausdorff spaces with $B$ weakly locally compact (every point has a compact neighbourhood), and $f : E \to M$ with values in a commutative additive monoid, such that for every compact $K\subseteq B$ the set $p^{-1}(K)\cap \operatorname{supp}f$ is compact, where the topological support is the closure of $\{f\neq 0\}$. Suppose for every $e\in E$ we are given a map $\sigma_e : B\to E$, continuous at $p(e)$, with $\sigma_e(p(e))=e$ and $p(\sigma_e(b))=b$ for $b$ near $p(e)$ (a local section through $e$). Then for each $b_0\in B$ there is a finite set $F$ of points of the fiber over $b_0$ such that, for all $b$ near $b_0$, $\sum_{e\in p^{-1}(b)} f(e)=\sum_{e\in F} f(\sigma_e(b))$. So fiber sums of such a function are locally finite sums of $f$ composed with sections, which is how regularity of fiber sums (for instance for the source map of an etale groupoid) is reduced to regularity of $f\circ\sigma_e$.

- No tests.

## Lean subtleties
The left side is a `finsum` (`∑ᶠ`), which is defined as $0$ when the support of the summand is infinite; the hypothesis on compact preimages of the support is what makes the fiber sum a genuine finite sum, and the conclusion expresses it as one. `T2Space` and `WeaklyLocallyCompactSpace` are typeclass hypotheses on the spaces. Only continuity of each $\sigma_e$ at the single point $p(e)$ is assumed, not on a neighbourhood. $F$ may be empty, in which case the fiber sum vanishes near $b_0$.

## What it says
For a local homeomorphism $p : E\to B$, a point $b\in B$ and a subset $s\subseteq E$, if $p^{-1}(\{b\})\cap s$ is compact then it is finite. This is because the fiber $p^{-1}(\{b\})$ of a local homeomorphism is discrete as a subspace, and a compact discrete set is finite.

## What it says
Let $p : E \to B$ be a local homeomorphism and $e \in E$. Mathlib's `localInverseAt` gives a local homeomorphism $L$ from $B$ to $E$ (defined on an open set of $B$, the target of $L$ in the sense below) which inverts a chart of $p$ at $e$. Suppose $\varphi : E \to E$ is continuous at $z$, satisfies $p\circ\varphi = p$ on a neighbourhood of $z$, and sends $z$ into the domain of $L$ (called `target` of the symmetric partial homeomorphism). Then $L\circ p = \varphi$ on a neighbourhood of $z$. In words, a continuous local deck transformation near $z$ is determined by where it sends $z$ once a local inverse is fixed. Proof idea: near $z$, $\varphi(w)$ lies in the open domain of $L$ and $p(\varphi(w))=p(w)$, so $L(p(w)) = L(p(\varphi(w))) = \varphi(w)$ since $L$ inverts $p$ there.

## What it says
Let $p : E \to B$ be a local homeomorphism (every point of $E$ has an open neighbourhood mapped homeomorphically onto an open subset of $B$) and suppose $B$ is locally path-connected, meaning every point has a neighbourhood basis of path-connected sets. Then $E$ is locally path-connected. The idea: pull a path-connected neighbourhood of $p(e)$ back through a local inverse at $e$, which is a homeomorphism onto an open set, so path-connected open sets map to path-connected open sets. This is the standard fact that local path-connectedness is local and passes to open subspaces; applied to a covering map it says the total space of a covering of a locally path-connected space is locally path-connected, as the docstring notes.

## What it says
Let $f : X\to Y$ be a local homeomorphism and $g : Z\to Y$ continuous. The fiber product $X\times_Y Z=\{(x,z) : f(x)=g(z)\}$, with the subspace topology from $X\times Z$, maps to $Z$ by the second projection, and this projection is a local homeomorphism: local homeomorphisms are stable under base change. Over a chart $e$ of $f$ the fiber product is identified with $g^{-1}(\text{target of }e)$ via $(x,z)\mapsto z$ with inverse $z\mapsto(e^{-1}(g z), z)$.

## What it says

## What it says
Let $I$ be a finite index set, $G$ a group (with decidable equality), and $R^I$ the module of functions $I \to R$ with a right $C$-comodule structure. Let $f : C \to R[G]$ be a coalgebra morphism into the group algebra and $\mathrm{wt} : I \to G$. The hypothesis says that the corestriction of $R^I$ along $f$ is the diagonal comodule on the standard basis $e_a$ with weights $\mathrm{wt}(a)$, that is $e_a \mapsto e_a \otimes \mathrm{wt}(a)$. Then for every subcomodule $N$, every $v \in N$ and every $g \in G$, the vector $w$ with $w_a = v_a$ if $\mathrm{wt}(a) = g$ and $w_a = 0$ otherwise lies in $N$. In words: a subcomodule contains the full weight-$g$ component of each of its vectors, whether or not distinct coordinates share weights (weights are not assumed injective). The proof applies the weight projection of the corestricted comodule, which preserves subcomodules, and computes it on the diagonal comodule.

## Lean subtleties

Throughout, `AddCircle p` is the quotient group $\mathbb K/p\mathbb Z$ of the additive group of $\mathbb K$ by the subgroup generated by $p$, with no topology involved, and `[x]` denotes the class of $x$. `(AddCircle p)[n]` is the subgroup of elements killed by $n$. For $n\ne0$ the image of $\mathbb Z/n\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is exactly the $n$-torsion subgroup of $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Together with injectivity this identifies $\mathbb Z/n$ with the $n$-torsion of $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$.

The hypothesis is the typeclass `[NeZero n]`. For $n=0$ the image is trivial while the $0$-torsion is the whole group $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, so the statement would be false there. The range is the range of the bundled additive homomorphism, a subgroup.

## What it says
A $C^n$ map $f$, $n \ge 1$, from an open subset of a real or complex Banach space $E$ to a Banach space $F$ is an immersion at each point $x$ where its derivative has a continuous linear left inverse: in suitable local $C^n$ charts around $x$ and $f(x)$ it is the inclusion of $E$ as a factor.

- `[RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field $𝕜$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a Banach space over $𝕜$, of any dimension.
- `[NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] [CompleteSpace F]`: so is $F$.
- `(hf : ContDiffOn 𝕜 n f s)`: $f : E \to F$ is $C^n$ on the set $s \subseteq E$, where the order $n$ ranges over `WithTop ℕ∞`: a natural number, $\infty$ (smooth) or $\omega$ (analytic).
- `(hs : IsOpen s)`: $s$ is open.
- `(hx : x ∈ s)`: the point $x$ lies in $s$.
- `(hn : 1 ≤ n)`: $f$ is at least $C^1$.
- `(hdf : (fderiv 𝕜 f x).HasLeftInverse)`: the derivative $Df(x) : E \to F$ has a left inverse that is a continuous linear map $F \to E$; equivalently, $Df(x)$ is injective and its image is closed with a closed complement.
- The conclusion: with $E$ and $F$ seen as manifolds modelled on themselves (`modelWithCornersSelf`), $f$ is a $C^n$ immersion at $x$ (`Manifold.IsImmersionAt`): there are charts of their $C^n$ structures around $x$ and $f(x)$ in which $f$ reads $u \mapsto (u, 0)$, into $E$ times a complement, identified linearly with $F$.

This is the local immersion theorem in its Banach-space form. In infinite dimensions injectivity of $Df(x)$ is not enough, and the split condition, a continuous left inverse, is the standard hypothesis; in finite dimensions it says just that $Df(x)$ is injective.

## References and tests
- Hirsch, *Differential Topology*, Ch. 1 §3 — the local immersion theorem, there for finite-dimensional manifolds; cited by Voyager's announcement of this result.
- Glöckner, Fundamentals of Submersions and Immersions — immersions between infinite-dimensional manifolds, the setting where a continuous linear left inverse of the derivative is the split-immersion condition ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05795)); only the abstract was read in this review, so the exact statement was not checked.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `fderiv 𝕜 f x` is $Df(x)$ when $f$ is differentiable at $x$, and $0$ otherwise; `hf`, `hs`, `hx` and `hn` make $f$ differentiable at $x$, so `hdf` is about the true derivative.
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` has two tops: $\infty$ and, above it, $\omega$, which in Mathlib means analytic. For $n = \omega$ the charts are analytic.
- `modelWithCornersSelf 𝕜 E` makes $E$ a manifold whose one chart is the identity; `IsImmersionAt` allows any chart of the maximal $C^n$ atlas, that is, any local $C^n$ diffeomorphism, so the conclusion is the classical normal form.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, found by Lean; completeness of $E$ and $F$ is what the inverse function theorem behind the result needs.
- The statement is local: no injectivity of $f$ on $s$, closed image or embedding is claimed. For $E = 0$ the derivative is the zero map, which has a left inverse, and the conclusion holds trivially.

## What it says
A smooth (`C^infinity`) Riemannian metric `g` on the tangent bundle of a manifold `M` that already carries a metric space structure is said to induce the Riemannian distance when, with `g` installed as the Riemannian structure, `M` is a Riemannian manifold in Mathlib's sense: the ambient extended distance equals Mathlib's Riemannian extended distance `riemannianEDist` between any two points (`IsRiemannianManifold`).

## References and tests
- Mathlib's class `IsRiemannianManifold` is the definition it unfolds to.
No declaration tests it beyond its unfolding lemma.

## Lean subtleties
It is a `Prop`-valued definition that is the class `IsRiemannianManifold` stated after installing `g` with `letI`. The condition ties the ambient metric space structure to the Riemannian one; no new data is added.

## What it says
If the smooth Riemannian metric `g` induces the Riemannian distance, then with `g` installed as the Riemannian structure the manifold `M` satisfies `IsRiemannianManifold I M`.

## References and tests

## What it says
Two smooth Riemannian metrics of the same class `C^n` on a vector bundle are equal as soon as their fibrewise inner products agree at every point and for every pair of vectors. The other fields of a metric (symmetry, positivity, boundedness of the unit ball, smoothness) are propositions, so they carry no extra data.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's structure `Bundle.ContMDiffRiemannianMetric` (Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/VectorBundle/Riemannian.lean) has no extensionality lemma of its own; this one is registered as `@[ext]`.
No test names this lemma.

None: the proof destructs both structures and applies function and bilinear-map extensionality; the Prop fields are identified by proof irrelevance.

## What it says
If a `C^n` Riemannian metric `g` is installed as the `RiemannianBundle` structure on a vector bundle, then the fibre inner product of two vectors in the same fibre equals `g.inner x v w`.

## References and tests
- Dual to `Bundle.ContMDiffRiemannianMetric.ofIsContMDiffRiemannianBundle_inner`: installing a metric and reading it back gives the same inner product.
No other test.

## Lean subtleties

## What it says
Given a `C^n` Riemannian bundle (a bundle whose fibres carry inner products, with a `C^n` metric tensor as in Mathlib's `IsContMDiffRiemannianBundle`), this packages the fibre inner products as a bundled `C^n` Riemannian metric: the inner product at each point, symmetry, positivity, the von Neumann boundedness of the unit ball, and smoothness of the metric tensor viewed as a section.

## References and tests

No recorded test beyond its characterising lemma.

## Lean subtleties
It is a definition through the typeclass `RiemannianBundle V`, so the metric is the one the instance supplies; no choice is made beyond the existential witness used only inside the smoothness proof, which does not affect the data.

## What it says
The inner product of the metric packaged from a `C^n` Riemannian bundle at `x` on `v, w` is the bundle's fibre inner product. It is the characterising property of the packaging.

## References and tests

No other test.

## What it says
A continuous Riemannian bundle (a bundle with fibre inner products whose metric tensor is continuous) is a `C^0` Riemannian bundle, for any model with corners `IB`.

## References and tests
- Uses `IsContinuousRiemannianBundle.exists_continuous` and `contMDiff_zero_iff` (Mathlib).
No other test.

## Lean subtleties
`C^0` smoothness of a section agrees with continuity; here `n = 0` in the extended natural numbers `ℕ∞ω`, so no junk value is involved. It is a theorem, not an instance, as its docstring says, to avoid an inference loop.

## What it says
Let `f` be `C^n` from an open subset `U` of a real normed space to a manifold `M` whose tangent bundle carries a `C^m` Riemannian metric, with `m + 1 ≤ n`. For fixed vectors `ξ` and `η`, the function `z ↦ ⟪df_z ξ, df_z η⟫` of the Riemannian inner product is `C^m` on `U`. The loss of one derivative is that of the derivative of a `C^n` map being `C^(n-1)`.

## References and tests
- Uses `ContMDiffOn.contMDiffOn_totalSpaceMk_mfderiv_apply` (Tau Ceti, TauCeti/Geometry/Manifold/VectorField/Regularity.lean) and `ContMDiffOn.inner_bundle` (Mathlib).
No test declaration beyond its consumers in TauCeti/Geometry/Manifold/Riemannian/FirstVariation.lean.

## Lean subtleties
The smoothness class `m` ranges over `ℕ∞ω`, so `m = ω` (analytic) and `m = 0` (continuous) are covered; with `m = ω` the inequality `m + 1 ≤ n` forces `n = ω`. `ContDiffOn` is the vector-space smoothness of a real-valued function on `U`.

## What it says
For a fixed vector `ξ` in `F`, the Riemannian norm `‖df_z ξ‖` is continuous in `z` on the open set `U`, for `f` of class `C^n` with `1 ≤ n` on `U`.

## References and tests

Used in TauCeti/Geometry/Manifold/Riemannian/Geodesic/Corner.lean and TauCeti/Geometry/Manifold/Riemannian/Jacobi/Comparison.lean.
No test declaration.

## What it says
Let `f` be a map from an open subset `U` of a real normed space `F` to a manifold `M` with a continuous Riemannian structure on its tangent bundle, `C^n` on `U` with `1 ≤ n`. Then `(z, ξ) ↦ ‖df_z ξ‖`, where the norm is the Riemannian norm at `f z`, is continuous on `U × F`.

## References and tests

No other test.

## Lean subtleties
`mfderiv` takes a junk value (zero) where the map is not differentiable. This is harmless here, since `C^n` with `n ≥ 1` on an open set gives differentiability at each point of `U`. The set `U` is open so differentiability within `U` is differentiability. The hypothesis `1 ≤ n` is what makes the derivative exist; the statement is only claimed for `C^n` maps with `n ≥ 1`.

## What it says
A `C^n` Riemannian bundle, for any smoothness class `n` and any model with corners, is a continuous Riemannian bundle: a `C^n` metric tensor is in particular continuous.

## References and tests

No other test.

## What it says
Let $f : \gamma \to \alpha \to \beta$ be a family of maps whose joint map $(c,a)\mapsto f(c)(a)$ is measurable. Then $(\mu, c) \mapsto f(c)_*\mu$ is a measurable map from $\mathrm{FiniteMeasure}(\alpha) \times \gamma$ to the measures on $\beta$; the measure varies together with the parameter. Here finite measures carry the structure inherited as a subtype of measures.

- `hf : Measurable (Function.uncurry f)`: joint measurability of the family.
- The output is the underlying `Measure` (the coercion `(p.1 : Measure α)`), not a `FiniteMeasure`.
- Conclusion: `fun p => (p.1 : Measure α).map (f p.2)` is measurable.

Proof idea: $f(c)_*\mu = (\mathrm{uncurry} f)_*(\delta_c \otimes \mu)$, and $(\mu,c) \mapsto \delta_c \otimes \mu$ is measurable.

## References and tests
- The proof uses Mathlib's `FiniteMeasure.measurable_fun_prod`, `Measure.dirac_prod`, `Measure.map_map` and `Measure.measurable_map`.
- There is no test declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- The coercion from `FiniteMeasure α` to `Measure α` is applied before pushing forward, so the conclusion lands in all measures, which have no finiteness requirement in Lean's type.
- Since each `f c` is measurable, the pushforward is the ordinary one for every `c`.

## What it says
Fix a measure $\nu$ on $\beta$ that is s-finite (a countable sum of finite measures), and let $f : \alpha \to \beta \to \gamma$ be a family of maps such that the joint map $(a,b) \mapsto f(a)(b)$ on $\alpha \times \beta$ is measurable. Then $a \mapsto f(a)_*\nu$ is a measurable map from $\alpha$ to the space of measures on $\gamma$ (Giry structure).

- `[SFinite ν]`: $\nu$ is s-finite, a typeclass hypothesis Lean fills in by itself, true for finite and $\sigma$-finite measures.
- `hf : Measurable (Function.uncurry f)`: joint measurability in $(a,b)$, which is stronger than measurability of each $f(a)$.
- Conclusion: `fun a => ν.map (f a)` is measurable.

The argument is $f(a)_*\nu = (\mathrm{uncurry} f)_*(\nu \text{ pushed along } b \mapsto (a,b))$, composing the measurable pushforward along $\mathrm{uncurry} f$ with the measurable section map $a \mapsto (b \mapsto (a,b))_*\nu$.

## References and tests
- The proof uses Mathlib's `Measure.map_map`, `Measure.measurable_map` and `Measurable.map_prodMk_left` (measurability of $a \mapsto (\text{Prod.mk } a)_*\nu$ for s-finite $\nu$).
- There is no test declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- Measure maps are total in Lean; here every `f a` is measurable (a section of a measurable function), so `ν.map (f a)` is the ordinary pushforward for every `a`.
- `SFinite` is a typeclass argument in square brackets.
- `Type*` universe levels have no mathematical effect.

## What it says
For a measurable map $f : \alpha \to \beta$ between measurable spaces, the pushforward $P \mapsto f_*P$ is a measurable map from the space of probability measures on $\alpha$ to that on $\beta$. Both spaces of probability measures carry the $\sigma$-algebra they inherit as a subtype of all measures with the Giry structure.

- `{α β : Type*}` with `[MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β]`: the two spaces with their $\sigma$-algebras.
- `hf : Measurable f`: the map is measurable.
- Conclusion: `fun P : ProbabilityMeasure α => P.map f` is measurable.

It is the restriction to probability measures of the Giry-monad fact that pushforward along a fixed measurable map is measurable on measures.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Measure.measurable_map` (measurability of `Measure.map f` for measurable `f`), composed with the coercion from `ProbabilityMeasure α` to measures being measurable, is the whole proof.
- There is no test declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- `ProbabilityMeasure α` is a subtype of `Measure α`, and its measurable structure is the subtype one; the proof only uses this.
- `P.map f` is stated for any function `f`; the measurability hypothesis `hf` makes it the genuine pushforward here.

## What it says
The probability-measure version of the previous result: for a family $f : \gamma \to \alpha \to \beta$ with $(c,a)\mapsto f(c)(a)$ jointly measurable, the map $(P, c) \mapsto f(c)_*P$ from $\mathrm{ProbabilityMeasure}(\alpha)\times\gamma$ to $\mathrm{ProbabilityMeasure}(\beta)$ is measurable, with the subtype structures.

- `hf : Measurable (Function.uncurry f)`: joint measurability of the family.
- Conclusion: `fun p => p.1.map (f p.2)` is measurable, with values in `ProbabilityMeasure β`.

It follows from the finite-measure case by viewing a probability measure as a finite measure, then restricting the codomain to probability measures.

## References and tests
- The proof composes `TauCeti.MeasureTheory.measurable_map_finiteMeasure_of_measurable_uncurry` with the coercions between the subtype structures.
- There is no test declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- `ProbabilityMeasure` is a subtype of `Measure`, its measurable structure is the subtype one, and `p.1.map` is the pushforward of probability measures, which stays a probability measure.
- The map `f c` is measurable for each `c`, so no junk value of `Measure.map` occurs.

## What it says
Let $\beta$ be a measurable space, $\alpha$ a measurable space, $\iota$ a countable index set, $f : \beta \to \iota \to [0,\infty]$ and $g : \iota \to \alpha$ a fixed family of atoms. If each weight $b \mapsto f(b,i)$ is measurable, then $b \mapsto \sum_i f(b,i)\,\delta_{g(i)}$ is a measurable map from $\beta$ into the space of measures on $\alpha$, whose $\sigma$-algebra is generated by the evaluation maps $\mu \mapsto \mu(s)$ for measurable $s$ (the Giry structure).

- `{β ι α : Type*}`: the three spaces, as types (universe levels play no mathematical role).
- `[Countable ι]`: the index type is countable, so the sum is a countable mixture; $\alpha$ itself may be uncountable.
- `hf`: every coordinate weight is measurable, valued in extended nonnegative reals.
- Conclusion: the family of measures `Measure.sum fun i => f b i • Measure.dirac (g i)` is measurable in $b$.

On a measurable set $s$ the value is $\sum_i f(b,i)\,1_{s}(g(i))$, a countable sum of measurable functions, hence measurable; this is the standard way measurability into the Giry space is checked.

## References and tests
- No external reference: the proof uses the characterisation of measurability into the space of measures by evaluation on measurable sets (Mathlib's `Measure.measurable_measure`), then Mathlib's `Measure.sum_apply`, `Measure.dirac_apply'` and `Measurable.tsum`, as the file's own proof shows.
- There is no test declaration; consumers elsewhere in the library use it as a lemma.

## Lean subtleties
- Weights are in `ℝ≥0∞`, so a weight may be $\infty$; the measures need not be finite, and sums of weights are not required to be $1$.
- `Measure.sum` of a family indexed by the empty type is the zero measure.
- The atoms are arbitrary points: `g` need not be measurable, since `Measure.dirac` evaluates through measurable sets only (`dirac_apply'`).

## What it says
 If a random variable X has law μ.withDensity f (HasLaw X (μ.withDensity f) P) with f an a.e. measurable density with values in [0,∞], then X has a probability density function with respect to μ, in Mathlib's sense (HasPDF X P μ), i.e. X is a.e. measurable and its law is absolutely continuous with respect to μ.

## References and tests
 The proof is one application of Mathlib's hasPDF_of_map_eq_withDensity to HasLaw.aemeasurable and HasLaw.map_eq. Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
 The density f takes values in ℝ≥0∞ (it may be ∞ on a null set); the a.e. measurability hypothesis is what makes withDensity behave, since withDensity of a non-measurable function is a junk measure. HasLaw gives X a.e. measurable, so no separate hypothesis on X is needed.

## What it says
 If a finite measure ν equals μ.withDensity (ofReal ∘ ρ) for an a.e. measurable, a.e. nonnegative real function ρ, then ρ is μ-integrable.

## References and tests
 The proof applies TauCeti.Probability.integrable_withDensity_ofReal_iff to the constant function 1, which is ν-integrable because ν is finite. Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
 ν is given as an equality to a withDensity measure rather than defined by it, so the lemma applies to any measure presented this way. Nonnegativity is needed since ofReal truncates negative values: with ρ = -1 and ν = 0 the hypotheses hold while ρ is not integrable.

## What it says
 Let ρ be an a.e. measurable real function on (α, μ) that is a.e. nonnegative, and let ν = μ.withDensity (ofReal ∘ ρ), the measure with density ρ. For a function g into a real normed space, g is ν-integrable if and only if x ↦ ρ x • g x is μ-integrable.

## References and tests
 The proof uses Mathlib's integrable_withDensity_iff_integrable_smul₀' and ENNReal.toReal_ofReal. Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
 The density enters as ENNReal.ofReal ρ, which replaces negative values by 0; this agrees with ρ only where ρ ≥ 0, which is why nonnegativity is assumed: with ρ constantly -1 the measure is 0, every g is integrable against it, but ρ • g need not be. Integrable includes a.e. strong measurability, and the hypothesis hρ supplies measurability of the density.

## What it says
 For an a.e. measurable, a.e. nonnegative real density ρ and any g valued in a real normed space, the integral of g against μ.withDensity (ofReal ∘ ρ) equals the integral of ρ • g against μ.

## References and tests
 The proof specialises Mathlib's integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul₀ and uses ENNReal.toReal_ofReal on the set where ρ ≥ 0. Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
 No integrability hypothesis is needed: the Bochner integral of a non-integrable function is the junk value 0, and by TauCeti.Probability.integrable_withDensity_ofReal_iff the two sides are integrable together, so both are then 0. Nonnegativity is needed since ofReal truncates negative values: for μ the Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1], ρ = -1 and g = 1 the left side is 0 and the right side is -1.

## What it says
 Under the same hypotheses as hasPDF_of_hasLaw_withDensity, plus σ-finiteness of the reference measure μ, Mathlib's pdf X P μ (defined as a Radon-Nikodym derivative) equals the presenting density f μ-almost everywhere.

## References and tests
 The proof uses TauCeti.Probability.hasPDF_of_hasLaw_withDensity for the HasPDF instance and Mathlib's pdf.eq_of_map_eq_withDensity'. Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
 Equality is only almost everywhere, as it must be: f can be changed on a μ-null set without changing the law. pdf is a Radon-Nikodym derivative, a junk value unless the law is absolutely continuous; here HasPDF holds by the first theorem, so the junk case does not arise. The statement lives in ℝ≥0∞, so values of ∞ on a null set are allowed.

## What it says
Same setting as above, with $A$ reduced.

- `k : Type u`, `A : Type v`, `K : Type w`: types standing for underlying sets (the universe levels `u v w` do not affect the mathematics).
- `[Field k]`, `[CommRing A]`, `[Algebra k A]`: $k$ is a field and $A$ a commutative ring with $1$ that is a $k$-algebra.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra.

- `[IsReduced A]`: $A$ has no nonzero nilpotent elements.
- Conclusion: the evaluation map sending $x \in A$ to the function $f \mapsto f(x)$ on the set of $k$-algebra maps $A \to K$ is injective.

It is the point-separation principle phrased as injectivity of $A \to K^{\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,K)}$.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha,\beta,\varepsilon:\mathbb{N}\to R$. Then
$$\sum_{p<n}(-1)^p\Big(\prod_{i<p}\alpha_i\Big)\big(\varepsilon_p\beta_p+\alpha_p\varepsilon_{p+1}\big)\prod_{p<i<n}\beta_i=\varepsilon_0\prod_{i<n}\beta_i-(-1)^n\Big(\prod_{i<n}\alpha_i\Big)\varepsilon_n.$$

- `(n : ℕ)`, `(α β ε : ℕ → R)`: the number of terms and three sequences in $R$.
- On the left `Finset.range p` is $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and `Finset.Ico (p+1) n` is $\{p+1,\dots,n-1\}$; `(p : ℤ)` is the cast of $p$ to an integer, the exponent of the sign.

With $u_q=(-1)^q\prod_{i<q}\alpha_i\cdot\varepsilon_q\cdot\prod_{q\le i<n}\beta_i$, the $p$-th summand equals $u_p-u_{p+1}$, so the sum telescopes to $u_0-u_n$, as the docstring says.

## What it says
Let $C$ be a $k$-coalgebra with a chosen element $1 \in C$ and $V$ a right $C$-comodule. If $V$ is completely reducible, and every nonzero subcomodule $N$ of $V$ contains a nonzero vector $v$ with coaction $\rho(v) = v \otimes 1$ (a fixed vector), then the fixed subcomodule of $V$ is all of $V$.

- `[CommSemiring k]`, `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module k C] [Coalgebra k C]`, `[AddCommMonoid V] [Module k V] [Comodule k C V]`: $C$ is a $k$-coalgebra and $V$ a right $C$-comodule.
- `[One C]`: a distinguished element $1 \in C$; no axiom ties it to the comultiplication or counit.
- `(hcr : IsCompletelyReducible k C V)`: every subcomodule of $V$ has a complementary subcomodule.
- `(hfix : ∀ N, N ≠ ⊥ → ∃ v ∈ N, v ≠ 0 ∧ coact v = v ⊗ₜ 1)`: every nonzero subcomodule contains a nonzero fixed vector.
- The conclusion: `fixedSubcomodule k C V = ⊤`, that is, every vector of $V$ is fixed.

The argument: a complement $Q$ of the fixed subcomodule meets it in $0$; if $Q \neq 0$, it would contain a nonzero fixed vector, which lies in both, a contradiction; so $Q = 0$ and the fixed subcomodule is everything. For a group, this is the step showing that a completely reducible representation in which every nonzero subrepresentation has a nonzero invariant vector (for a unipotent group, by Kolchin's theorem) is trivial.

## What it says

Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $C$ a flat $R$-coalgebra and $V$ a right $C$-comodule, and let $S$ be an atom of the lattice of subcomodules of $V$, that is, a nonzero subcomodule with no subcomodule strictly between $0$ and $S$. `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]` and `(L : IntegralLattice V)` are the ambient rational vector space and an integral lattice in it, with its symmetric rational bilinear form $B$ (`L.form`). Equivalently the sign of the determinant is $(-1)^{n_-}$ (and the determinant is $0$ when `L` is degenerate). This is the standard fact that diagonalising $B$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives exactly $n_-$ negative entries, and a change of basis multiplies the determinant by a positive square.

An *arrow weight* is a function `wt` sending each arrow to an element of an additive monoid $M$; the weight of a path is the sum of the weights of its arrows (`Quiver.Path.addWeight wt`), and $0$ for a trivial path. The piece `gradeBy k wt m` is the $k$-span of the paths of weight $m$.

The decomposition homomorphism sends the basis element of a path $x$ to the element of the summand of weight $\mathrm{wt}(x)$ given by $x$ itself.

## What it says

A graph in Serre's sense. The data are a type of vertices `V`, a type of directed edges `E` (darts), a source map `src : E → V`, and a reversal `rev : E → E`. Loops and parallel edges are allowed; a loop still has two distinct darts, the dart and its reverse.

## What it says
The complex analytic Weierstrass preparation theorem, in one distinguished variable $w$ over a finite-dimensional parameter space. Let $f(x, w)$ be holomorphic near $(x_0, w_0)$ and suppose $w \mapsto f(x_0, w)$ vanishes to finite order $d$ at $w_0$. Then near $(x_0, w_0)$, $f(x, w) = P_x(w - w_0)\, u(x, w)$ with $P_x$ a monic polynomial of degree $d$ in $w - w_0$ whose coefficients are holomorphic in $x$ and vanish at $x_0$ (a Weierstrass polynomial), and $u$ holomorphic and nonzero at $(x_0, w_0)$.

- `{E : Type*}`, `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℂ E] [FiniteDimensional ℂ E]`: the parameter space, a finite-dimensional complex normed space; these are typeclass hypotheses, found by Lean.
- `{f : E × ℂ → ℂ} {x₀ : E} {w₀ : ℂ} {d : ℕ}`: the function, the base point and the order $d$.
- `(hf : AnalyticAt ℂ f (x₀, w₀))`: $f$ is given by a convergent power series near $(x_0, w_0)$, which in finite dimension is holomorphy in all variables jointly.
- `(hd : analyticOrderAt (fun w ↦ f (x₀, w)) w₀ = d)`: the order of vanishing of the slice $w \mapsto f(x_0, w)$ at $w_0$ is the natural number $d$. `analyticOrderAt` takes values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, so this hypothesis also says the slice is not identically zero near $w_0$.
- The conclusion: coefficient functions $c_0, \dots, c_{d-1} : E \to \mathbb{C}$ (`c : Fin d → E → ℂ`) analytic at $x_0$ and vanishing there, and $u$ analytic and nonzero at $(x_0, w_0)$, with $f(x, w) = P_x(w - w_0) \cdot u(x, w)$ for all $(x, w)$ in a neighbourhood of $(x_0, w_0)$ (`=ᶠ[𝓝 (x₀, w₀)]`). Here `TauCeti.Polynomial.monicOfCoeff (fun i ↦ c i x)` is the monic polynomial $T^d + \sum_{i < d} c_i(x) T^i$, evaluated at $T = w - w_0$.

This is the preparation theorem as Hörmander states it, with the parameter in a finite-dimensional space rather than $\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$ and the distinguished variable last.

## What it says
Doob's maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale in continuous time, with right-continuous paths: for a time $T$ and $\varepsilon \ge 0$,
$$\varepsilon\, P\bigl(\exists\, t \le T,\ \varepsilon < f_t\bigr) \le E[f_T].$$

- `{Ω ι : Type*}`, `{m0 : MeasurableSpace Ω}`, `{μ : Measure Ω}`: the sample space with its $\sigma$-algebra and measure, and the time set $\iota$.
- `[LinearOrder ι] [TopologicalSpace ι] [OrderTopology ι] [DenselyOrdered ι] [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace ι]`: the times are linearly ordered, carry the order topology, are dense (between two times there is a third) and separable, as $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is. These are typeclass hypotheses.
- `[IsFiniteMeasure μ]`: $\mu$ is a finite measure (a probability measure in applications).
- `(hf : Submartingale f ℱ μ)`: $f : \iota \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a submartingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$, in Mathlib's sense (adapted, integrable, $f_s \le E[f_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s]$ a.e. for $s \le t$).
- `(hnonneg : 0 ≤ f)`: $f_t(\omega) \ge 0$ for every $t$ and $\omega$.
- `{T : ι}`: the horizon.
- `(hcont : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∀ t < T, ContinuousWithinAt (fun u ↦ f u ω) (Ioi t) t)`: almost every path $t \mapsto f_t(\omega)$ is right-continuous at every time $t < T$.
- `(ε : ℝ≥0)`: the level, a nonnegative real.
- The conclusion: $\varepsilon$ times the measure of the set of $\omega$ for which some $t \le T$ has $f_t(\omega) > \varepsilon$ is at most $E[f_T]$, the right side read in $[0, \infty]$ through `ENNReal.ofReal`.

This is the continuous-time maximal inequality of Karatzas–Shreve and Revuz–Yor for right-continuous nonnegative submartingales, stated with a strict inequality $f_t > \varepsilon$ in the event; the nonstrict version follows by letting the level increase to $\varepsilon$.

## Lean subtleties
- The event $\{\omega \mid \exists t \le T, \varepsilon < f_t(\omega)\}$ is not assumed measurable: `μ` is applied to it as an outer measure, which is what makes the statement meaningful without a measurability proof of the running supremum.
- Multiplication `ε * μ {…}` is in `ℝ≥0∞`, with `0 * ∞ = 0`; for $\varepsilon = 0$ the inequality is trivial.
- `ENNReal.ofReal` sends a negative real to $0$; it does not matter here since $f_T \ge 0$.
- Right-continuity is only required almost surely and only at times before $T$; the path at $T$ itself is not constrained.
- `0 ≤ f` is pointwise for every $\omega$, not merely almost everywhere.

## What it says
The preprojective algebra of a finite simply-laced Dynkin diagram, for any orientation, is left self-injective over every field: the algebra is injective as a left module over itself.

- `(k : Type*) [Field k]`: the ground field, any field; carried as a typeclass.
- `{V : Type*} [Finite V]`: a finite vertex type.
- `{G : SimpleGraph V}`: a simple graph on $V$.
- `{t : DynkinType}`, `(e : G ≃g diagramGraph t.cartanMatrix)`: a Dynkin type $t$ and a graph isomorphism from $G$ onto the underlying simple graph of its Dynkin diagram. For the types $A_n$, $D_n$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$ this is the diagram itself; for $B_n$, $C_n$, $F_4$, $G_2$ the underlying simple graph forgets the multiple bonds and is a path, so these cases are again of type $A$.
- `(o : Orientation G)`: an orientation of the edges of $G$, making it a quiver `OrientedQuiver G o`.
- The conclusion, `Module.Injective (preprojectiveAlgebra k (OrientedQuiver G o)) (preprojectiveAlgebra k (OrientedQuiver G o))`: the preprojective algebra $\Pi$ of that quiver over $k$ is an injective $\Pi$-module, for the left action on itself.

This is the Frobenius, or self-injective, property of the preprojective algebras of Dynkin quivers. It is deduced here from the general theorem that a finite-dimensional preprojective algebra is self-injective and the finite-dimensionality of the Dynkin ones; the right-module version is `TauCeti.moduleInjective_op_preprojectiveAlgebra_of_iso`.

## What it says
The Iwasawa decomposition of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$ for $\Bbbk = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$: multiplication $(k, a, u) \mapsto kau$ is a homeomorphism from $K \times A \times N$ onto $\mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$, where $K$ is the unitary group $\mathrm{U}(n)$ (the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(n)$ when $\Bbbk = \mathbb{R}$), $A$ the group of diagonal matrices with positive real diagonal entries and $N$ the group of upper unitriangular matrices. So every invertible $n \times n$ matrix over $\Bbbk$ is $kau$ for exactly one such triple, and the three factors depend continuously on the matrix.

- `(𝕜 : Type u_1)`, `[RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field, carried as a typeclass; `RCLike` is Mathlib's class of fields that are $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ (a complete normed field with a conjugation and real part behaving as in those two).
- `(n : ℕ)`: the size $n$ of the matrices, a natural number.
- The type: a homeomorphism (`≃ₜ`) from the product of three subgroups, with the product topology, to `GL (Fin n) 𝕜`. The first, `unitarySubgroup (GL (Fin n) 𝕜)`, is the group of $g$ with $g^* g = g g^* = 1$, where $g^*$ is the conjugate transpose: $\mathrm{U}(n)$, which is $\mathrm{O}(n)$ over $\mathbb{R}$. The second, `posDiagonalSubgroup (Fin n) ℝ`, is $A$: the invertible real diagonal matrices with positive diagonal entries, which act on $\Bbbk^n$ through `Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.map (algebraMap ℝ 𝕜)`, the entrywise inclusion of $\mathbb{R}$ in $\Bbbk$ (the identity when $\Bbbk = \mathbb{R}$). The third, `upperUnitriangularGroup (Fin n) 𝕜`, is $N$: the upper triangular matrices over $\Bbbk$ with $1$ on the diagonal.

Its value: the map is $(k, a, u) \mapsto k a u$; its inverse sends $g$ to `iwasawaUnitary g`, `iwasawaDiagonal g` and `iwasawaUnitriangular g`, computed from the Cholesky factorisation of $g^* g$, and the proofs show that the two maps are inverse to each other and continuous.

This is the standard Iwasawa decomposition $G = KAN$ for $G = \mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$ with $K = \mathrm{U}(n)$, in the usual order $k \cdot a \cdot u$; equivalently, the $QR$ factorisation $g = QR$ of Gram–Schmidt, with $R = au$ normalised to have a positive diagonal. Knapp states the decomposition as a diffeomorphism; only the homeomorphism is stated here.

## Lean subtleties
- `GL (Fin n) 𝕜` is the group of invertible $n \times n$ matrices over $\Bbbk$, with rows and columns indexed by `Fin n` $= \{0, \dots, n-1\}$; "upper" in $N$ refers to the usual order of these indices.
- The star operation on matrices is the conjugate transpose, which over $\mathbb{R}$ is the transpose, so `unitarySubgroup` is $\mathrm{U}(n)$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and all of $\mathrm{O}(n)$, not $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, over $\mathbb{R}$.
- The factor $A$ is a group of real matrices for every $\Bbbk$: positivity of its diagonal entries is a condition on real numbers, and `GeneralLinearGroup.map (algebraMap ℝ 𝕜)` embeds it in $\mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$.
- `↥H` is the subgroup $H$ seen as a type, the type of its elements, with the topology induced from $\mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$.
- Lean topologises $\mathrm{GL}_n(\Bbbk)$ as a group of units: the coarsest topology making $g \mapsto g$ and $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ continuous into matrices. As matrix inversion is continuous, this is the usual topology of an open subset of $\Bbbk^{n \times n}$.
- `≃ₜ` is a homeomorphism: a bijection, continuous in both directions, recorded together with its inverse.
- For $n = 0$ all four groups are trivial, and the statement is about one-point spaces.

## What it says
A compact normal operator on a complex Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

- `{E : Type u_1}`: a type $E$, the underlying set of the space; `u_1` is a universe level with no mathematical content.
- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℂ E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a complex inner product space, complete for the norm $\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle}$, so a Hilbert space.
- `{T : E →L[ℂ] E}`: a bounded linear operator on $E$.
- `(hT : IsStarNormal T)`: $T$ is normal, $T^*T = TT^*$, where `star` is the Hilbert adjoint.
- `(hc : IsCompactOperator T)`: $T$ is compact: the image of the unit ball is relatively compact.
- The conclusion: there are a set $s \subseteq E$, a Hilbert basis `b : HilbertBasis s ℂ E` indexed by $s$ (an orthonormal family with dense span, packaged as an isometric isomorphism $E \cong \ell^2(s)$) and a function `nu : s → ℂ` such that the basis vector at index $x$ is $x$ itself (`⇑b = Subtype.val`) and each $x \in s$ is an eigenvector of $T$ for the eigenvalue `nu x`: `HasEigenvector T μ x` means $Tx = \mu x$ and $x \neq 0$.

This is the spectral theorem for compact normal operators in its eigenbasis form, as in Conway, Section II.7: complex scalars, no separability, the basis indexed by its own vectors. The eigenvalue $0$ is allowed, so $\ker T$ is spanned by basis vectors too.

- The scalars are fixed to $\mathbb{C}$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ the statement is false: a rotation of the plane is compact and normal without eigenvectors.
- `HilbertBasis` requires orthonormality, so every $x \in s$ has norm $1$; `nu` need not be injective, since an eigenvalue of multiplicity $m$ is listed once per basis vector.
- When $E = \{0\}$, $s = \varnothing$ and the statement holds with the empty basis.
- `(T : Module.End ℂ E)` coerces the bounded operator to a plain linear map, the form `HasEigenvector` takes.

## What it says
For a compact normal operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space $E$, the space is the direct sum of $\ker T$ and the closed span of the eigenspaces of $T$ at nonzero eigenvalues.

- `{E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℂ E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a complex Hilbert space.
- `{T : E →L[ℂ] E}`: a bounded linear operator on $E$.
- `(hT : IsStarNormal T)`: $T$ is normal, $T^*T = TT^*$.
- `(hc : IsCompactOperator T)`: $T$ is compact: the image of the unit ball is relatively compact.
- The conclusion, `IsCompl P Q` for the submodules $P$ = `LinearMap.ker (T : E →ₗ[ℂ] E)`, the kernel of $T$, and $Q$ = `(⨆ (μ) (_ : μ ≠ 0), eigenspace T μ).topologicalClosure`: $P \cap Q = \{0\}$ and $P + Q = E$. Here `eigenspace T μ` is $\{x : Tx = \mu x\}$, `⨆` over the $\mu \neq 0$ is the smallest submodule containing them all, the sum $\sum_{\mu \ne 0} E_\mu$, and `topologicalClosure` is its closure in $E$.

This is the decomposition $H = \ker T \oplus \overline{\bigoplus_{\lambda \neq 0} \ker(T - \lambda)}$ of the spectral theorem for compact normal operators (Conway, Section II.7). The companion `IsStarNormal.topologicalClosure_iSup_eigenspaces_ne_zero` identifies the second summand with $(\ker T)^\perp$, so the sum is in fact orthogonal; `IsCompl` records only that it is direct.

## What it says
The Fefferman–Stein inequality: on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \geq 1$, for $1 < p < \infty$ and integrable $f$, $\|f\|_{L^p} \leq C(n, p)\, \|f^\#\|_{L^p}$ with an explicit constant.

- `{ι : Type u_1} [Fintype ι]`: a finite index type; the space is $\mathbb{R}^n$ = `ι → ℝ`, with $n$ = `Fintype.card ι`.
- `{F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [CompleteSpace F]`: $f$ takes values in a real Banach space $F$.
- `[Nonempty ι]`: $n \geq 1$.
- `{f : (ι → ℝ) → F} (hf : Integrable f volume)`: $f$ is a.e. strongly measurable with $\int \|f\| < \infty$ for Lebesgue measure `volume` on `ι → ℝ`.
- `{p : ℝ≥0∞} (hp : 1 < p) (hp_top : p ≠ ⊤)`: an exponent $1 < p < \infty$ in the extended nonnegative reals; `p.toReal` is $p$ as a real number.
- The conclusion: `eLpNorm f p volume` is $\|f\|_{L^p} = (\int \|f\|^p)^{1/p}$, in $[0, \infty]$; `sharpMaximalFunction volume f` is $f^\#(x) = \sup_{B \ni x} \frac{1}{|B|}\int_B \|f - f_B\|$, the supremum over all open balls $B$ containing $x$ (not only those centred at $x$) of the mean oscillation of $f$ about its average $f_B$; the constant is $\bigl(2^{p+1}\, 2^{(p + 2n + 2)p}\bigr)^{1/p}$.

This is the inequality of Fefferman and Stein in the form $\|f\|_p \leq C\|f^\#\|_p$ (Stein, Chapter IV, §2; Grafakos, Section 3.4). Two differences from the usual statement: the a priori hypothesis is $f \in L^1$ rather than $f \in L^{p_0}$ for some $p_0 \leq p$, a special case; and $f$ may be Banach-space valued. Balls are those of the sup distance on `ι → ℝ`, that is, cubes, and the constant is for that choice.

## What it says
The Schmidt (singular value) decomposition: a compact operator $T$ from a Hilbert space $E$ to an inner product space $F$ is $T = \sum_i \sigma_i \langle e_i, \cdot\rangle f_i$ in operator norm, with $(e_i)$, $(f_i)$ countable orthonormal families and $\sigma_i > 0$, $\sigma_i \to 0$; the $\sigma_i$ in decreasing order are the approximation numbers of $T$.

- `{𝕜 : Type u_1} [RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `{F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 F]`: $F$ is an inner product space, not assumed complete.
- `{E : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a Hilbert space.
- `{T : E →L[𝕜] F} (hTc : IsCompactOperator T)`: $T$ is bounded linear and compact (the image of the unit ball is relatively compact).
- The conclusion: there are an index type $\iota$ and families `e : ι → E`, `f : ι → F`, `σ : ι → ℝ` with `Countable ι`; `Orthonormal 𝕜 e` and `Orthonormal 𝕜 f` ($\|e_i\| = 1$ and $\langle e_i, e_j\rangle = 0$ for $i \neq j$, likewise for $f$); $\sigma_i > 0$; `Tendsto σ cofinite (𝓝 0)`, that is, for each $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many $\sigma_i \geq \varepsilon$; `HasSum (fun i ↦ (σ i : 𝕜) • rankOne 𝕜 (f i) (e i)) T`, the convergence to $T$ in operator norm of the finite partial sums of the rank-one operators $x \mapsto \sigma_i \langle e_i, x\rangle f_i$ (`rankOne 𝕜 y x` is $z \mapsto \langle x, z\rangle y$); and for every $n$, `T.singularValue n`, the $n$-th approximation number $a_n(T) = \inf\{\|T - R\| : \operatorname{rank} R \leq n\}$ (zero-based, $a_0(T) = \|T\|$), equals `TauCeti.decreasingRearrangement σ n`, the $n$-th entry of the $\sigma_i$ listed in nonincreasing order with multiplicity and padded by zeros.

This is the Schmidt expansion of a compact operator (Gohberg–Krein, Chapter II, §2) together with the identification of its singular numbers with the approximation numbers (Pietsch, §2.11). Differences: the target need not be complete, the index set is not enumerated (the order is recorded through the decreasing rearrangement), and $a_n$ is numbered from $0$, so $a_n(T)$ is $s_{n+1}(T)$ in the one-based convention.

## What it says
The method of continuity: along a family of bounded operators $L_t : E \to F$ from a Banach space, continuous in $t$ on a preconnected parameter set $S$ and satisfying a uniform a priori estimate $\|x\| \leq C\|L_t x\|$, either every $L_t$ is onto or none is.

- `{𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]`: a field with a nontrivial absolute value, such as $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `{E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a Banach space over $\mathbb{k}$.
- `{F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]`: $F$ is a normed space, not assumed complete.
- `{X : Type u_4} [TopologicalSpace X] {S : Set X}`: a topological parameter space and a subset $S$ of it.
- `{L : X → E →L[𝕜] F}`: the family $t \mapsto L_t$. `{C : ℝ}`: a constant. `{s t : X}`: two parameters.
- `(hS : IsPreconnected S)`: $S$ cannot be split by two disjoint open sets.
- `(hL : ContinuousOn L S)`: $t \mapsto L_t$ is continuous on $S$ for the operator norm.
- `(hC : ∀ t ∈ S, ∀ x, ‖x‖ ≤ C * ‖L t x‖)`: the a priori estimate, with one constant for all $t \in S$.
- `(hs : s ∈ S) (ht : t ∈ S)`.
- The conclusion: $L_s$ is surjective if and only if $L_t$ is.

This is Theorem 5.2 of Gilbarg–Trudinger, stated there for the segment $L_t = (1 - t)L_0 + tL_1$, $t \in [0, 1]$, here for any preconnected family continuous in operator norm; the segment form is `ContinuousLinearMap.surjective_iff_of_forall_norm_le_lineMap`. As in the source, the target is only normed.

## What it says
The method of continuity in its textbook form: for bounded operators $L_0, L_1 : E \to F$ from a Banach space, if the segment $L_t = (1 - t)L_0 + tL_1$, $t \in [0, 1]$, satisfies a uniform a priori estimate $\|x\| \leq C\|L_t x\|$, then $L_0$ is onto if and only if $L_1$ is.

- `{𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]`: a field with a nontrivial absolute value, such as $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `{E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]`: $E$ is a Banach space over $\mathbb{k}$.
- `{F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]`: $F$ is a normed space, not assumed complete.
- `{C : ℝ}`: a constant.
- `[NormedSpace ℝ F] [SMulCommClass 𝕜 ℝ F]`: a real scalar action on $F$ commuting with the $\mathbb{k}$-action, so that the real parameter $t$ can multiply operators $E \to F$; for $\mathbb{k} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with the real structure obtained by restricting scalars, these hold.
- `{L₀ L₁ : E →L[𝕜] F}`: two bounded linear operators.
- `(hC : ∀ t ∈ Icc 0 1, ∀ x, ‖x‖ ≤ C * ‖AffineMap.lineMap L₀ L₁ t x‖)`: for every $t$ in the closed interval $[0, 1]$ and every $x$, $\|x\| \leq C\|L_t x\|$, where `AffineMap.lineMap L₀ L₁ t` is $L_0 + t(L_1 - L_0) = (1 - t)L_0 + tL_1$.
- The conclusion: $L_0$ is surjective if and only if $L_1$ is.

This is Theorem 5.2 of Gilbarg–Trudinger as stated there: a Banach space $E$, a normed space $F$, the segment between $L_0$ and $L_1$, one constant for the whole segment. It is the case $S = [0, 1]$ of `IsPreconnected.surjective_iff_of_forall_norm_le`.

## What it says
The Johnson–Sinclair theorem, nonunital form: every derivation of a semisimple complex Banach algebra, with or without a unit, is continuous.

- `{B : Type u_1} [NonUnitalNormedRing B]`: a ring $B$, not assumed to have a unit, with a norm satisfying $\|xy\| \leq \|x\|\,\|y\|$.
- `[NormedSpace ℂ B]`: $B$ is a complex normed vector space, $\|cx\| = |c|\,\|x\|$.
- `[IsScalarTower ℂ B B] [SMulCommClass ℂ B B]`: $(cx)y = c(xy)$ and $x(cy) = c(xy)$; with the previous lines, $B$ is a complex normed algebra without unit.
- `[CompleteSpace B]`: $B$ is complete, so a Banach algebra.
- `(D : B →ₗ[ℂ] B)`: a $\mathbb{C}$-linear map, with no continuity assumed.
- `(hD : ∀ x y, D (x * y) = x * D y + D x * y)`: the Leibniz rule, so $D$ is a derivation.
- `(hB : TauCeti.nonUnitalJacobson ℂ B = ⊥)`: the Jacobson radical of $B$ is $\{0\}$, that is, $B$ is semisimple. `TauCeti.nonUnitalJacobson ℂ B` is the two-sided ideal of the $b \in B$ whose image in the unitization $\mathbb{C} \oplus B$ (`Unitization ℂ B`) lies in the Jacobson radical of that unital ring; `⊥` is the zero ideal.
- The conclusion, `Continuous ⇑D`: $D$ is continuous, hence bounded.

This is the theorem of Johnson and Sinclair that a derivation of a semisimple Banach algebra is automatically continuous, for complex algebras as in the source, with no unit required: the unital case is `LinearMap.continuous_of_derivation_of_jacobson_eq_bot`, and this form answers the roadmap's request for nonunital versions via unitization.

## What it says

- `{u v : Lp ℂ 2 volume}`: two complex-valued square-integrable functions, as classes modulo null sets.

- `{f : E → ℝ} {K : ℝ≥0}`: a real function and a nonnegative real constant.
- `(hf : ContDiff ℝ 1 f)`: $f$ is continuously differentiable.
- `(hK : ∀ x, ‖fderiv ℝ f x‖ ≤ K)`: the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$, a linear functional on $E$, has operator norm at most $K$ at every point: $\|\nabla f(x)\| \leq K$.
- `{ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 ≤ ε)`: a nonnegative threshold.
- The conclusion: `stdGaussian E` is the standard Gaussian measure on $E$ (the image of a product of $N(0, 1)$ laws under an orthonormal basis, independent of the basis); `.real` is its value as a real number; the set is $\{x : \varepsilon \leq |f(x) - \int f\, d\gamma|\}$; the bound is $2\exp(-2\varepsilon^2/(\pi^2K^2))$.

This is the Gaussian concentration inequality of the Maurey–Pisier interpolation argument (Pisier, Theorem 2.2), with its constant $2/\pi^2$ rather than the sharp $1/2$ of the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality. ## What it says
The regular-crossing formula in finite dimensions: along a continuous path of symmetric bilinear forms on $[a, b]$ with nondegenerate endpoints and only regular crossings, the drop of the negative index from $a$ to $b$ is the sum, over the crossings, of the signatures of the crossing forms.

- `{E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
- `{V V' : ℝ → E →L[ℝ] E →L[ℝ] ℝ}`: a path $V$ of continuous bilinear forms on $E$ (in curried form, $E \to E^*$) and a path $V'$ of candidate derivatives.
- `{a b : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b)`: the interval.
- `(hc : ContinuousOn V (Icc a b))`: $V$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ in operator norm.
- `(hsymm : ∀ t ∈ Icc a b, (V t).toBilinForm.IsSymm)`: each $V_t$, as a bilinear form (`toBilinForm`), is symmetric.
- `(ha) (hb)`: $V_a$ and $V_b$ are nondegenerate (`Nondegenerate`: no nonzero vector pairs to $0$ with every vector).
- `(hV : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, ¬(V t).toBilinForm.Nondegenerate → HasDerivAt V (V' t) t)`: at every crossing $t \in (a, b)$, a parameter where $V_t$ is degenerate, $V$ is differentiable at $t$ with derivative $V'_t$.
- `(hreg : …)`: at every crossing the crossing form `crossingForm (V t) (V' t)`, the quadratic form $v \mapsto V'_t(v, v)$ restricted to $\ker V_t$, is nondegenerate: the crossing is regular.
- The conclusion, in $\mathbb{Z}$: $\operatorname{sigNeg}(V_a) - \operatorname{sigNeg}(V_b) = \sum_{t \in (a, b)} \bigl(\operatorname{sigPos}\Gamma_t - \operatorname{sigNeg}\Gamma_t\bigr)$, where `sigNeg Q` is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $Q$ is negative definite, `sigPos Q` likewise with positive definite, `toQuadraticMap` is $v \mapsto V_t(v, v)$, and `∑ᶠ` is the finite sum over the $t$ with a nonzero term.

This is the formula of Robbin and Salamon for the spectral flow of a path with regular crossings as the sum of the signatures of its crossing forms (1995, Section 4; crossing forms as in 1993, Section 2), a positive definite crossing form counting positively. In finite dimensions the spectral flow, the net number of eigenvalues crossing from negative to positive, is the drop in the negative index, which is the left side. The source treats paths of self-adjoint Fredholm operators on a Hilbert space; this is the finite-dimensional case.

## What it says
`amiceEquiv p h S` is Amice's map $(c_n)_n \mapsto \sum_n e_{h,n}\,c_n$, with $e_{h,n}(x) = \lfloor n/p^h\rfloor!\binom{x}{n}$, packaged as a norm-preserving linear bijection from the null sequences in $E$ onto the analytic stage $\mathrm{LA}_h(E)$.

- `(p h : ℕ)`, `[Fact (Nat.Prime p)]`: a natural number $p$, its primality a typeclass hypothesis, and the level $h \ge 0$.
- `{E : Type u_1}` with `[NormedAddCommGroup E]`, `[Module ℤ_[p] E]`, `[IsBoundedSMul ℤ_[p] E]`, `[IsUltrametricDist E]`, `[CompleteSpace E]`: a complete normed abelian group $E$ with the strong triangle inequality $\|x+y\| \le \max(\|x\|,\|y\|)$ and an action of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $\|a x\| \le \|a\|\,\|x\|$, so a contractive one. No torsion-freeness is asked.
- `(S : Type u_2)` with `[Semiring S]`, `[Module S E]`, `[ContinuousConstSMul S E]`, `[SMulCommClass ℤ_[p] S E]`: a semiring of scalars acting continuously on $E$ and commuting with $\mathbb{Z}_p$; the equivalence is $S$-linear. $S = \mathbb{Z}_p$ gives the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear statement.
- The type `C₀(ℕ, E) ≃ₗᵢ[S] AnalyticStage p h E`: an $S$-linear isometric bijection between `C₀(ℕ, E)`, the sequences $(c_n)$ in $E$ with $c_n \to 0$ under $\sup_n \|c_n\|$, and `AnalyticStage p h E`, which is `C₀(ZMod (p ^ h) × ℕ, E)`: families $c(a,k)$, indexed by the residues $a$ modulo $p^h$ and $k \ge 0$, tending to $0$, under the supremum norm. This is the coefficient model of $\mathrm{LA}_h(E)$: $c(a,\cdot)$ are the coefficients of a power series in $w = (x-a)/p^h$ on the disc $a + p^h\mathbb{Z}_p$.
- Its value: the underlying map is `amiceMap p h S` (`amiceEquiv_apply`), $(c_n) \mapsto \sum_n$ `amiceTerm p h n (c n)`, where `amiceTerm p h n e` has at $(a,k)$ the $k$-th coefficient of `TauCeti.amicePolynomial p h n a`, the polynomial with value $\lfloor n/p^h\rfloor!\binom{a+p^h w}{n}$ at $w$, times $e$: the disc expansions of $e_{h,n}$.

This is Amice's theorem as in Colmez §I.4: the $e_{h,n}$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{LA}_h$, so the series $\sum_n e_{h,n}c_n$ with $c_n \to 0$ exhaust $\mathrm{LA}_h$ and have norm $\sup_n\|c_n\|$. Here $E$ is more general than $\mathbb{Q}_p$ or a Banach space, the stage is its coefficient model, and the centres are the representatives $0 \le a < p^h$ rather than Colmez's $-a$.

`periodPolynomialEquiv hk` is the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism at level one, $M_k(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})) \oplus S_k(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})) \cong W_w$ for $k = w + 2$.

- `ModularForm 𝒮ℒ k × CuspForm 𝒮ℒ k`: pairs $(f, g)$ of a modular form and a cusp form of weight $k$ for `𝒮ℒ`, the image of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, the full modular group.
- `↥(periodPolynomials ℂ w)`: the period-polynomial space $W_w = \ker(1+S) \cap \ker(1+U+U^2)$ inside the binary forms of degree $w$ with complex coefficients, for the right action $(P|M)(X,Y) = P(aX+bY, cX+dY)$, $S = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $U = TS = \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; `↥` makes the subspace a type.
- `≃ₗ[ℂ]`: a $\mathbb{C}$-linear bijection.
- Its value: $(f, g) \mapsto$ `extendedEvenPeriodPolynomialEquiv hk f` $+$ `oddPeriodPolynomialEquiv hk g` (`coe_periodPolynomialEquiv_apply`). The odd part is $r_g^- = \tfrac12\,(r_g(X,Y) - r_g(-X,Y))$, with $r_g(X,Y) = \int_0^{i\infty} g(\tau)(X - \tau Y)^w\,d\tau$, a bijection $S_k \to W_w^-$. The even part restricts to $r_f^+$ on cusp forms and, for positive even $w$, sends the normalised Eisenstein series `ModularForm.E` to $X^w - Y^w$; for $w = 0$ or $w$ odd both sides are $0$ and it is the zero map.

This is the theorem of Eichler, Shimura and Manin as stated in Kohnen–Zagier §1.1: $r^-$ is an isomorphism $S_k \to W_w^-$, $r^+$ is injective with $W_w^+ = r^+(S_k) \oplus \mathbb{C}(X^w - Y^w)$. The extension to $M_k$ is normalised here by $E \mapsto X^w - Y^w$; the literature's extension differs by a scalar on the Eisenstein line.

## What it says
For an elliptic curve over a nonarchimedean local field and $m$ invertible in $K$, the local Tate pairing on $H^1(K, E[m])$ is perfect: pairing with a class is a bijection from $H^1(K, E[m])$ onto its additive characters with values in $\mathbb{Z}/m$.

- `{K : Type} [Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: a nonarchimedean local field $K$, its valuation, topology and local-field property given as typeclasses.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K) [W.IsElliptic]`: an elliptic curve $E$ given by a Weierstrass equation with nonzero discriminant.
- `(m : ℕ) (hm : IsUnit (m : K))`: $m$ invertible in $K$.
- The conclusion `Function.Bijective ⇑(W.localTateWeilPairing m hm)`: the map $H^1(K, E[m]) \to \mathrm{Hom}(H^1(K, E[m]), \mathbb{Z}/m)$, $a \mapsto \langle a, \cdot\rangle$, is injective and surjective, where $\langle a, b\rangle$ is the invariant in $\mathbb{Z}/m$ of the cup product of $a$ and $b$ along the Weil pairing $e_m$. `⇑` reads the additive map as a function.

Since $H^1(K, E[m])$ is killed by $m$, its homomorphisms to $\mathbb{Z}/m$ are all its characters, so this is the statement that the pairing is nondegenerate on both sides between finite groups: local Tate duality, Milne, *Arithmetic Duality Theorems*, I, Theorem 2.1, for $M = E[m]$ in degree $1$, with $M^D = \mathrm{Hom}(E[m], \mu_m)$ identified with $E[m]$ by the Weil pairing. No rationality of the torsion or of $\mu_m$ is assumed; in mixed characteristic $m$ may be divisible by the residue characteristic.

`IsDerivedComplete I M` says that the $R$-module $M$ is derived $I$-complete: for every $f \in I$, the telescope map $(x_n)_n \mapsto (x_n - f x_{n+1})_n$ on sequences in $M$ is bijective.

## What it says
An oriented real vector bundle with a nowhere-vanishing continuous section has Euler class $0$.

- `{B : Type w} [TopologicalSpace B]`: the base space.
- `{F : Type w} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]`: the model fibre, a real normed space.
- `{E : B → Type w}` with `[TopologicalSpace (TotalSpace F E)]`, `[∀ b, AddCommMonoid (E b)]`, `[∀ b, Module ℝ (E b)]`, `[∀ b, TopologicalSpace (E b)]`, `[FiberBundle F E]`, `[VectorBundle ℝ F E]`: a topological real vector bundle with fibres $E_b$ and model fibre $F$.
- `{n : ℕ}`, `(o : VectorBundleOrientation F E (Fin (n + 1)))`: an orientation of the bundle, one of each fibre varying continuously.
- `(hF : finrank ℝ F = n + 1)`: the rank is $n + 1$.
- `{s : ∀ b, E b}`: a section, a function assigning to each $b$ a vector of $E_b$.
- `(hs : Continuous fun b ↦ TotalSpace.mk' F b (s b))`: $b \mapsto (b, s(b))$ is continuous into the total space, so $s$ is a continuous section.
- `(hs₀ : ∀ b, s b ≠ 0)`: the section vanishes nowhere.
- The conclusion: `o.eulerClass hF = 0` in $H^{n+1}(B; \mathbb{Z})$, where `o.eulerClass hF` is the pull-back along the zero section of the Thom class of $(E, o)$ restricted to $E$.

This is Property 9.7 of Milnor and Stasheff, over an arbitrary base: the zero section is homotopic through $t \cdot s$ to $s$, which lands in $E_0$, where every relative class restricts to $0$.
