name: Joyal's special outer horn theorem
text: an edge of a quasicategory is an equivalence exactly when every outer horn Λⁿ₀ with n ≥ 2 whose initial edge it is extends to an n-simplex (Lurie, *Higher Topos Theory*, Prop. 1.2.4.3).

name: Kőnig's theorem, capacitated form
text: in a bipartite multigraph with vertex capacities b, the maximum size of a b-matching equals the minimum weight Σ_{v∈C} b(v) of a vertex cover; b ≡ 1 is the classical matching–cover equality (Schrijver, *Combinatorial Optimization*, §21.1).

name: The Euler characteristic of a closed odd-dimensional manifold is zero
text: for a compact smooth manifold M without boundary of odd dimension, Σ(−1)ⁱ dim Hᵢ(M; V) = 0 for every finite-dimensional module V over a division ring (Milnor, *Morse Theory*, §5).

name: Derivations of C^∞(M) are smooth vector fields
text: on a finite-dimensional Hausdorff manifold without boundary, every ℝ-linear derivation of C^∞(M, ℝ) is differentiation along a unique smooth vector field, with no continuity assumed, and commutators go to Lie brackets (Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Prop. 8.15).

name: The degree formulas for groups with polynomial invariants
text: if a finite group G acts faithfully on an n-dimensional space over a field of characteristic 0 and Sym^G is polynomial on invariants of degrees d₁, …, dₙ, then ∏dᵢ = |G| and Σdᵢ = n + #pseudoreflections (Humphreys, *Reflection Groups and Coxeter Groups*, Thm 3.9).

name: The Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality on a closed Riemannian manifold
text: on a compact connected Riemannian manifold without boundary and for 1 ≤ p < ∞, ‖u − ⨍u‖_{Lᵖ} ≤ C ‖∇u‖_{Lᵖ} for every C¹ function u, now on manifolds after the domain versions announced earlier (Hebey, *Nonlinear Analysis on Manifolds*, Ch. 3).

name: Analytic adic spaces
text: an adic space every point of which has an open Tate affinoid neighbourhood, equivalently a local pseudouniformiser; every morphism into one is adic, and the locally noetherian analytic spaces of Huber's étale cohomology are defined alongside (Huber, *Étale Cohomology of Rigid Analytic Varieties and Adic Spaces*, §1.1).

name: Pisot numbers
text: a real algebraic integer θ > 1 all of whose other conjugates lie in the open unit disc, with the root criterion for monic integer polynomials and the golden ratio as an example (Smyth, *Seventy years of Salem numbers*, 2015, §1).

name: The spectral theorem for bounded normal operators
text: a bounded normal operator a on a complex Hilbert space is a = ∫ z dP(z) for a unique projection-valued measure P on its spectrum, which gives the Borel functional calculus f ↦ f(a) (Rudin, *Functional Analysis*, Thms 12.23–12.24).

name: Von Neumann's bicommutant theorem
text: a unital *-subalgebra of B(H) equals its double commutant iff it is closed in the weak operator topology, iff it is closed in the strong operator topology (Kadison–Ringrose, *Fundamentals I*, Thm 5.3.1).

name: The Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem
text: now in full: a finite group acting faithfully on a vector space in characteristic zero is generated by pseudoreflections iff its polynomial invariants form a polynomial algebra (Bourbaki, *Lie*, V §5 Thm 4).

name: The Eichler–Selberg trace formula at level one
text: now in full: for even k ≥ 4, tr(Tₙ | S_k(SL₂(ℤ))) = −½ Σ_{t² ≤ 4n} H(4n − t²) P_k(t, n) − ½ Σ_{dd′ = n} min(d, d′)^{k−1}, H the Hurwitz class number (Zagier's appendix to Lang, *Introduction to Modular Forms*).

name: Uniformization of complex elliptic curves
text: now in full: every elliptic curve over ℂ has E(ℂ) ≅ ℂ/Λ as abelian groups, via (℘, ℘′/2), for some lattice Λ, and every (g₂, g₃) with nonzero discriminant comes from a lattice (Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*, VI.5.1).

name: Tate's uniformization theorem
text: over a complete non-archimedean field K with |q| < 1, the Tate curve satisfies E_q(L) ≅ Lˣ/q^ℤ as groups for every complete extension L, Galois-equivariantly (Silverman, *Advanced Topics*, Thm V.3.1).

name: The Dunford–Pettis theorem
text: for a finite measure, a subset of L¹ is relatively weakly compact iff it is norm bounded and uniformly integrable (Dunford–Schwartz, *Linear Operators I*, IV.8.11).

name: Laurent's theorem
text: a function holomorphic on an open annulus, with values in a complex Banach space, is the sum there of a unique two-sided power series, whose coefficients are circle integrals (Conway, *Functions of One Complex Variable I*, V.1.11).

name: Stickelberger's relation
text: in the m-th cyclotomic field, for an ideal A prime to m, the Gauss-sum power Φ(A) generates A^γ, where γ = Σ_{(t,m)=1} t σ_t⁻¹ (Washington, *Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields*, §6.2).

name: Surjectivity of the exponential map of a compact connected Lie group
text: every element of a compact connected Lie group is the exponential of an element of its Lie algebra (Knapp, *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction*, Cor. 4.48).

name: The sharp Sobolev inequality in BV
text: ‖u‖_{n/(n−1)} ≤ (n ωₙ^{1/n})⁻¹ |Du|(ℝⁿ) for every integrable u on ℝⁿ, n ≥ 2, the isoperimetric constant replacing the unspecified constant announced earlier (Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter*, Thm 12.37).

name: Craig interpolation for L_{ω₁ω}
text: if φ entails ψ in L_{ω₁ω}, over any language, some sentence θ in their common function and relation symbols has φ ⊨ θ and θ ⊨ ψ (Keisler, *Model Theory for Infinitary Logic*).

name: The omitting types theorem for countable fragments of L_{ω₁ω}
text: a satisfiable theory in a countable formation-closed fragment has a countable model omitting any countable family of non-isolated types (Marker, *Lectures on Infinitary Model Theory*, Ch. 4).

name: Steiner symmetrization does not increase perimeter
text: for every null-measurable set of finite volume in ℝⁿ and every direction, the Steiner symmetral has De Giorgi perimeter at most that of the set (Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter*, Thm 14.4).

name: The Fredholm alternative for the Dirichlet problem
text: now with the compatibility condition: under Gårding's inequality, B(u, ·) = ℓ is solvable in H¹₀(Ω) iff ℓ ∈ H⁻¹ vanishes on the adjoint kernel, whose dimension equals the kernel's (Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, §6.2.3 Thm 4).

name: The Efron–Stein inequality
text: for a square-integrable function of finitely many independent variables, Var f ≤ Σᵢ E[Varᵢ f], the sum of the expected variances in each coordinate (Boucheron–Lugosi–Massart, *Concentration Inequalities*, Thm 3.1).

name: The cup-length lower bound for the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category
text: the cup length of H*(X; R) is at most the normalized Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of X, so a smooth function on a compact manifold has at least cup length + 1 critical points (Cornea–Lupton–Oprea–Tanré, *Lusternik–Schnirelmann Category*, Prop. 1.5).

name: The Gauss–Brent–Salamin formula
text: π = 4 M(1, 1/√2)² / (1 − Σ_{j ≥ 1} 2^{j+1} (aⱼ² − gⱼ²)), with M the arithmetic–geometric mean and (aⱼ, gⱼ) its iterates (Borwein–Borwein, *Pi and the AGM*, §2.4).

name: The presentation of the simplex category
text: Mathlib's category generated by faces and degeneracies modulo the simplicial identities is equivalent to the simplex category Δ, the comparison Mathlib leaves open (Mac Lane, *Categories for the Working Mathematician*, VII.5).

name: Hamilton's principle of stationary action
text: a C^n path, n ≥ 2, is a stationary point of the action ∫ L(t, q, q′) dt among fixed-endpoint variations iff it satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations (Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, §13).

name: Agueh–Carlier's theorem on Gaussian barycenters
text: the W₂-barycenter of Gaussians N(mⱼ, Cⱼ), one of them nondegenerate, is the Gaussian with mean Σ wⱼ mⱼ and covariance the unique positive-definite solution of S = Σ wⱼ (S^{1/2} Cⱼ S^{1/2})^{1/2} (Agueh–Carlier 2011, Thm 6.1).

name: The dispersive estimate for the free Schrödinger equation
text: for f ∈ L¹ ∩ L²(ℝⁿ) and t ≠ 0, ‖e^{itΔ} f‖_∞ ≤ (4π|t|)^{−n/2} ‖f‖₁ (Tao, *Nonlinear Dispersive Equations*, §2.2).

name: Concavity of the von Neumann entropy
text: S(Σ pᵢ ρᵢ) ≥ Σ pᵢ S(ρᵢ) on positive semidefinite matrices, with the upper bound S(Σ pᵢ ρᵢ) ≤ Σ pᵢ S(ρᵢ) + H(p) (Nielsen–Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum Information*, Thm 11.10).

name: The real-analytic Weierstrass preparation and division theorems
text: now for real-analytic germs on ℝⁿ⁻¹ × ℝ: a germ of finite order d in the last variable is a unit times a degree-d Weierstrass polynomial with analytic coefficients (Krantz–Parks, *A Primer of Real Analytic Functions*, §6.1).

name: Sard's theorem on manifolds
text: now for smooth maps between manifolds of any two dimensions, the domain Lindelöf and boundaryless: the critical values form a null set (Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Thm 6.10).

name: The second Bianchi identity with torsion
text: now for any tangent connection: the cyclic sum of (∇ᵤR)(v, w) equals minus the cyclic sum of R(T(u, v), w), T the torsion (Kobayashi–Nomizu I, Thm III.5.3).

name: The Lagrange–Dirichlet stability theorem
text: on a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space, an equilibrium at a strict local minimum of the Hamiltonian is Lyapunov stable (Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, §22).

name: The divisor bound
text: for every ε > 0 there is a constant C with d(n) ≤ C n^ε for all n, d(n) the number of divisors (Hardy–Wright, Thm 315).

name: The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex
text: the cochain complex of alternating maps Λⁿ L → M with the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential, over any commutative ring, and Lie algebra cohomology Hⁿ(L; M) in every degree; Mathlib has degrees at most 2 (Weibel, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*, §7.7).

name: The Nisnevich topology
text: the subcanonical Grothendieck topology on schemes whose covers are étale families in which every point lifts with the same residue field, between the Zariski and étale topologies (Morel–Voevodsky, *𝔸¹-homotopy theory of schemes*, §3.1).

name: Lie algebroids
text: a vector bundle over a manifold with a Lie bracket on sections and an anchor to the tangent bundle satisfying the Leibniz rule; the anchor is then a Lie homomorphism, and the tangent bundle is one (Mackenzie, *General Theory of Lie Groupoids and Lie Algebroids*, Ch. 3).

name: The wave front set of a distribution
text: the closed conic set of (x, ξ) at which a distribution is not microlocally smooth, refining the singular support by direction, with WF(δ) = {x₀} × (ℝⁿ ∖ 0) (Hörmander, *The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I*, Def. 8.1.2).

name: The perfection of a scheme over 𝔽ₚ
text: the limit of X along Frobenius: a perfect scheme with a universal homeomorphism to X, universal among perfect schemes over X (Bhatt–Scholze, *Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian*, §3).

name: The Dixmier trace
text: a linear tracial functional on the weak trace-class ideal L^{1,∞}, vanishing on trace-class operators, built from a dilation-invariant generalized limit, with Dixmier measurability (Connes, *Noncommutative Geometry*, IV.2.β).

name: Bergman spaces
text: the closed subspace A²(U) of L²(U) of holomorphic functions on an open U ⊆ ℂ, with restriction to a relatively compact subdomain a compact operator (Forster, *Lectures on Riemann Surfaces*, §14).

## What it says
The Efron–Stein inequality: for a square-integrable function $f$ of finitely many independent coordinates, $\operatorname{Var} f(X) \le \sum_i \mathbb{E}\,[\operatorname{Var}_i f(X)]$, where $\operatorname{Var}_i$ is the variance in the $i$-th coordinate alone, the others frozen.

- `{ι : Type u_1} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]`: a finite index set $I$ of coordinates, with decidable equality (used to replace one coordinate).
- `{α : ι → Type u} [∀ i, MeasurableSpace (α i)]`: a measurable space $\alpha_i$ for each $i$; the coordinate spaces may differ.
- `(μ : ∀ i, Measure (α i)) [∀ i, IsProbabilityMeasure (μ i)]`: a probability measure $\mu_i$ on each $\alpha_i$; `Measure.pi μ` is the product measure, the law of independent $X_i \sim \mu_i$.
- `{f : (∀ i, α i) → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f) (hL : MemLp f 2 (Measure.pi μ))`: a real function on the product, measurable and square-integrable.
- The conclusion: `evariance f (Measure.pi μ)`, the variance $\int |f - \mathbb{E} f|^2$ in $[0,\infty]$, is at most $\sum_i \int \operatorname{Var}_{\mu_i}\big(y \mapsto f(x \text{ with } x_i := y)\big)\,d(\prod_j \mu_j)(x)$; `Function.update x i y` is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate replaced by $y$.

This is Theorem 3.1 of Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, $\operatorname{Var}(Z) \le \sum_i \mathbb{E}[(Z - \mathbb{E}^{(i)} Z)^2]$, for the same data: finitely many independent coordinates of arbitrary type and a square-integrable $f$. The form with independent copies, $\tfrac12 \sum_i \mathbb{E}[(f(X) - f(X^{(i)}))^2]$, is not part of this statement.

## What it says
Laurent's theorem: a function holomorphic on an open concentric annulus $r < |w - c| < R$, with values in a complex Banach space, is the sum there of its Laurent series, whose coefficients are the circle integrals on any circle $|z - c| = \rho$ inside the annulus.

- `{E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℂ E] [CompleteSpace E]`: a complex Banach space $E$.
- `{f : ℂ → E} {c : ℂ} {r ρ : ℝ} {R : ℝ≥0∞}`: a function $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$, a centre $c$, real radii $r, \rho$ and an extended radius $R \in [0,\infty]$.
- `(hf : DifferentiableOn ℂ f (eball c R \ closedBall c r))`: $f$ is complex-differentiable at every point of the open annulus $\{w : r < |w - c| < R\}$; `eball c R` is the open ball of extended radius $R$, all of $\mathbb{C}$ when $R = \infty$.
- `(hr : 0 ≤ r) (hrρ : r < ρ) (hρR : ENNReal.ofReal ρ < R)`: $0 \le r < \rho < R$, so the circle of radius $\rho$ lies in the annulus.
- The conclusion: `HasLaurentSeriesOnAnnulus f a c r R` with $a_n$ = `circleLaurentCoeff f c ρ n` $= \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-c|=\rho} (z-c)^{-n-1} f(z)\,dz$: it packages $0 \le r < R$ and that for every $w$ in the annulus the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (w-c)^n a_n$ has sum $f(w)$.

This is the Laurent expansion of Conway, Chapter V, §1, and Ahlfors, Chapter 5, §1.2, for the same annuli and with the classical coefficient formula; here the values lie in any Banach space, and $r = 0$ (a punctured disc) and $R = \infty$ are allowed. Uniqueness of the coefficients is the separate `TauCeti.HasLaurentSeriesOnAnnulus.coeff_unique`.

## What it says
The Dunford–Pettis theorem in its classical form: for a finite measure, a set of integrable functions is relatively weakly compact in $L^1$ exactly when it is bounded in norm and its integrals are uniformly absolutely continuous.

- `{α 𝕜 : Type*} [RCLike 𝕜]`: a measurable space $\alpha$ and a scalar field $\mathbb{K}$, which is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `{m : MeasurableSpace α} {μ : Measure α} [IsFiniteMeasure μ]`: a measure $\mu$ on $\alpha$ with $\mu(\alpha) < \infty$.
- `{A : Set (Lp 𝕜 1 μ)}`: a set $A$ of elements of $L^1(\mu)$, classes of integrable functions modulo null sets.
- The left side: `toWeakSpace 𝕜 (Lp 𝕜 1 μ) '' A` is $A$ read in $L^1(\mu)$ with its weak topology; the condition is that its weak closure is weakly compact, that is, $A$ is relatively weakly compact.
- The right side: `IsBounded A`, $A$ is bounded in the $L^1$ norm, and for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $\int_s \|f\|\,d\mu \le \varepsilon$ for every $f \in A$ and every measurable $s$ with $\mu(s) \le \delta$.

This is the Dunford–Pettis criterion as in Albiac and Kalton, §5.2: in $L^1$ of a finite measure, relative weak compactness is boundedness plus uniform integrability, written here as uniform absolute continuity of the integrals. Real and complex scalars are covered; the measure is finite, so no tightness condition enters. The same file states the criterion with Mathlib's `UniformIntegrable` and `UnifIntegrable`.

## What it says
The Eichler–Selberg trace formula at level one: for even weight $k \ge 4$ and $n \ge 1$,
$$\operatorname{tr}\big(T_n \mid S_k(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}))\big) = -\tfrac12 \sum_{t \in \mathbb{Z},\ t^2 \le 4n} H(4n - t^2)\,P_k(t,n) - \tfrac12 \sum_{dd' = n} \min(d,d')^{k-1}.$$

- `{k : ℤ} {w : ℕ} (hk : k = w + 2) (hw : Even w) (hw₀ : w ≠ 0)`: an integer weight $k = w + 2$ with $w$ even and nonzero, so $k \in \{4, 6, 8, \dots\}$.
- `(n : ℕ) [NeZero n]`: the index $n \ge 1$ of the Hecke operator.
- The left side: `LinearMap.trace ℂ _ (heckeTCuspLevelOne k n)`, the trace of $T_n$ on the cusp forms of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. $T_n$ is $f \mapsto \sum f|_k \left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over the upper-triangular representatives of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \backslash \{\det = n\}$, with Mathlib's slash $f|_k \gamma(\tau) = (\det\gamma)^{k-1} (c\tau + d)^{-k} f(\gamma\tau)$: the classical $T_n$, with eigenvalue $a_n$ on a normalised eigenform.
- The first sum runs over the integers $t$ with $t^2 \le 4n$, written as a filter of $[-4n, 4n]$. `hurwitzClassNumber D` is the Hurwitz class number $H(D) \in \mathbb{Q}$: $H(0) = -1/12$, and for $D > 0$ the number of classes of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms of discriminant $-D$, counted by reduced forms, the multiples of $x^2 + y^2$ with weight $1/2$ and those of $x^2 + xy + y^2$ with weight $1/3$. `(dickson 2 n w).eval t` is $P_k(t,n) = E_w(t)$, the Dickson polynomial of the second kind: $E_0 = 1$, $E_1 = X$, $E_{j+2} = X E_{j+1} - n E_j$, so $\sum_j E_j(t) x^j = (1 - tx + nx^2)^{-1}$.
- The second sum runs over `n.divisorsAntidiagonal`, the pairs $(d, d')$ of positive integers with $dd' = n$; the exponent $w + 1$ is $k - 1$. Everything is cast to $\mathbb{C}$.

This is Theorem 1 of Popa and Zagier, in Zagier's normalisation, where $H(0) = -1/12$ makes the $t^2 = 4n$ terms absorb the scalar matrices. The weight $k = 2$, where the formula carries a correction term, is excluded.

## What it says
The Gauss–Brent–Salamin formula: with the arithmetic–geometric mean iteration started at $a_0 = 1$, $g_0 = 1/\sqrt 2$, and $c_j^2 = a_j^2 - g_j^2$,
$$\pi = \frac{4\,M(1, 1/\sqrt 2)^2}{1 - \sum_{j \ge 1} 2^{j+1} c_j^2}.$$

The statement has no hypotheses. `π` is `Real.pi`. `agm 1 (NNReal.sqrt 2)⁻¹` is Mathlib's `NNReal.agm`, the common limit $M(1, 1/\sqrt 2)$ of $a_{j+1} = (a_j + g_j)/2$, $g_{j+1} = \sqrt{a_j g_j}$; the right side is $4M^2$ divided by $1 - \sum'_n 2^{n+2}\big((\texttt{agmSequences}\ 1\ (1/\sqrt 2)\ n).2^2 - (\dots).1^2\big)$. Mathlib's `agmSequences x y n` is the pair $(g_{n+1}, a_{n+1})$ of the iteration started at $(x, y)$, geometric mean first; so the $n$-th term is $2^{n+2}(a_{n+1}^2 - g_{n+1}^2) = 2^{j+1} c_j^2$ with $j = n + 1$, and the sum over $n \ge 0$ is the sum over $j \ge 1$. This is the formula of Salamin and Brent as in Borwein and Borwein, §2.4, with the same corrections $c_j$; it is the self-complementary case $x = y = 1/\sqrt 2$ of Salamin's formula for complementary moduli $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, `TauCeti.Real.pi_eq_four_mul_agm_mul_agm_div_one_sub_tsum`. Truncating the sum and the AGM is the Brent–Salamin algorithm.

## What it says
Stickelberger's relation: in the $m$-th cyclotomic field, the principal ideal generated by the Gauss-sum power $\Phi(A)$ of an ideal $A$ prime to $m$ is $A^\gamma$, with $\gamma = \sum_{1 \le t < m,\ (t,m) = 1} t\,\sigma_t^{-1}$ the Stickelberger element.

- `{K : Type*} [Field K] [NumberField K] {m : ℕ} [NeZero m] [IsCyclotomicExtension {m} ℚ K]`: a number field $K$ which is the $m$-th cyclotomic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, $K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$, with $m \ne 0$.
- `[HasEnoughRootsOfUnity (𝓞 K) m]`: the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ contains a primitive $m$-th root of unity and its $m$-th roots of unity form a cyclic group.
- `(hm : 2 ≤ m)`: $m \ge 2$.
- `{A : Ideal (𝓞 K)} (hA : (absNorm A).Coprime m)`: an ideal $A$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ whose absolute norm $N(A) = [\mathcal{O}_K : A]$, a natural number, is coprime to $m$.
- The conclusion: `span {stickelbergerPhi A m}`, the principal ideal $(\Phi(A))$, equals $\prod_{\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})} (\sigma^{-1} A)^{c(\sigma)}$. Here $\Phi(P) = g(\chi_P, \psi)^m \in \mathcal{O}_K$ for a prime $P$ with $N(P)$ prime to $m$, the $m$-th power of the Gauss sum of the inverse $m$-th power residue character, defined through Jacobi sums and extended multiplicatively (`Ideal.stickelbergerPhi`); `σ⁻¹ • A` is the image of $A$ under $\sigma^{-1}$; and $c(\sigma) \in \{1, \dots, m-1\}$ represents the class of $\sigma$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$ under `galEquivZMod`, so that $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{c(\sigma)}$ for the $m$-th roots of unity.

So $(\Phi(A)) = \prod_t \sigma_t^{-1}(A)^t = A^\gamma$, as in Washington, §6.2, and Adhikari, §4, Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 (iii), for every $m \ge 2$ and every ideal prime to $m$, not only primes, with no restriction on the rational primes below $A$: $p = 2$ is included.

## What it says
The Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem, both directions: a finite group acting faithfully on a finite-dimensional vector space in characteristic zero is generated by pseudoreflections if and only if its algebra of polynomial invariants is a polynomial algebra on homogeneous invariants of positive degree.

- `{K G V : Type*} [Field K] [CharZero K] [Group G] [Finite G] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] [FiniteDimensional K V]`: a field $K$ of characteristic zero, a finite group $G$, and a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $V$.
- `(ρ : Representation K G V)`: a linear action $\rho : G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$.
- `(hρ : Function.Injective ρ)`: the action is faithful.
- The left side: `ρ.pseudoreflectionSubgroup = ⊤`, the subgroup generated by the $g \in G$ whose fixed space $V^g$ has codimension one (`finrank K (V ⧸ (ρ g).fixedSubmodule) = 1`) is all of $G$.
- The right side: there are $n = \dim_K V$ elements $f_1, \dots, f_n$ of `ρ.dual.symmetricAlgebraInvariants`, the subalgebra $\operatorname{Sym}(V^*)^G$ fixed by the contragredient action $\rho^*(g)\varphi = \varphi \circ \rho(g^{-1})$, each in `homogeneousSubmodule K (Dual K V) d` for some $d > 0$, the degree-$d$ part of $\operatorname{Sym}(V^*)$, such that the $K$-algebra map `MvPolynomial.aeval f` $: K[X_1, \dots, X_n] \to \operatorname{Sym}(V^*)^G$, $X_i \mapsto f_i$, is bijective.

This is the theorem of Chevalley and of Shephard and Todd as in Kane, §§17–18, Smith, §7.2, and Stanley, Section 4. The usual setting is $K = \mathbb{C}$ or algebraically closed of characteristic zero; here any field of characteristic zero serves, and the number of generators is fixed at $\dim V$.

## What it says
The Fredholm compatibility condition for the weak Dirichlet problem: under Gårding's inequality on a bounded open set, $B(u, \cdot) = \ell$ has a solution $u \in H^1_0(\Omega)$ exactly when $\ell$ vanishes on the weak solutions of the homogeneous adjoint problem.

This is $\dim N = \dim N^*$ in Evans, §6.2.3, Theorem 4, and Gilbarg–Trudinger, Theorem 8.6, with Gårding's inequality as hypothesis in place of the uniform ellipticity from which the textbooks derive it. ## What it says
For a compact connected real Lie group $G$ of finite dimension, every element of $G$ is the exponential of an element of its Lie algebra: $\exp : \mathfrak g \to G$ is onto.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, the model space of the charts.
- `{H : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H] {I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H} [I.Boundaryless]`: a model with corners $I$, Mathlib's device for manifolds with or without boundary; `I.Boundaryless` says its range is all of $E$, so it models manifolds without boundary.
- `{G : Type*} [TopologicalSpace G] [ChartedSpace H G] [Group G] [LieGroup I ∞ G]`: a group $G$ with charts modelled on $I$ which is a $C^\infty$ manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion: a real Lie group.
- `[CompactSpace G] [ConnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is compact and connected.
- The statement opens with `let _ : T2Space G := I.t2Space_of_lieGroup ∞`: Lean needs $G$ Hausdorff to speak of `lieExp`, and derives this from the Lie-group structure instead of assuming it.
- The conclusion, `Function.Surjective (lieExp (I := I) (G := G))`: `lieExp : LeftInvariantDerivation I G → G` is the exponential map on Mathlib's Lie algebra of left-invariant derivations of $C^\infty(G)$: a derivation is identified with a tangent vector $v$ at $1$, and `lieExp` is the value at time $1$ of the one-parameter subgroup with velocity $v$. Surjective: every $g \in G$ is `lieExp X` for some $X$.

This is the classical theorem that the exponential map of a compact connected Lie group is surjective (Knapp, Corollary 4.48), for the same groups: real, finite-dimensional, compact, connected. Knapp argues through maximal tori; here an $\mathrm{Ad}$-invariant inner product is obtained by averaging, the bi-invariant metric is complete and its geodesics through $1$ are the one-parameter subgroups, so Hopf–Rinow reaches every point. The only hypothesis without a counterpart in the book is the boundaryless model, which every Lie group in the usual sense satisfies.

## What it says
Craig interpolation for the infinitary logic $L_{\omega_1\omega}$: if a sentence $\varphi$ entails a sentence $\psi$, some sentence $\theta$ using only the function and relation symbols common to $\varphi$ and $\psi$ satisfies $\varphi \models \theta$ and $\theta \models \psi$.

- `{L : Language.{u, v}}`: a first-order language, a family of function symbols and of relation symbols of each arity, of any cardinality (`u`, `v` are universe levels and do not affect the mathematics).
- `(φ ψ : L.Sentenceω)`: two sentences of $L_{\omega_1\omega}$: formulas built from atomic formulas (equality of terms, and relation symbols applied to terms) by implication, universal quantification, and conjunctions and disjunctions over countable families indexed by $\mathbb N$, with no free variables.
- `(h : φ.Entails ψ)`: every nonempty structure for $L$ satisfying $\varphi$ satisfies $\psi$.
- The conclusion: there is a sentence $\theta$ with `θ.functionsIn ⊆ φ.functionsIn ∩ ψ.functionsIn`, every function symbol occurring in $\theta$ (constants included, as functions of arity $0$) occurs in both $\varphi$ and $\psi$; `θ.relationsIn ⊆ φ.relationsIn ∩ ψ.relationsIn`, likewise for relation symbols; and $\varphi \models \theta$, $\theta \models \psi$.

This is López-Escobar's interpolation theorem for $L_{\omega_1\omega}$, with both symbol bounds, for a language of any size with function symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and may appear in $\theta$ freely, as in the classical statement.

## What it says
The omitting types theorem for a countable fragment of $L_{\omega_1\omega}$: a satisfiable theory inside a countable formation-closed fragment has a countable model omitting any countable family of partial types of the fragment that the theory does not isolate.

- `{L : Language.{u, v}} {A : Fragment L} {T : L.Theoryω}`: a language $L$; a fragment $A$, a set of $L_{\omega_1\omega}$ formulas without free variables, each tagged with its number $n$ of bound-variable slots, closed under subformulas; a theory $T$, a set of sentences.
- `(hAc : (A : Set _).Countable)`: $A$ is countable.
- `(hA : A.FormationClosed)`: $A$ contains $\bot$ and every atomic formula at every arity, and is closed under implication, universal quantification and relabelling of bound positions.
- `(hT : ∀ φ ∈ T, ⟨0, φ⟩ ∈ A)`: every sentence of $T$ lies in $A$.
- `(hTs : T.IsSatisfiable)`: $T$ has a nonempty model.
- `{ι : Type*} [Countable ι] {n : ι → ℕ} (p : ∀ i, Set (L.BoundedFormulaω Empty (n i)))`: a countable family of partial types $p_i$, each a set of formulas in $n_i$ variables.
- `(hp : ∀ i, ∀ ψ ∈ p i, ⟨n i, ψ⟩ ∈ A)`: each $p_i$ lies in $A$.
- `(hnp : ∀ i, ¬IsolatesIn A T (p i))`: no $p_i$ is isolated over $T$ in $A$: there is no $\varphi \in A$ in $n_i$ variables with $T \cup \{\exists \bar x\, \varphi\}$ satisfiable and $T \models \forall \bar x\,(\varphi \to \psi)$ for every $\psi \in p_i$.
- The conclusion: there are a type `M : Type w`, in any universe `w`, and an $L$-structure on it, with $M$ countable, nonempty, a model of $T$, and `OmitsType M (p i)` for each $i$: no $n_i$-tuple of $M$ satisfies every formula of $p_i$.

This is Keisler's omitting types theorem for countable fragments, as in Marker's Chapter 4, with the same notion of isolation. Countability of the language is not assumed: it follows from that of a formation-closed fragment, which contains every atomic formula.

## What it says
The complex uniformization of the elliptic curve of a lattice: $\mathbb C/\Lambda$ is isomorphic, as an abelian group, to the group of complex points of the Weierstrass curve $E_\Lambda$, by the map induced by $z \mapsto (\wp(z), \wp'(z)/2)$.

- `(L : PeriodPair)`: a pair $(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ of complex numbers linearly independent over $\mathbb R$; `L.lattice` is $\Lambda = \mathbb Z\omega_1 + \mathbb Z\omega_2$ as a $\mathbb Z$-submodule of $\mathbb C$, and `L.lattice.toAddSubgroup` the same set as an additive subgroup, so `ℂ ⧸ L.lattice.toAddSubgroup` is the group $\mathbb C/\Lambda$.
- `L.weierstrassCurve`: the Weierstrass curve $y^2 = x^3 - (g_2/4)x - g_3/4$ over $\mathbb C$, with $g_2 = 60\sum' \lambda^{-4}$ and $g_3 = 140\sum' \lambda^{-6}$ over $\lambda \in \Lambda \setminus 0$ (Mathlib's `PeriodPair.g₂`, `PeriodPair.g₃`); `.toAffine.Point` is the set of its nonsingular affine points $(x, y)$ together with the point at infinity $0$, with Mathlib's chord-and-tangent group law. The discriminant $g_2^3 - 27g_3^2$ does not vanish, so this is $E_\Lambda(\mathbb C)$.
- The value: the additive-group isomorphism (`≃+`) obtained by `QuotientAddGroup.liftEquiv` from the homomorphism `weierstrassPointHom : ℂ →+ E_Λ(ℂ)`, $z \mapsto (\wp(z), \wp'(z)/2)$ for $z \notin \Lambda$ and $z \mapsto 0$ for $z \in \Lambda$, which is surjective (`weierstrassPoint_surjective`) with kernel $\Lambda$ (`ker_weierstrassPointHom`). The class of $z$ goes to `weierstrassPoint z`.

This is the isomorphism $\mathbb C/\Lambda \cong E_\Lambda(\mathbb C)$ of Silverman §VI.3, up to normalisation: the book's curve is $y^2 = 4x^3 - g_2x - g_3$ with the map $(\wp, \wp')$; dividing $y$ by $2$ gives the monic form Mathlib's `WeierstrassCurve` requires. Only the group structure is identified: the library gives $E(\mathbb C)$ no complex-manifold structure, so no analytic isomorphism is stated.

## What it says
The Pólya–Szegő inequality in $BV$ form: the symmetric decreasing (Schwarz) rearrangement of the positive part of an integrable function has total variation at most that of the function.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [Nontrivial E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: a finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension at least $1$, with Lebesgue measure `volume`.
- `{u : E → ℝ} (hu : Integrable u volume)`: an integrable real function.
- `fun y ↦ ENNReal.ofReal (u y)`: the positive part $u^+ = \max(u, 0)$, viewed as a function with values in $[0, \infty]$.
- `schwarzRearrangement volume f`: for $f : E \to [0, \infty]$, the function $f^*(x) = \sup\{t : |B(0, \|x\|)| < |\{f > t\}|\}$: radial, nonincreasing in $\|x\|$, with superlevel set $\{f^* > t\}$ the open ball centred at $0$ of the same volume as $\{f > t\}$, or the whole space if that volume is infinite. This is the symmetric decreasing rearrangement.
- `(… x).toReal`: the value converted back to a real number, with $\infty \mapsto 0$.
- `totalVariationOn volume ⊤ v`: the total variation $|Dv|(E)$ on the whole space, $\sup \int v \operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields $\varphi$ with $\|\varphi\| \le 1$, in $[0, \infty]$.
- The conclusion: $|D(u^+)^*|(E) \le |Du|(E)$.

This is the $BV$ case of the Pólya–Szegő principle (Maggi, Chapter 14; Lieb–Loss, Chapter 3), for the rearrangement of $u^+$; for nonnegative $u$ it is the usual $|Du^*| \le |Du|$. Nothing is assumed beyond integrability: no bounded support, no finite variation. The proof compares superlevel sets level by level through the sharp isoperimetric inequality and the exact perimeter of a ball, and integrates with the coarea formula for $BV$.

- The value: a cochain complex of $R$-modules indexed by $\mathbb N$, assembled by `CochainComplex.of`. ## What it says
The big Nisnevich topology on the category of schemes.

- No explicit arguments, only a universe `u`. The value is a Grothendieck topology on `Scheme.{u}`, the schemes of that universe: for every scheme $S$ a family of covering sieves on $S$ (a sieve being a set of morphisms into $S$ closed under precomposition), such that the maximal sieve covers, covering sieves pull back along every morphism, and a sieve covers once its pullbacks along a covering sieve cover.
- It is `nisnevichPrecoverage.toGrothendieck`, the topology generated by the Nisnevich covering families by closing under these axioms. Since Nisnevich coverings contain the isomorphisms and are stable under base change and composition, `mem_nisnevichTopology_iff` says a sieve on $S$ covers exactly when it contains a Nisnevich covering family.
- A family $\{p_i : X_i \to S\}$ is a Nisnevich covering (`IsNisnevichCovering`) when every $p_i$ is étale and every point $s \in S$ has a preimage $x \in X_i$, for some $i$, at which the induced map of residue fields $\kappa(s) \to \kappa(x)$ (`residueFieldMap`) is an isomorphism.

This is the Nisnevich topology of Morel–Voevodsky, §3.1, Definition 1.2, placed on all schemes rather than on smooth schemes over a base; covering families are indexed by arbitrary types and need not be finite.

## What it says
The spectral measure, or resolution of the identity, of a bounded normal operator.

- `{H : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]`: a complex Hilbert space $H$.

In Tau Ceti this is a family $B \mapsto P(B)$ of operators on $H$, $B$ measurable, with $P(\sigma(a)) = 1$ and $P(B_1)P(B_2) = P(B_1 \cap B_2)$, together with finite scalar measures $\mu_\xi$ (`diag`) with $\langle \xi, P(B)\xi\rangle = \mu_\xi(B)$; from these, each $P(B)$ is an orthogonal projection and $P$ is countably additive in the strong topology.
- It is `ProjValMeasure.ofRepresentation (cfcHom _)`, the projection-valued measure of the continuous functional calculus $\pi = $ `cfcHom`, the unital star homomorphism $C(\sigma(a), \mathbb C) \to B(H)$ with $\pi(z) = a$: $P(B) = \tilde\pi(\mathbf 1_B)$ for $\tilde\pi$ the extension of $\pi$ to bounded Borel functions, and $\mu_\xi$ the Riesz measure of $f \mapsto \langle \xi, \pi(f)\xi\rangle$.

This is the resolution of the identity $E$ of Rudin's Theorem 12.23 and the spectral measure of Conway's §IX.2: the projection-valued measure on the Borel sets of $\sigma(a)$ with $a = \int \lambda\, dE(\lambda)$. Here it is built from the continuous calculus and characterised by `eq_spectralPVM_iff` as the only projection-valued measure on $\sigma(a)$ whose integrals of continuous functions give the continuous calculus.

## What it says
Uniqueness of the spectral measure of a bounded normal operator.

- `{H : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]`: a complex Hilbert space $H$.
- `(a : H →L[ℂ] H)` and `[IsStarNormal a]`: a bounded normal operator on $H$.
- `(P : ProjValMeasure (spectrum ℂ a) H)`: any projection-valued measure on the Borel sets of the spectrum $\sigma(a)$: projections $P(B)$ with $P(\sigma(a)) = 1$, $P(B_1)P(B_2) = P(B_1 \cap B_2)$, and finite diagonal measures $\mu_\xi$ with $\langle \xi, P(B)\xi\rangle = \mu_\xi(B)$.
- The conclusion: $P$ is the spectral measure `spectralPVM` of $a$ if and only if, for every continuous $f : \sigma(a) \to \mathbb C$, the integral $\int f\, dP$ (`P.integral`, applied to $f$ regarded as a bounded Borel function by `ofContinuousMap`) equals $f(a)$, the continuous functional calculus `cfcHom f`.

This is the uniqueness in Rudin's Theorem 12.23, with one difference of form: Rudin determines the resolution of the identity by the single identity $T = \int \lambda\, dE(\lambda)$, while here agreement is asked on all continuous functions. The two are equivalent, since integration against a projection-valued measure is a star homomorphism, so agreement on $z$ gives agreement on polynomials in $z, \bar z$, dense in $C(\sigma(a))$; the recorded statement is the second form. No regularity of $P$ is assumed, finite Borel measures on the compact metrizable $\sigma(a)$ being regular.

## What it says
The Lagrange–Dirichlet theorem: a strict local minimum of a Hamiltonian $H$ on a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space is Lyapunov stable for the Hamiltonian flow.

- `{V : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup V] [NormedSpace ℝ V] [FiniteDimensional ℝ V]`: a finite-dimensional real normed space; the norm only fixes the topology and the derivatives.
- `(ω : SymplecticForm V)`: an alternating nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. It enters through `ω.hamiltonianVectorField H`, the field $X_H$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega = dH$, built from `fderiv ℝ H`.
- `{H : V → ℝ}`, `{x : V}`; `hs : s ∈ 𝓝 x`, `hH : ContinuousOn H s`: $H$ is continuous on a neighbourhood $s$ of $x$.
- `hmin : ∀ᶠ y in 𝓝[≠] x, H x < H y`: $H(x) < H(y)$ for all $y \neq x$ near $x$, a strict local minimum.
- `hU : U ∈ 𝓝 x`: a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$.
- Conclusion: for all $y$ in some neighbourhood of $x$ (`∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x`), every curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to V$ and open preconnected set of times $T$ (an open interval) such that $\gamma'(t) = X_H(\gamma(t))$ for $t \in T$, $H$ is differentiable at $\gamma(t)$ for $t \in T$, and $\gamma(t_0) = y$ for some $t_0 \in T$, satisfy $\gamma(t) \in U$ for all $t \in T$.

This is the classical statement: trajectories passing close enough to a strict minimum of the energy stay in any prescribed neighbourhood, in the past as in the future. Arnold states it for a minimum of the potential energy of a natural system; here it is for any continuous Hamiltonian on a symplectic vector space, with no nondegeneracy of the minimum and no completeness of the flow.

## What it says
The cup-length lower bound for the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category, unnormalized: on a nonempty space, the number of categorical opens needed to cover it exceeds the cup length.

- `{X : Type u} [TopologicalSpace X]`: a topological space; `{R : Type u} [CommRing R]`: a commutative coefficient ring in the same universe; `[Nonempty X]`: $X$ has a point.
- Left side: `lsCupLength X R : ℕ∞` is the supremum in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ of the lengths $n$ of nonzero products $a_1 \smile \cdots \smile a_n$ of positive-degree classes in the singular cohomology $H^*(X; R)$ (`IsPositiveDegreeCupProduct`), $0$ when every positive-degree class vanishes. The cohomology is Tau Ceti's singular cohomology of `TopCat.of X` with coefficients $R$, and the cup product is `singularCup` with the unitors of `ModuleCat R` as diagonal and multiplication.
- Right side: `lsCategoryCount X univ : ℕ∞` is the least $r$ such that $X$ has an `LSCategoricalCover` of size $r$: $r$ open sets covering $X$, each with nullhomotopic inclusion into $X$; it is $\infty$ when there is no finite such cover.
- Conclusion: $\operatorname{cuplength}(X; R) + 1 \le \operatorname{count}(X)$.

This is the classical $\operatorname{cup}(X) \le \operatorname{cat}(X)$ of Cornea–Lupton–Oprea–Tanré in the counting convention where a contractible space has count $1$; on a nonempty space the count is the normalized category plus one. The proof is the standard one: a positive-degree class restricts to zero on a categorical open, so a product of $r$ classes lifts to $H^*(X, U_1 \cup \cdots \cup U_r) = H^*(X, X) = 0$.

## What it says
The cup-length lower bound for the normalized Lusternik–Schnirelmann category, on every space.

- `{X : Type u} [TopologicalSpace X]`: a topological space; `{R : Type u} [CommRing R]`: a commutative coefficient ring in the same universe.
- Left side: `lsCupLength X R : ℕ∞` is the supremum in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ of the lengths $n$ of nonzero products $a_1 \smile \cdots \smile a_n$ of positive-degree classes in the singular cohomology $H^*(X; R)$ (`IsPositiveDegreeCupProduct`), $0$ when every positive-degree class vanishes. The cohomology is Tau Ceti's singular cohomology of `TopCat.of X` with coefficients $R$.
- Right side: `normalizedLSCategory X : ℕ∞` is `lsCategoryCount X univ - 1`, one less than the least number of open sets with nullhomotopic inclusion needed to cover $X$, or $\infty$ when there is no finite such cover.
- Conclusion: $\operatorname{cuplength}(X; R) \le \operatorname{cat}(X)$.

This is the bound of Cornea–Lupton–Oprea–Tanré in their normalization $\operatorname{cat}(\mathrm{point}) = 0$, for any commutative coefficient ring. It follows from the unnormalized form `lsCupLength_add_one_le_lsCategoryCount_univ` on nonempty spaces, and holds on the empty space because both sides are $0$ there.

- `TauCeti.lsCupLength_of_contractibleSpace` — a contractible space has cup length $0$: its normalized category is $0$, so the bound forces every product of positive-degree classes to vanish.

The contractible case checks the bound where the right side is known to be $0$, and recovers the vanishing of $H^{>0}$ of a contractible space from it.

## Lean subtleties
- Subtraction in `ℕ∞` is truncated: $0 - 1 = 0$, which is why the normalized category of the empty space is $0$ and no `Nonempty X` is needed; also $\infty - 1 = \infty$.
- `univ` is the whole space as a subset; `lsCategoryCount` is defined for subsets of $X$.
- $R$ must share the universe of $X$, a Lean restriction without mathematical content.
- The cup length is $\infty$ when nonzero products of every length exist.

## What it says
Tate's uniformisation of the Tate curve as a group isomorphism $K^\times / q^{\mathbb{Z}} \cong E_q(K)$.

- `{K : Type*} [NormedField K] [CompleteSpace K] [IsUltrametricDist K]`: a complete non-archimedean normed field; the valuation need not be discrete and the characteristic is arbitrary.
- `[DecidableEq K]`: a decidable equality on $K$, which Mathlib's group law on the points of a Weierstrass curve asks for.
- `(q : Kˣ) (hq : ‖(q : K)‖ < 1)`: a unit $q$ of norm less than $1$.
- Source: `Additive (Kˣ ⧸ Subgroup.zpowers q)`, the quotient of $K^\times$ by the subgroup $q^{\mathbb{Z}}$ of integer powers of $q$, its group law written additively.
- Target: `(tateCurveAt q hq).toAffine.Point`, the group of points of the Tate curve $E_q : y^2 + xy = x^3 + a_4(q)\,x + a_6(q)$, whose coefficients are the values at $q$ of the integral $q$-series of `tateCurve`; Mathlib's `Point` is the point at infinity together with the nonsingular affine solutions.
- Value: the map is `tateUniformization q hq`: the identity class goes to the point at infinity, and the class of $u \notin q^{\mathbb{Z}}$ to the point with coordinates the Tate series $X(u) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^n u}{(1 - q^n u)^2} - 2\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{n q^n}{1 - q^n}$ and $Y(u)$ (`tateUniformizationX`, `tateUniformizationY`). It is assembled from `tateUniformizationHom` (additivity, injectivity) and the surjectivity proved in this file.

This is Tate's theorem as in Silverman, Advanced Topics, Chapter V, Section 3, for the field $K$ itself; the same file gives it over every complete normed extension $L$ of $K$ (`tateUniformizationBaseChangeEquiv`), with Galois equivariance for algebraic $L / K$.

## What it says
Von Neumann's bicommutant theorem in the form: a unital $*$-subalgebra of the bounded operators on a Hilbert space is its own double commutant exactly when it is closed in the weak operator topology.

- `{𝕜 H : Type*} [RCLike 𝕜] [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 H] [CompleteSpace H]`: $\mathbb{k}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and $H$ is a Hilbert space over it.
- `(S : StarSubalgebra 𝕜 (H →L[𝕜] H))`: a subalgebra of $B(H)$ containing the scalars, hence the identity, and closed under `star`, the adjoint.
- Left side: `(S : Set (H →L[𝕜] H))` is the underlying set of $S$; `.centralizer` is the set of operators commuting with every element of it, the commutant $S'$; so the left side says $S'' = S$ as sets of operators.
- Right side: `ContinuousLinearMapWOT.ofCLM` is the identity map from $B(H)$ to Mathlib's copy `H →WOT[𝕜] H` of the same operators carrying the weak operator topology, the coarsest for which every $T \mapsto \langle y, T x\rangle$ is continuous; `''` is the image of a set; `IsClosed` of that image says that $S$ is weak-operator closed.

This is Theorem 5.3.1 of Kadison–Ringrose, which identifies the weak and strong operator closures of a self-adjoint algebra containing $I$ with its double commutant; the equivalence is its immediate consequence, and the strong-operator form is `double_commutant_iff_isClosed_image_toPointwiseConvergenceCLM` in the same file. The book works over $\mathbb{C}$; the statement here also covers real Hilbert spaces.

The special case connects the theorem with Mathlib's definition of a von Neumann algebra by the double commutant, giving it the closure property that the usual definition takes as primary.

- The commutants are taken in `Set (H →L[𝕜] H)`, and $S'' = S$ is an equality of sets, via the coercion of $S$.
- Closedness is in the weak operator topology on the type copy, not in the operator norm: a norm-closed $C^*$-subalgebra need satisfy neither side.
- `star` on `H →L[𝕜] H` is the adjoint, available because $H$ is complete.
- On $H = 0$ both sides hold trivially.

## What it says
The universal property of the quotient of a scheme by a finite group: every $G$-invariant morphism out of $X$ factors uniquely through the projection $X \to X/G$.

- `{X : Scheme.{u}}`, `{G : Type v} [Group G] [Finite G]`, `{σ : G →* Aut X}`: a scheme, a finite group, and an action by automorphisms, given as a homomorphism into the automorphism group of $X$ among schemes.
- `{Z : Scheme.{u}}`: the target scheme, in the universe of $X$.
- `hσ : HasInvariantAffineCover σ`: every point of $X$ lies in an affine open $U$ with $\sigma(g)^{-1}(U) = U$ for all $g$ (`Opens.IsInvariant`). This holds for affine $X$ (`hasInvariantAffineCover_of_isAffine`) and when $G$ acts over a base along an affine morphism.
- `f : X ⟶ Z`, `hf : ∀ g, (σ g).asIso.hom ≫ f = f`: $f \circ \sigma(g) = f$ for every $g$; `(σ g).asIso.hom` is the morphism $X \to X$ underlying the automorphism, and `≫` is composition in diagrammatic order.
- Conclusion `∃! h : quotient σ ⟶ Z, projection σ hσ ≫ h = f`: exactly one $h : X/G \to Z$ has $h \circ \pi = f$. Here `quotient σ` is glued from the affine invariant quotients $\operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, U)^G$ over the invariant affine opens $U$ (the colimit of `chartDiagram σ`), and `projection σ hσ` is $\pi : X \to X/G$, glued from the affine projections $\operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, U) \to \operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(X, U)^G$.

This is the categorical-quotient part of SGA 1, Exposé V, Proposition 1.8, under its hypothesis that every orbit lies in an affine open, here as a cover by invariant affine opens; no separatedness of $X$ is assumed. The same file shows $\pi$ surjective, integral and an epimorphism.

## What it says
The interior Calderón–Zygmund $W^{2,p}$ estimate for a non-divergence-form operator with continuous principal coefficients and bounded lower-order terms: on a compact $K \subseteq \Omega$, the Hessian of a strong solution of $\sum_{ij} a_{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u + b \cdot \nabla u + c u = f$ is bounded in $L^p(K)$ by $f$ and $u$ in $L^p(\Omega)$.

- `hn : 0 < n`; `{p : ℝ≥0∞} [Fact (1 ≤ p)]`, `hp : 1 < p`, `hp_top : p ≠ ⊤`: dimension $n \ge 1$ and exponent $1 < p < \infty$, the typeclass `Fact` repeating $1 \le p$ so that the Sobolev space can be formed.
- `{Omega : Opens (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))}`, `hK : IsCompact K`, `hKΩ : K ⊆ Omega`: an open $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and a compact $K \subseteq \Omega$.
- `a : ℝⁿ → Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ`: `ha`, measurable on $\Omega$ (`AEStronglyMeasurable` for Lebesgue measure restricted to $\Omega$); `hcont`, continuous at every point of $K$; `hell`, at every $x \in K$ some $\lambda > 0$ has $\lambda\|\xi\|^2 \le \xi^{\mathsf T} a(x)\,\xi$ for all $\xi$ (`Matrix.toQuadraticForm'`). Away from $K$ only measurability is asked.
- `b`, `β`, `hb`, `hbβ`: a measurable vector field with $\|b\| \le \beta$ a.e. on $\Omega$; `c`, `γ`, `hc`, `hcγ`: a measurable function with $|c| \le \gamma$ a.e. on $\Omega$.
- Conclusion: there is a real $C$ such that for every `u : Wkp volume Omega p 2`, Tau Ceti's weak Sobolev space $W^{2,p}(\Omega)$, and every `f : Lp ℝ p (volume.restrict Omega)`, i.e. $f \in L^p(\Omega)$, if for a.e. $x \in \Omega$
$$\textstyle\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}(x)\,\langle D^2u(x)\,e_i, e_j\rangle + \langle b(x), \nabla u(x)\rangle + c(x)\,u(x) = f(x),$$
then $\|D^2 u\|_{L^p(K)} \le C\,(\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)} + \|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)})$. Here `Wkp.iteratedGradient 1 u` is the weak Hessian, an $L^p$ function valued in the linear maps $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$; `Wkp.iteratedGradient 0 (Wkp.lowerOrder 1 u)` is the weak gradient; `Wkp.value 2 u` is $u$ as an element of $L^p(\Omega)$; `lpNorm g p μ` is $(\int |g|^p\,d\mu)^{1/p}$ as a real number.

Gilbarg–Trudinger, Theorem 9.11, is the interior $W^{2,p}$ estimate for this operator, with coefficients continuous and uniformly elliptic on $\Omega$ and a bound on the $W^{2,p}$ norm of $u$ on a relatively compact subdomain; here ellipticity and continuity are asked only at the points of $K$, $u$ is taken in $W^{2,p}(\Omega)$, and only the Hessian is bounded. No boundary condition and no regularity of $\partial\Omega$ enter.

## What it says
The permutation model of the Mathieu group $M_{12}$ has order $95040 = 12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8$.

- `M12 : Subgroup (Equiv.Perm (Fin 12))` is the subgroup of the permutations of $\{0, \dots, 11\}$ generated by two explicit permutations `M12.a` and `M12.b`, transcribed from the ATLAS files `M12G1-p12aB0.m1` and `.m2`: in the files' numbering $1, \dots, 12$, $a = (1,4)(3,10)(5,11)(6,12)$ and $b = (1,8,9)(2,3,4)(5,12,11)(6,10,7)$, each point shifted down by one.
- `Nat.card M12`: the number of elements of the subgroup, regarded as a type.
- The conclusion: this number is $95040$.

The statement is about the model, a subgroup of $S_{12}$ given by generators; it identifies it with nothing abstract, such as the sharply $5$-transitive group of degree $12$. The orders $2$, $3$ and $11$ of $a$, $b$ and $ab$ (`M12.orderOf_a`, `M12.orderOf_b`, `M12.orderOf_a_mul_b`) are the recorded checks that the transcription is the ATLAS pair. ## What it says
The Higman–Sims permutation model `TauCeti.Sporadic.HS`, the subgroup of the symmetric group on $100$ points generated by the two permutations `HS.a` and `HS.b` transcribed from the ATLAS files `HSG1-p100B0.m1` and `.m2`, has exactly $44\,352\,000$ elements.

## What it says
For any base point $x$ of the Kodaira–Thurston manifold and any point $e$ of the cover $\mathbb{R}^4$ lying over $x$, a group isomorphism from the fundamental group $\pi_1(KT, x)$ onto the deck group $\Gamma = H(\mathbb{Z}) \times \mathbb{Z}$.

- `{x : KodairaThurston}`: a point of `TauCeti.KodairaThurston`, the orbit space of $\mathbb{R}^4$ (`Cover`, coordinates $(x, y, z, t)$) under the deck group acting by $((a,b,c),n)\cdot(x,y,z,t) = (a+x,\ b+y,\ c+z+ay,\ n+t)$.
- `(e : mk ⁻¹' {x})`: a point of the fibre of the projection `mk : Cover → KodairaThurston` over $x$, a chosen lift of the base point.
- The value: a `≃*`, a group isomorphism, from `FundamentalGroup KodairaThurston x`, the homotopy classes of loops at $x$ under concatenation, to `DeckGroup`, which is `HeisenbergGroup ℤ × Multiplicative ℤ`: the integer Heisenberg group of triples with product $(x,y,z)(x',y',z') = (x+x',\ y+y',\ z+z'+xy')$, times $\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively.

The map is Mathlib's `IsQuotientCoveringMap.fundamentalGroupEquiv`, which identifies $\pi_1$ of the quotient of the contractible cover by the free, properly discontinuous action with the opposite group $\Gamma^{\mathrm{op}}$, followed by the inverse of the anti-automorphism $((x,y,z),n) \mapsto ((x,y,xy-z),n)$ of $\Gamma$ (`DeckGroup.opMulEquiv`). So a loop whose lift from $e$ ends at $h\cdot e$, $h = ((a,b,c),n)$, goes to $((a,b,ab-c),n)$ (`fundamentalGroupMulEquiv_apply_eq_iff`). This is Hatcher's Proposition 1.40 for Thurston's example; the only difference from the bare "$\pi_1(KT) \cong \Gamma$" is the explicit twist, needed because the monodromy of a composite loop applies the second loop first.

## What it says
Finitely many Gaussian laws on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with weights summing to one, one of them nondegenerate with positive weight, have a unique quadratic Wasserstein barycenter: the Gaussian law with the averaged mean and a positive-definite covariance $S$ solving $S = \sum_j w_j\,(S^{1/2} C_j S^{1/2})^{1/2}$.

- `{ι} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]`: a finite index set; the space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ ι` $= \mathbb{R}^\iota$. `{J} [Fintype J]`: a finite index set for the inputs.

The von Neumann entropy is a concave function on the cone of positive semidefinite matrices: for positive semidefinite $x, y$ and $a, b \ge 0$ with $a + b = 1$, $a\,S(x) + b\,S(y) \le S(ax + by)$.

as endomorphisms of the fibre $V_x$.

- The ambient data: a $C^\infty$ manifold $M$ modelled on a finite-dimensional real space $E$ through `I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H` (boundary and corners allowed), Hausdorff (`T2Space M`); a smooth real vector bundle $V \to M$ with finite-dimensional fibre $F$.
- `(cov : CovariantDerivative I F V) [ContMDiffCovariantDerivative cov ∞]`: a covariant derivative on $V$, smooth.
- `(covT : CovariantDerivative I E (TangentSpace I))`: a covariant derivative on the tangent bundle, with no smoothness assumed.
- `(x : M) (u v w : TangentSpace I x)`: a point and three tangent vectors there.
- `cov.curvatureTensor x u v` is $R(u,v) : V_x \to V_x$ with Lee's sign, $R(X,Y)\sigma = \nabla_X \nabla_Y \sigma - \nabla_Y \nabla_X \sigma - \nabla_{[X,Y]}\sigma$; `cov.derivCurvatureTensor covT x u v w` is $(\nabla_u R)(v,w)$, with $(\nabla_X R)(Y,Z)\sigma = \nabla_X(R(Y,Z)\sigma) - R(\nabla^T_X Y, Z)\sigma - R(Y, \nabla^T_X Z)\sigma - R(Y,Z)\nabla_X \sigma$; `covT.torsion x u v` is $T(u,v) = \nabla^T_u v - \nabla^T_v u - [u,v]$.

This is the second Bianchi identity in Kobayashi–Nomizu's form $\mathfrak{S}\{(\nabla_X R)(Y,Z) + R(T(X,Y),Z)\} = 0$, extended from affine connections to a connection on any vector bundle differentiated with an auxiliary tangent connection; when $T$ vanishes at $x$ it reduces to $\mathfrak{S}\,(\nabla_u R)(v,w) = 0$. No metric is used.

## What it says
On an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, a function $u$ with values in a finite-dimensional complex space satisfies $\bar\partial u = 0$ in the sense of distributions, and is locally integrable, if and only if it agrees almost everywhere on $\Omega$ with a holomorphic function.

- `{F} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℂ F] [FiniteDimensional ℂ F]`: the values lie in a finite-dimensional complex normed space.
- `{μ : Measure ℂ} [μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]`: a Haar measure on $\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}^2$, for instance Lebesgue measure.
- `{Ω : Opens ℂ}`: an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$; `{u : ℂ → F}`: a function.
- The left side, `HasWeakConjWirtingerDerivOn μ Ω u 0`: $F$ is complete (automatic here), $u$ and $0$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$, and for every real-valued test function $\varphi \in C^\infty_c(\Omega)$, $\int (\partial_x \varphi)\, u\, d\mu + i \int (\partial_y \varphi)\, u\, d\mu = -2 \int \varphi \cdot 0\, d\mu = 0$. With $\bar\partial = \tfrac12(\partial_x + i\,\partial_y)$ this is the weak form of $\bar\partial u = 0$.
- The right side: there is $v : \mathbb{C} \to F$ complex-differentiable on $\Omega$ (`DifferentiableOn ℂ v Ω`) with $u = v$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\Omega$ (`=ᵐ[μ.restrict Ω]`).

This is Weyl's lemma for the Cauchy–Riemann operator as in McDuff and Salamon's Appendix B: a weak solution of $\bar\partial u = 0$ is holomorphic after modification on a null set, and conversely. It is derived from the harmonic Weyl lemma applied to the real and imaginary parts. Nothing is assumed of $u$ beyond the local integrability in the left side.

## What it says

- `{f : (ι → ℝ) × ℝ → ℝ} {x₀ : ι → ℝ} {t₀ : ℝ} {d : ℕ}`: the function, the base point and the order.
- `(hf : AnalyticAt ℝ f (x₀, t₀))`: $f$ is the sum of a convergent power series near $(x_0, t_0)$.
- `(hd : analyticOrderAt (fun t ↦ f (x₀, t)) t₀ = d)`: the one-variable function $t \mapsto f(x_0, t)$ vanishes to order exactly $d$ at $t_0$; `analyticOrderAt` takes values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, so this excludes a slice identically zero near $t_0$.
- The conclusion: there are $c_0, \dots, c_{d-1} : \mathbb{R}^\iota \to \mathbb{R}$ and $u : \mathbb{R}^\iota \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, each $c_i$ analytic at $x_0$ with $c_i(x_0) = 0$, $u$ analytic at $(x_0, t_0)$ with $u(x_0, t_0) \ne 0$, such that for all $(x, t)$ in some neighbourhood of $(x_0, t_0)$ (`=ᶠ[𝓝 (x₀, t₀)]`)

It is deduced from the complex theorem `AnalyticAt.exists_weierstrassPreparation` by complexification: uniqueness of the complex preparation makes the coefficients and the unit commute with conjugation, hence real at real points.

## What it says
Mathlib's comparison functor from the category presented by faces and degeneracies modulo the simplicial identities to the simplex category is an equivalence of categories.

- The instance has no binders. `SimplexCategoryGenRel` is the category whose objects are `mk n` for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and whose morphisms are generated by faces $\delta_i : [n] \to [n+1]$, $i \in \{0, \dots, n+1\}$, and degeneracies $\sigma_i : [n+1] \to [n]$, $i \in \{0, \dots, n\}$, subject to the simplicial identities (`FreeSimplexQuiver.homRel`): $\delta_{j+1}\delta_i = \delta_i\delta_j$ for $i \le j$, $\sigma_j \sigma_{i} = \sigma_i \sigma_{j+1}$ for $i \le j$, and the three cases of $\sigma_j \delta_i$. `SimplexCategory` is the usual simplex category $\Delta$: objects the finite nonempty ordinals $[n] = \{0 < \dots < n\}$, morphisms the monotone maps.
- `toSimplexCategory` sends `mk n` to $[n]$, $\delta_i$ to the $i$-th coface (the monotone injection missing $i$) and $\sigma_i$ to the $i$-th codegeneracy (the monotone surjection taking the value $i$ twice).
- What it provides: `Functor.IsEquivalence`, Mathlib's Prop recording that the functor is full, faithful and essentially surjective, which Mathlib takes as the definition of an equivalence; `toSimplexCategory.asEquivalence` then supplies a quasi-inverse.

This is the classical presentation of $\Delta$ by generators and relations: every monotone map factors uniquely as codegeneracies followed by cofaces, and the simplicial identities suffice to identify any two words with the same monotone map (Mac Lane VII.5; Kerodon 04FQ, 04FT). The Lean statement is exactly that, for Mathlib's categories, $[0]$ included.

## What it says

- The left side `α.IsContactForm`: at every $x$ the covector $\alpha_x$ is contact for the bilinear form $d\alpha_x$ (`Module.Dual.IsContact`): $\alpha_x \ne 0$ and $d\alpha_x$ restricted to the hyperplane $\ker \alpha_x$ is nondegenerate.

## What it says
A cone over a diagram $p\colon K \to C$ of simplicial sets is a *limit cone* when it is a terminal vertex of the slice $C_{/p}$.

- `{K C : SSet.{u}}`: two simplicial sets in one universe `u`.
- `(p : K ⟶ C)`: a map of simplicial sets, the diagram.
- `(c : (slice p) _⦋0⦌)`: a vertex of `slice p`, the simplicial set $C_{/p}$ whose $n$-simplices are the maps $\Delta[n] \star K \to C$ restricting to $p$ on $K$. A vertex is a map $\Delta[0] \star K \to C$ extending $p$: a cone over $p$.
- The value: `(slice p).IsTerminalVertex c`: for every $n$, every map $\sigma_0\colon \partial\Delta[n+1] \to C_{/p}$ whose last vertex is $c$ extends to $\Delta[n+1]$.

This is Lurie's definition of a limit of $p$ as a final object of $C_{/p}$ (Higher Topos Theory, Definition 1.2.13.4), with Joyal's extension condition as the definition of a final object. It is stated for every simplicial set $C$, with no `Quasicategory` instance; it is the intended notion when $C$ is a quasicategory.

The empty-diagram and nerve cases recover terminal objects, and the equivalence lemma gives uniqueness up to equivalence, as the definition should.

- When $K$ is empty, $\Delta[0] \star K = \Delta[0]$ and $C_{/p}$ is $C$ itself.
- `IsLimit` is a proposition about a given cone; it asserts no existence of limits.

## What it says
Vaught's conjecture in perfect-set form, as a proposition: every $L_{\omega_1\omega}$ sentence in a countable relational language has countably many countable models up to isomorphism, or perfectly many.

- `∀ (L : Language.{0, 0})`: a first-order language whose symbol sets live in universe $0$.
- `[L.IsRelational]`: no function symbols (hence no constants).
- `[Countable (Σ n, L.Relations n)]`: countably many relation symbols in all.
- `(φ : L.Sentenceω)`: an $L_{\omega_1\omega}$ sentence: conjunctions and disjunctions indexed by $\mathbb N$, finite quantifier strings, no free variables.
- The value: `HasVaughtDichotomy φ`, that is `countableModelCount φ ≤ ℵ₀ ∨ HasPerfectlyManyCountableModels φ`. The count is the number of isomorphism classes of models of $\varphi$ with carrier $\mathbb N$ or $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ for some $n$, finite and empty models included; the alternative says that, on $\mathbb N$ or on some finite carrier, the models of $\varphi$ (as assignments of truth values to atoms) contain a nonempty perfect set of pairwise non-isomorphic ones.

This is the perfect-set (Steel's "strong") form of Vaught's conjecture for $L_{\omega_1\omega}$ sentences. Relational languages in universe $0$ lose nothing, since a countable language has such a presentation; counting finite models is harmless by `vaughtConjecture_iff_nat`. The library asserts neither the conjecture nor its negation.

- The perfect set lives in the space of configurations `Atom L V → Bool` with the product topology; a finite carrier can carry one when the language is infinite. Empty carriers are allowed as models.

## What it says
The Bergman space of an open $U \subseteq \mathbb C$: the subspace of $L^2(U)$ of classes with a holomorphic representative.

- `(F : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℂ F]`: a complex normed space of values; the classical case is $F = \mathbb C$.
- `(U : Opens ℂ)`: an open subset of $\mathbb C$.
- The value: a $\mathbb C$-submodule of `Lp F 2 (volume.restrict (U : Set ℂ))`, the space $L^2(U, F)$ for Lebesgue measure restricted to $U$. Its carrier is $\{u \mid \exists f\colon \mathbb C \to F,\ f \text{ holomorphic on } U,\ u = f \text{ a.e. on } U\}$; the proof fields check that $0$, sums and scalar multiples stay in it.

This is the Bergman space $A^2(U)$ with its usual $L^2$ norm, as in Forster §14 and Conway, allowing vector values. The norm is inherited from $L^2$, not an auxiliary supremum norm.

- `TauCeti.BergmanSpace.isCompactOperator_restrictBounded` — for proper $F$ (in particular finite-dimensional), restriction to a relatively compact open subset is a compact operator.

Closedness and compact restriction are what make $A^2(U)$ a Bergman space rather than an arbitrary subspace of $L^2$.

- $U$ may be empty, giving the zero space, or of infinite measure.

## What it says
Harish-Chandra induction is left adjoint to Harish-Chandra restriction, for any subgroup with a quotient and any commutative coefficient ring.

- `(k : Type u) [CommRing k]`: the coefficient ring.
- `{G : Type v} [Group G] (P : Subgroup G)`: a group and a subgroup.
- `{L : Type v'} [Group L] (π : P →* L) (hπ : Function.Surjective π)`: a surjective homomorphism $\pi\colon P \to L$; write $U = \ker\pi$, so $P/U \cong L$.
- The value: an adjunction `harishChandraInd k P π ⊣ harishChandraRes k P π hπ` between Mathlib's categories `Rep k L` and `Rep k G`. Here $R(M) = \mathrm{Ind}_P^G(\mathrm{Inf}_L^P M) = k[G] \otimes_{k[P]} M$, with $P$ acting on $M$ through $\pi$, and ${}^*R(N) = N^U$ with $L \cong P/U$ acting. The adjunction gives natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}_G(R(M), N) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_L(M, N^U)$; it composes Frobenius reciprocity $\mathrm{Ind} \dashv \mathrm{Res}$ with $\mathrm{Inf} \dashv (-)^U$.

For a finite reductive group and a parabolic $P = L \ltimes U$ these are the Harish-Chandra functors of Dudas–Michel §7 and Howlett–Lehrer; the declaration states the adjunction for an abstract subgroup with a surjection onto a quotient. The other adjunction ${}^*R \dashv R$ is `Rep.harishChandraResIndAdjunction`, under finite index and $|U|$ invertible in $k$; this one needs neither.

## What it says
Almostification $M \mapsto M^a$ is left adjoint to the functor of almost elements $M \mapsto M_*$.

- `{V : Type u} [CommRing V]`: a commutative ring.
- `(S : BasicSetup V)`: a basic setup $(V, \mathfrak m)$: an ideal with $\mathfrak m^2 = \mathfrak m$ such that $\tilde{\mathfrak m} = \mathfrak m \otimes_V \mathfrak m$ is flat.
- `toAlmost S : ModuleCat V ⥤ Module S`: almostification, from $V$-modules to the category `Module S` of almost $V$-modules, the Serre quotient by the almost zero modules (those killed by $\mathfrak m$).
- `elements S : Module S ⥤ ModuleCat V`: $M \mapsto M_* = \mathrm{Hom}(V^a, M)$, with the $V$-module structure of Hom-modules of almost modules.
- The value: an adjunction $(-)^a \dashv (-)_*$: natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}(M^a, N) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_V(M, N_*)$ with unit and counit. The unit $M \to (M^a)_*$ sends $x$ to the almostification of $V \to M$, $1 \mapsto x$.

This is Gabber–Ramero's Proposition 2.2.13 (ii) for an arbitrary basic setup, obtained by transport from Bhatt's firm-module model, in which $M_*$ becomes $\mathrm{Hom}_V(\tilde{\mathfrak m}, -)$.

## What it says
On a closed Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ with $\mathrm{Ric} \geq (n-1)k\,g$, a smooth function with $\Delta f = -nk f$ satisfies $\mathrm{Hess} f = -k f\, g$ everywhere.

- Section variables: `M` a Hausdorff, compact, boundaryless smooth manifold modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space `E` (`[IsManifold I ∞ M] [I.Boundaryless] [CompactSpace M] [T2Space M]`), with a Borel structure and a smooth Riemannian metric on its tangent bundle (`[RiemannianBundle …] [IsContMDiffRiemannianBundle I ∞ E …]`); `f : M → ℝ`, `k : ℝ`.
- `hf`: $f$ is smooth.
- `heig`: for every $x$, `laplaceBeltrami I f x = -n * k * f x`, with $n$ = `Module.finrank ℝ E`. The Laplacian is $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}$, so this says $-\Delta f = nk f$: $f$ is an eigenfunction of the positive Laplacian with eigenvalue $nk$.
- `hRic`: for every $x$ and $v \in T_xM$, $(n-1)k\|v\|^2 \leq \mathrm{Ric}(v,v)$, the Ricci tensor of the Levi-Civita connection, $\mathrm{Ric}(u,v) = \operatorname{tr}(w \mapsto R(w,u)v)$.
- `(x : M) (u v : TangentSpace I x)`.
- The conclusion: `hessian I f x u v = -k * f x * ⟪u, v⟫_ℝ`, where $\mathrm{Hess} f(u,v) = \langle \nabla_u \operatorname{grad} f, v\rangle$.

This is the Hessian equation in the equality case $\lambda_1 = nk$ of the Lichnerowicz estimate, Petersen's Chapter 9. Differences from the book: no connectedness, no $k > 0$, no $f \neq 0$, and dimensions $0$ and $1$ are allowed. The rigidity conclusion, that $M$ is a round sphere, is not part of this statement.

No tests are recorded.

## Lean subtleties

- `‖v‖` and `⟪u, v⟫_ℝ` come from the Riemannian metric on `TangentSpace I x`, a copy of `E`.
- $n = 0$: tangent spaces are zero and both sides vanish. $n = 1$: the Ricci tensor is $0$, so `hRic` holds vacuously and the only input is $\Delta f = -k f$.
- $f = 0$ satisfies the hypotheses for every $k$; $k$ may be negative or zero.
- `[MeasurableSpace M] [BorelSpace M]` fix the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, used by the proof's integration; they add no condition on $M$.

## What it says
For a continuous family $A(s)$ of operators on a finite-dimensional inner product space with hyperbolic limits at $\pm\infty$, $u \mapsto u' + Au$ from $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R, E)$ to $L^2(\mathbb R, E)$ is Fredholm.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: a finite-dimensional real inner product space.
- `{A : ℝ → E →L[ℝ] E}`, `hA : Continuous A`: a continuous family of bounded operators.
- `{Aminus Aplus : E →L[ℝ] E}`, `hminus`, `hplus`: each has a Lyapunov form (`HasLyapunovForm`): a symmetric $S$ and $c > 0$ with $c\|v\|^2 \leq \langle S A_\pm v, v\rangle$ for all $v$. In finite dimensions this characterises hyperbolic operators (no eigenvalue on the imaginary axis); only the easy direction is formalised.
- `hbot`, `htop`: $A(s) \to A_\mp$ as $s \to \mp\infty$.
- `(AL : Lp (E →L[ℝ] E) ∞ (volume.restrict ⊤))`, `hAL : AL =ᵐ A`: an $L^\infty$ class of operator-valued functions on $\mathbb R$, equal to $A$ almost everywhere.
- The conclusion: `(trajectoryOperator (p := 2) AL).IsFredholm`. The domain `WeakDerivStep volume ⊤ 2 (ContinuousLinearMap.id …)` is $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R, E)$: pairs $(u, u')$ in $L^2$ with $u'$ the weak derivative of $u$, with the graph norm. Mathlib's `IsFredholm`: closed range, finite-dimensional kernel, finitely generated cokernel.

This is the Fredholm half of Robbin–Salamon's theory of $d/ds + A(s)$ with hyperbolic limits (their §3). Neither symmetry nor differentiability of $A$ is assumed; the spectral-flow index formula is a separate statement.

- The sign is $u' + Au$; Robbin–Salamon's $d/ds - A$ is the case $A \mapsto -A$.
- Symmetric invertible operators have a Lyapunov form, so the symmetric case is included.

## What it says
A compact manifold carrying a smooth function with exactly two critical points, degenerate or not, is the union of two open subsets each homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^m$.

- Section variables: `M` a Hausdorff compact smooth manifold, without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space `E` (`[IsManifold I ∞ M] [I.Boundaryless] [T2Space M] [CompactSpace M]`); `f : M → ℝ`.
- `hf`: $f$ is smooth.
- `h2`: `totalCriticalCount I f = 2`, the cardinality in $\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$ of `criticalPoints I f = {x | mvfderiv I f x = 0}`: $f$ has exactly two critical points.
- The conclusion: open sets $U, V \subseteq M$ with $U \cup V = M$ and homeomorphisms $U \cong \mathbb R^m$, $V \cong \mathbb R^m$, where $m = \dim E$ and $\mathbb R^m$ is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)`.

This is the cover step of Reeb's sphere theorem for functions with possibly degenerate critical points, Milnor (1959), Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, and Rosen (1960), Lemma 1. No Hessian condition is assumed, so the Morse lemma is not used: the proof flows the complement of a coordinate ball about the maximum into one about the minimum. The conclusion $M \cong S^m$ needs Brown's generalised Schoenflies theorem and is not part of this statement.

## Lean subtleties
- A point where $f$ is not differentiable has `mvfderiv I f x = 0` by convention and would count as critical; moot for smooth $f$.
- `totalCriticalCount` takes values in `ℕ∞`, so `= 2` means exactly two points.
- `U ≃ₜ EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)` is a homeomorphism from the subspace $U$ (a subtype of $M$) to $\mathbb R^m$; `Nonempty` asserts one exists. $m$ is the dimension of the model `E`, hence of every component of $M$.
- Dimension $0$, or constant $f$: every point is critical, so $M$ is the two critical points, each open and homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^m$.

## What it says
For topological spaces $X$ and $Y$ with $Y$ second countable, a subset $s$ of $X \times Y$ with the Baire property is comeagre exactly when, for comeagrely many $x \in X$, its section $s_x = \{y \mid (x, y) \in s\}$ is comeagre in $Y$.

- `{X Y : Type*}`, `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: two topological spaces, with no separation or Baire-space assumption.
- `[SecondCountableTopology Y]`: $Y$ has a countable base. Nothing is assumed of $X$.
- `{s : Set (X × Y)}`, `(hs : BaireMeasurableSet s)`: $s$ has the Baire property: it differs from a Borel set (equivalently, an open set) by a meagre set.
- The conclusion is an equivalence. `∀ᵇ x : X, ∀ᵇ y : Y, (x, y) ∈ s` says that the set of $x$ whose section $s_x$ is comeagre in $Y$ is comeagre in $X$; `s ∈ residual (X × Y)` says that $s$ is comeagre in the product. `residual Z` is the filter of comeagre sets of $Z$, those containing a countable intersection of dense open sets, and `∀ᵇ` quantifies along it.

This is the Kuratowski–Ulam theorem, the category analogue of Fubini's theorem, in its comeagre wording; the meagre wording is `BaireMeasurableSet.eventually_isMeagre_curry_left_iff_isMeagre`. Kechris states it for second countable $X$ and $Y$; here only $Y$ is second countable. The direction "comeagre implies comeagrely many comeagre sections" holds for every $s$ (`TauCeti.curry_le_residual`); the Baire property enters only in the converse.
