- Roadmap BorelEquivalenceRelations, Layer 1.1 Kuratowski–Ulam ([README, line 305](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/BorelEquivalenceRelations/README.md#L305)).

No tests are recorded for this declaration, and the roadmap states no Checks for this target.

## Lean subtleties
- `∀ᵇ x : X, p x` is `Filter.Eventually p (residual X)`: $p$ holds on a comeagre set. With no Baire hypothesis a comeagre set may be empty (in $\mathbb{Q}$ every set is comeagre), so "comeagrely many" does not imply "some"; the equivalence holds as stated.
- `BaireMeasurableSet s` is measurability for the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the Borel sets and the meagre sets.
- The outer quantifier is over $x$. The form with $y$ outermost is `BaireMeasurableSet.eventually_eventually_right_iff_mem_residual`, under `[SecondCountableTopology X]`; exchanging the two (`BaireMeasurableSet.eventually_eventually_swap`) needs both.
- `[SecondCountableTopology Y]` is carried as a typeclass, found by Lean itself.
- If $X$ or $Y$ is empty, every subset of the product is comeagre and both sides are true.

## What it says
In a finite-dimensional real inner product space $E$ of dimension $n$, a bounded set $s$ has outer measure at most $(\operatorname{diam} s / 2)^n$ times the measure of the unit ball, for any additive Haar measure $\mu$: $\mu(s) \le \omega_n (\operatorname{diam} s/2)^n$ with $\omega_n = \mu(B(0,1))$.

- `{E : Type*}`, `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$.
- `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ carries its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
- `(μ : Measure E) [μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]`: $\mu$ is translation invariant, finite on compact sets and positive on open sets; Lebesgue measure `volume` is one, and every other is a positive multiple of it.
- `{s : Set E}`, `(hs : Bornology.IsBounded s)`: $s$ is bounded. No measurability is asked.
- The conclusion: `μ s ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ((diam s / 2) ^ Module.finrank ℝ E) * μ (ball 0 1)`. `Module.finrank ℝ E` is $n = \dim E$, `diam s` the diameter as a real number, `ball 0 1` the open unit ball, and `ENNReal.ofReal` reads the real $(\operatorname{diam} s/2)^n$ as an extended nonnegative real, the kind of value $\mu$ takes.

This is the isodiametric inequality of Evans and Gariepy, Theorem 2.4, $\mathcal{L}^n(A) \le \alpha(n)(\operatorname{diam} A/2)^n$ for every $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, with Lebesgue measure replaced by any Haar measure and $\omega_n$ read as its unit-ball volume. The set is assumed bounded; the unbounded case, where the right side is $\infty$, is `MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_le_ediam_div_two_pow_mul_addHaar_ball`. The constant is sharp, since a closed ball of radius $\operatorname{diam} s / 2$ has diameter $\operatorname{diam} s$.

## References and tests
- L. C. Evans and R. F. Gariepy, *Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions*, Theorem 2.4.
- Roadmap Isoperimetry, I2 ([README, line 176](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/Isoperimetry/README.md#L176)): the sharp isodiametric inequality $|E| \le \omega_n(\operatorname{diam} E/2)^n$.

No tests are recorded for this declaration, and the roadmap states no Checks for this target.

## Lean subtleties
- `diam s` is `ENNReal.toReal (ediam s)`, and is $0$ for an unbounded set; `hs` rules that case out.
- $\mu(s)$ is an outer measure: Mathlib's measures are defined on all sets, so no measurability hypothesis is needed.
- `ball 0 1` is the open ball; a Haar measure gives the closed ball the same measure, so $\omega_n$ is the usual constant for Lebesgue measure.
- When $\dim E = 0$ the space is a point, the unit ball is the whole space, $(\operatorname{diam} s/2)^0 = 1$, and the inequality reads $\mu(s) \le \mu(E)$.
- `InnerProductSpace ℝ E` restricts to Euclidean norms; the statement is not made for an arbitrary norm.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, found by Lean automatically.

## What it says
In a finite-dimensional real inner product space $E$, a nonempty closed bounded set $s$ has the measure of a closed ball of radius $\operatorname{diam} s / 2$, for an additive Haar measure $\mu$, exactly when $s$ is itself a closed ball of radius $\operatorname{diam} s / 2$.

- `{E : Type*}`, `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ is a Euclidean space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
- `(μ : Measure E) [μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]`: $\mu$ is translation invariant, finite on compacts and positive on open sets, such as Lebesgue measure.
- `{s : Set E}`, `(hsc : IsClosed s)`, `(hs : Bornology.IsBounded s)`, `(hne : s.Nonempty)`: $s$ is closed, bounded and nonempty, so a nonempty compact set; a convex body is an instance.
- `(x : E)`: any point, the centre of the comparison ball; by translation invariance it does not matter which.
- The conclusion: `μ s = μ (closedBall x (diam s / 2))` if and only if `∃ c, s = closedBall c (diam s / 2)`, that is, $s$ is the closed ball of radius $\operatorname{diam} s / 2$ about some centre $c$.

This is the equality case of the isodiametric inequality: $\mu(s) = \omega_n(\operatorname{diam} s/2)^n$ forces $s$ to be a ball. The a.e. version for bounded null-measurable sets is `MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_eq_addHaar_closedBall_diam_div_two_iff_exists_ae_eq`, and the containment statement for arbitrary bounded sets is `MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_subset_closedBall_diam_div_two_of_addHaar_ge`. The radius is that of $s$ itself: a null modification can enlarge the diameter without changing the measure, which is why the closed and the a.e. forms are stated apart.

## References and tests
- Roadmap Isoperimetry, I2 ([README, line 176](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/Isoperimetry/README.md#L176)): "the volume-maximizing convex-body case has ball rigidity; supply the equality proof."
- R. Schneider, *Convex Bodies: The Brunn–Minkowski Theory*, 2nd ed., Theorem 7.1.1, the equality case of Brunn–Minkowski for convex bodies, cited by the module for the step the proof rests on.
- L. C. Evans and R. F. Gariepy, *Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions*, Theorem 2.4, the inequality whose equality case this is.

No tests are recorded for this declaration, and the roadmap states no Checks for this target.

## Lean subtleties
- `hne` is needed: in positive dimension the empty set has measure $0 = \mu(\overline{B}(x, 0))$ but is no ball. A singleton $\{a\}$ has diameter $0$ and is the closed ball of radius $0$ about $a$, so both sides hold there.
- `diam s` is $0$ for unbounded sets; `hs` excludes them. Closed sets are Borel, so no measurability hypothesis appears.
- The norm is the Euclidean one from `InnerProductSpace ℝ E`, not an arbitrary norm.
- When $\dim E = 0$ the only nonempty closed set is the point, a closed ball of radius $0$.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, found by Lean automatically.

## What it says
The diamond operator $\langle d \rangle$ on modular forms of weight $k$ for $\Gamma_1(N)$, indexed by a unit $d \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, as a $\mathbb{C}$-linear endomorphism of $M_k(\Gamma_1(N))$.

- `{N : ℕ}`: the level, a natural number.
- `(k : ℤ)`: the weight, any integer.
- `(d : (ZMod N)ˣ)`: a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.
- The value is a linear map `ModularForm ((Gamma1 N).map (mapGL ℝ)) k →ₗ[ℂ] ModularForm ((Gamma1 N).map (mapGL ℝ)) k`. `(Gamma1 N).map (mapGL ℝ)` is $\Gamma_1(N)$ written as a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, and `ModularForm Γ k` is the space $M_k(\Gamma)$ of holomorphic weight-$k$ forms for $\Gamma$ bounded at the cusps.

The definition picks $\gamma = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & \delta \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(N)$ with $\delta \equiv d \pmod N$, which exists since the lower-right entry `Gamma0Map N` maps $\Gamma_0(N)$ onto $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, and sends $f$ to $f \mid_k \gamma$, carried back to level $\Gamma_1(N)$ because $\Gamma_1(N)$ is normal in $\Gamma_0(N)$. Two choices of $\gamma$ differ by an element of $\Gamma_1(N)$, under which $f$ is invariant, so the operator does not depend on the choice. This is $\langle d \rangle f = f[\gamma]_k$ of Diamond and Shurman; Mathlib's slash agrees with theirs for determinant $1$: $(f \mid_k \gamma)(\tau) = f(\gamma\tau)(c\tau + \delta)^{-k}$. The character spaces $M_k(\Gamma_1(N), \chi)$ are its simultaneous eigenspaces (`TauCeti.modFormCharSpace`).

## References and tests
- F. Diamond and J. Shurman, *A First Course in Modular Forms*, §5.2.
- T. Miyake, *Modular Forms*, §4.5.
- Roadmap ModularForms, "Diamond operators first" ([README, line 268](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/ModularForms/README.md#L268)), which pins the AINTLIB names `diamondOp`, `diamondOpCusp` and `diamondOpHom`.
- `TauCeti.diamondOp_one` — at $d = 1$ the operator is the identity.
- `TauCeti.coe_diamondOp` — for any $\gamma \in \Gamma_0(N)$ with lower-right entry $d$, $\langle d \rangle f$ is the function $f \mid_k \gamma$.
- `TauCeti.diamondOp_mul` — $\langle d_1 d_2 \rangle = \langle d_1 \rangle \circ \langle d_2 \rangle$.

The first and third show that $d \mapsto \langle d \rangle$ is an action of $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, as in the book; the second that the operator is the classical one, independent of the lift. The roadmap states no Checks for this target.

## Lean subtleties
- The representative $\gamma$ is chosen by classical choice (`Exists.choose`), so the definition is noncomputable; its independence of the choice is the theorem `TauCeti.coe_diamondOp`.
- $N = 0$ is allowed: `ZMod 0` is $\mathbb{Z}$, whose units are $\pm 1$.
- The weight $k$ is any integer, including negative and odd weights.
- The slash goes through `mapGL ℝ`, the inclusion $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$; for determinant $1$ the factor $|\det|^{k-1}$ in Mathlib's `∣[k]` is $1$.
- The cusp-form counterpart is `TauCeti.diamondOpCusp`; `TauCeti.diamondOp_coe_cuspForm` says the two agree on cusp forms.

## What it says
The Lagrange–Dirichlet theorem: a strict local minimum of a Hamiltonian $H$ on a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space is Lyapunov stable for the Hamiltonian flow.

- `{V : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup V] [NormedSpace ℝ V] [FiniteDimensional ℝ V]`: a finite-dimensional real normed space; the norm only fixes the topology and the derivatives.
- `(ω : SymplecticForm V)`: an alternating nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. It enters through `ω.hamiltonianVectorField H`, the field $X_H$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega = dH$, built from `fderiv ℝ H`.
- `{H : V → ℝ}`, `{x : V}`; `hs : s ∈ 𝓝 x`, `hH : ContinuousOn H s`: $H$ is continuous on a neighbourhood $s$ of $x$.
- `hmin : ∀ᶠ y in 𝓝[≠] x, H x < H y`: $H(x) < H(y)$ for all $y \neq x$ near $x$, a strict local minimum.
- `hU : U ∈ 𝓝 x`: a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$.
- Conclusion: for all $y$ in some neighbourhood of $x$ (`∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x`), every curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to V$ and open preconnected set of times $T$ (an open interval) such that $\gamma'(t) = X_H(\gamma(t))$ for $t \in T$, $H$ is differentiable at $\gamma(t)$ for $t \in T$, and $\gamma(t_0) = y$ for some $t_0 \in T$, satisfy $\gamma(t) \in U$ for all $t \in T$.

This is the classical statement: trajectories passing close enough to a strict minimum of the energy stay in any prescribed neighbourhood, in the past as in the future. Arnold states it for a minimum of the potential energy of a natural system; here it is for any continuous Hamiltonian on a symplectic vector space, with no nondegeneracy of the minimum and no completeness of the flow.

## References and tests
- V. I. Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, 2nd ed., Lagrange's theorem on the stability of an equilibrium at a strict minimum of the potential energy.
- M. W. Hirsch, S. Smale, R. L. Devaney, *Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos*, 3rd ed., Section 9.2.
- Roadmap [SymplecticGeometry/IntegrableSystems, milestone I4, planar central force](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/SymplecticGeometry/IntegrableSystems/README.md#L243-L244): "A nondegenerate reduced minimum is Lyapunov-stable elliptic".
- `TauCeti.eventually_forall_mem_of_strictLocalMin_effectivePotential` — the special case of the reduced central-force Hamiltonian $p_r^2/2m + U_\ell(r)$ on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ with the standard symplectic form: a strict local minimum of the effective potential at $r_0$ makes the circular orbit $(r_0, 0)$ stable.

The special case instantiates $V$, $\omega$ and $H$ concretely and recovers the textbook stability of circular orbits.

## Lean subtleties
- `𝓝[≠] x` is the punctured neighbourhood filter: the inequality is asked only for $y \neq x$.
- `hamiltonianVectorField` is defined through `fderiv`, which is $0$ where $H$ is not differentiable; the differentiability of $H$ along $\gamma$ removes this junk value and makes the energy constant along $\gamma$.
- Nothing asserts that $x$ is an equilibrium: $H$ need not be differentiable at $x$. When it is, the strict minimum is a critical point and $X_H(x) = 0$.
- $T$ is any open interval on which $\gamma$ solves the equation, not necessarily maximal, and may contain times before $t_0$.

text:
## What it says
The Hilbert class field of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ is $\mathbb{Q}(i, \sqrt{5})$.

- `(hd : Squarefree (-5 : ℤ))`: the integer $-5$ is squarefree. This is true; it is an argument because the genus field `candidateGenusField hd` is constructed from it.
- `candidateGenusFieldBase hd`: the copy of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ inside `candidateGenusField hd`, a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by a chosen square root of $-5$.
- `hilbertClassField K`: for a number field $K$, the ray class field of the trivial modulus inside a separable closure `SeparableClosure K`: the abelian extension that the global class field correspondence attaches to the class group $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$, that is, the maximal abelian extension of $K$ unramified at every place, the real places included. The narrow Hilbert class field, unramified at the finite places only and attached to the narrow class group, is a different declaration.
- `adjoin ℚ {Complex.I, (Real.sqrt 5 : ℂ)}`: the subfield $\mathbb{Q}(i, \sqrt 5)$ of $\mathbb{C}$.
- The conclusion `Nonempty (… ≃ₐ[ℚ] …)`: there exists an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras between $H(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}))$ and $\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt 5)$.

This is the classical example of Cox §6.A: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ has class number $2$, so its Hilbert class field has degree $2$ over it, and the genus field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-1}, \sqrt{5})$ of discriminant $-20$, unramified everywhere over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$, exhausts it. The companions `finrank_hilbertClassField_sqrt_neg_five` (degree $2$) and `fieldRange_candidateGenusField_neg_five_eq_hilbertClassField` (the identification for every embedding of the genus field) are the two halves. Since $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ has no real place, the Hilbert and narrow Hilbert class fields coincide, and the narrow one has the same presentation (`nonempty_algEquiv_narrowHilbertClassField_sqrt_neg_five`).

## References and tests
- Cox, *Primes of the Form $x^2 + ny^2$*, §6.A (the genus field of discriminant $-20$).
- Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, Chapter VI, §6 (the Hilbert class field).
- Roadmap: [ClassFieldTheory, §5.7 Downstream worked examples](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/ClassFieldTheory/README.md#L2031): "Compute the Hilbert and narrow Hilbert class fields in small quadratic examples".

No tests are recorded for this declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- The two fields live in different ambient fields, an abstract separable closure of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$ and $\mathbb{C}$, so the statement is an isomorphism over $\mathbb{Q}$; it does not say that the isomorphism matches the two copies of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$, although the proof builds one that does.
- The Hilbert class field is a priori an algebra over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$, not over $\mathbb{Q}$; the $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra structure that `≃ₐ[ℚ]` uses is the one every field of characteristic zero carries, and it is the only one, so no choice is involved.
- `Nonempty` asserts that an isomorphism exists and chooses none.
- `Real.sqrt 5` is the nonnegative real root, cast into $\mathbb{C}$. Which root of $-5$ generates the base is a choice made in `candidateGenusFieldBaseRoot`; both signs give the same subfield.
- `↥` turns an intermediate field into a type; `≃ₐ[ℚ]` is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras, here of fields.
- `hd` is provable (`by norm_num`), so the statement is not vacuous.

The result should still be true if DenselyOrdered and SeparableSpace are replaced by SecondCountableTopology?

Yes. `SecondCountableTopology ι` would suffice and is strictly weaker: Mathlib's `SecondCountableTopology.of_separableSpace_orderTopology` derives it from `DenselyOrdered` + `SeparableSpace` + `OrderTopology`, while ℕ, ℤ or `ℝ ×ₗ ℤ` are second countable but not densely ordered.

The two hypotheses enter only through `TopologicalSpace.exists_countable_subset_Iic_exists_mem_lt` (TauCeti/Topology/Order/LeftRight.lean), whose witness is `{T} ∪ (D ∩ Iic T)` for a countable dense `D`. Under second countability one can instead take `{T} ∪ ((D ∪ {t | ∃ b, t ⋖ b}) ∩ Iic T)`: by `nhdsGT_eq_bot_iff` a time `t < T` is right-isolated exactly when some `b` covers it, these form a countable set by `countable_setOfPred_covBy_right`, and at any other `t < T` right-continuity gives a nonempty open subset of `(t, T)` on which `f > ε`, which meets `D`. So the generalisation is an improvement; I could not run Lean here, so this proof sketch is unchecked.

That is weaker, since Mathlib derives second countability from those two together with the order topology, and it now includes discrete times such as ℕ. The key step is the lemma `TopologicalSpace.exists_countable_subset_Iic_exists_mem_lt`. Its countable set now also contains the points below `T` that are isolated on the right. Mathlib's `countable_setOfPred_covBy_right` shows these are countable. `Dense.exists_mem_insert_inter_Iic_lt` was generalised the same way. Everything that imports these modules builds.

## What it says
A continuous self-map of a nonempty closed convex set in a real normed space, whose image is relatively compact, has a fixed point.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {C : Set E}` (section variables): a real normed space $E$, not assumed complete, and a subset $C$.
- `(hC : IsClosed C) (hconv : Convex ℝ C) (hne : C.Nonempty)`: $C$ is closed, convex and nonempty.
- `{f : E → E} (hf : ContinuousOn f C) (hfC : MapsTo f C C)`: a function on all of $E$, continuous at the points of $C$ relative to $C$, with $f(C) \subseteq C$.
- `(hK : IsCompact (closure (f '' C)))`: the closure of the image $f(C)$ is compact.
- Conclusion `∃ x ∈ C, IsFixedPt f x`: some $x \in C$ has $f(x) = x$.

This is Schauder's theorem as in Corollary 11.2 of Gilbarg–Trudinger, with two hypotheses dropped: $E$ need not be a Banach space and $C$ need not be bounded, since the compactness of $\overline{f(C)}$ does the work of both. Their Theorem 11.1, for compact convex $C$, is the specialisation below.

## References and tests
- J. Schauder, *Der Fixpunktsatz in Funktionalräumen*, Studia Math. 2 (1930), 171–180.
- D. Gilbarg and N. S. Trudinger, *Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order*, Theorem 11.1 and Corollary 11.2.
- Roadmap: [BanachAlgebras, §8.2 "Schauder and Lomonosov"](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/BanachAlgebras/README.md#L1964), target `schauder_fixedPoint`, stated there for a closed bounded convex set in a real Banach space.
- `TauCeti.schauderFixedPoint_compactConvex` — the compact-convex specialisation, in any dimension.
- `TauCeti.schauderFixedPoint_closedConvex` — the same for a bundled map `C(C, C)`, by extending the map by the identity off $C$.
- `TauCeti.leraySchauderFixedPoint_closedBall` — the Leray–Schauder form on a ball, by applying this theorem to $T$ followed by the radial retraction.

## What it says
A continuous map of a real normed space sending bounded sets to relatively compact sets has a fixed point, provided the solutions of $u = \theta T u$ for $0 < \theta < 1$ form a bounded set.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]` (section variables): a real normed space, not assumed complete.
- `{T : E → E} (hT : Continuous T)`: a continuous map of $E$ into itself.
- `(hK : ∀ s, Bornology.IsBounded s → IsCompact (closure (T '' s)))`: the image of every bounded set has compact closure, so $T$ is a compact map.
- `(hbd : Bornology.IsBounded {u | ∃ θ ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1, u = θ • T u})`: the set of all $u$ with $u = \theta T u$ for some $\theta \in (0, 1)$ is bounded: the a priori bound.
- Conclusion `∃ u, IsFixedPt T u`: some $u$ has $T u = u$.

This is Schaefer's theorem, Theorem 11.3 of Gilbarg–Trudinger, which assumes a Banach space and a uniform bound on the solutions of $u = \sigma T u$ for $0 \le \sigma \le 1$. Here the bound is asked only over $0 < \theta < 1$, which the closed-interval bound implies, and completeness is not used, so the statement is at least as strong as the book's. The proof applies `TauCeti.leraySchauderFixedPoint_closedBall` on a ball of radius larger than the bound.

## What it says
Meyers' planar example: for every exponent $p > 2$ there is a uniformly elliptic coefficient field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a weak solution in $H^1$ that is not in $W^{1,p}$.

- Conclusion: there is a real $\mu$ with $0 < \mu < 1$ such that for every open $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ (`Opens (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))`), bounded and containing the origin:
  - some `u : W1p volume Ω 2`, an element of $H^1(\Omega)$ for Lebesgue measure, has `W1p.value u`, its $L^2$ class, equal almost everywhere on $\Omega$ to `meyersSolution μ`, the function $x \mapsto |x|^{\mu - 1} x_0$ (`x 0` is the first coordinate);
  - for every `v : W1p0 volume Ω 2`, an element of $H^1_0(\Omega)$, `energyFormH1 (meyersCoefficient μ) 0 0 u v = 0`: $\int_\Omega \langle a \nabla u, \nabla v \rangle = 0$ with no lower-order terms, so $u$ is a weak solution of $\operatorname{div}(a \nabla u) = 0$ for $a = $ `meyersCoefficient μ`, the field $\mu^2 I + (1 - \mu^2)\, x x^{\mathsf T}/|x|^2$;
  - no `w : W1p volume Ω p` has value almost everywhere equal to `meyersSolution μ`: the solution is not in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

This is the example of Meyers, §5: the exponent of his higher integrability theorem cannot be chosen independently of the ellipticity ratio. Here $a$ is uniformly elliptic with constants $\mu^2$ and $1$, and the proof takes $\mu = 1 - 2/q$ with $q = \min(p, 4)$.

## What it says
The symmetrization inequality with a ghost sample: for a finite family of centred real random variables $X_i$ with an independent copy $X'_i$, signs $\varepsilon_i = \pm 1$ independent of the differences, and a convex $\Phi$,
$$\mathbb{E}\,\Phi\Big(\sum_i X_i\Big) \le \mathbb{E}\,\Phi\Big(\sum_i (X_i - X'_i)\Big) = \mathbb{E}\,\Phi\Big(\sum_i \varepsilon_i (X_i - X'_i)\Big).$$

- `{Ω ι : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [Fintype ι] {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]`: a probability space and a finite index set.
- `{X X' ε : ι → Ω → ℝ} {Φ : ℝ → ℝ}`: three families of real random variables and a function $\Phi$.
- `(hΦ : ConvexOn ℝ univ Φ)`: $\Phi$ is convex on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
- `(hind : iIndepFun (Sum.elim X X') μ)`: the $2|\iota|$ variables $X_i, X'_i$ are jointly independent.
- `(hid : ∀ i, IdentDistrib (X i) (X' i) μ μ)`: $X_i$ and $X'_i$ have the same law.
- `(hX) (hX') (hε) (hint) (h0)`: all variables are measurable, and the $X_i$ are integrable and centred.
- `(hindep : IndepFun (fun ω i ↦ ε i ω) (fun ω i ↦ X i ω - X' i ω) μ)`: the vector $(\varepsilon_i)_i$ is independent of the vector $(X_i - X'_i)_i$.
- `(hsign : ∀ i, ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ε i ω = 1 ∨ ε i ω = -1)`: each sign is almost surely $\pm 1$.
- `(h1) (h2)`: $\Phi(\sum_i X_i)$ and $\Phi(\sum_i (X_i - X'_i))$ are integrable.
- Conclusion: the inequality and the equality above, as a conjunction.

The inequality is Jensen's inequality conditioned on $X'$; the equality holds because swapping $X_i$ with $X'_i$ where $\varepsilon_i = -1$ preserves the joint law. This is the chain the roadmap states. Ledoux–Talagrand's lemma is for Banach-space-valued sums with $\Phi$ applied to the norm and continues to $\mathbb{E}\,\Phi(2\|\sum_i \varepsilon_i X_i\|)$; that step is not part of this declaration.

## What it says
Over a left and right noetherian ring, a module is totally reflexive if and only if it is Gorenstein-projective: the theorem of Auslander and Bridger on modules of Gorenstein dimension zero.

- `universe u`, `{A : Type u} [Ring A]` (section variables): a ring $A$, not necessarily commutative.
- `[IsNoetherianRing A] [IsNoetherianRing Aᵐᵒᵖ]`: $A$ is left and right noetherian, the latter phrased as noetherianity of the opposite ring.
- `(M : ModuleCat.{u} A)`: a left $A$-module, as an object of the category of $A$-modules.
- Conclusion: `IsTotallyReflexive A M ↔ IsGorensteinProjective A M`.

`IsTotallyReflexive A M` has four fields: $M$ is finitely generated; evaluation `opDualEval A M` from $M$ to $M^{**} = \operatorname{Hom}_{A^{\mathrm{op}}}(\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A), A)$ is bijective; $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}_A(M, A) = 0$ for every $n$; and $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}_{A^{\mathrm{op}}}(M^*, A) = 0$ for every $n$, where $M^* = \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A)$ is a right module. `IsGorensteinProjective A M` says $M$ is isomorphic to the degree-zero cycles of a totally acyclic complex: a $\mathbb{Z}$-indexed cochain complex of finitely generated projective modules that is acyclic and whose dual $\operatorname{Hom}_A(P, A)$ is acyclic.

This is condition (c) of Proposition (3.8) of Auslander–Bridger, and Theorem 3.1 of Avramov–Martsinkovsky with $g = 0$, (i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iv), who name these modules totally reflexive. The direction from Gorenstein-projective to totally reflexive holds over any ring.

## What it says
The Modulus Lemma: a total function is computable in a c.e. set $Z$ exactly when it is the limit of a computable approximation with a modulus computable in $Z$.

- `{g : ℕ → ℕ}` (section variable): a total function on the natural numbers.
- `{Z : Set ℕ} (hZ : REPred (· ∈ Z))`: a computably enumerable set: membership in $Z$ is the domain of a partial computable function.
- Left side `ComputableIn {Z.oracle} g`: $g$ is computable relative to the single oracle `Z.oracle`, the characteristic function of $Z$ (value $1$ on $Z$, $0$ off it) as a total partial function; that is, $g \le_T Z$.
- Right side: there are `f : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` and `m : ℕ → ℕ` with `Computable₂ f`, $f$ computable as a function of the pair $(s, x)$, stage first; `ComputableIn {Z.oracle} m`, $m \le_T Z$; and `IsModulus f g m`, which unfolds to $f_s(x) = g(x)$ for all $x$ and all $s \ge m(x)$: the approximation settles at $x$ by stage $m(x)$.

This is Lemma III.3.2 of Soare for total natural-valued functions: if $A$ is c.e. and $f \le_T A$, then $f$ has a computable approximation with a modulus $m \le_T A$. The declaration adds the converse, the easy direction: a limit with an oracle-computable modulus is oracle-computable.

## What it says
The Witten deformation of the exterior derivative, $d_t = e^{-tf} \circ d \circ e^{tf}$, as a linear map from smooth $k$-forms to smooth $(k+1)$-forms.

- `{E H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [TopologicalSpace H] {I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H} {M : Type*} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]` (section variables): a manifold $M$ modelled on $E$ through the model with corners $I$.
- `[IsManifold I 2 M]`: the charts are compatible to order $C^2$, the regularity under which Tau Ceti defines the exterior derivative of smooth forms.
- `(f : C^∞⟮I, M; ℝ⟯)`: a smooth real function on $M$; `(t : ℝ)`: a real parameter; `(k : ℕ)`: the degree.
- Value: a linear map `SmoothForm I M ℝ k →ₗ[ℝ] SmoothForm I M ℝ (k + 1)`, the composite of `expSMulEquiv k f t`, multiplication of $k$-forms by $e^{tf}$, then `mextDerivₗ I k`, the exterior derivative, then `expSMulEquiv (k + 1) f (-t)`, multiplication by $e^{-tf}$: $d_t \varphi = e^{-tf}\, d(e^{tf} \varphi)$.

This is the deformed differential of Witten, §2, with his sign, so that $d_t = d + t\, df \wedge$. No metric enters; the Witten Laplacian, which needs one, is not defined here. Being conjugate to $d$, $d_t$ squares to zero and its cohomology is de Rham cohomology.

## Lean subtleties
- The sign convention is Witten's, $e^{-tf} d e^{tf}$; the other convention $e^{tf} d e^{-tf}$ is $t \mapsto -t$ here and gives $d - t\, df \wedge$.
- `SmoothForm I M ℝ k` are the $C^\infty$ $k$-forms with real coefficients, as a real vector space; `C^∞⟮I, M; ℝ⟯` is Mathlib's type of smooth maps $M \to \mathbb{R}$.
- Since $e^{tf}$ never vanishes, `expSMulEquiv` is an automorphism and no junk value arises; the definition is `noncomputable` only because real exponentials are. $t$ may be negative or zero, and $M$ may be empty.

## What it says
For a scheme $X$ and an ideal sheaf $I$ on $X$, the formal completion of $X$ along the closed subscheme $V(I)$, kept as the tower of its infinitesimal neighbourhoods $V(I^{n+1})$.

- `(X : Scheme)`: a scheme, in universe `u`.
- `(I : X.IdealSheafData)`: a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf on $X$, an ideal of $\Gamma(X, U)$ for each affine open $U$, compatible with restriction.
- The value is an `AdicThickeningSystem` with four fields: level `X n` is `(I ^ (n + 1)).subscheme`, the closed subscheme $V(I^{n+1})$; transition `ι n` is the `inclusion` $V(I^{n+1}) \to V(I^{n+2})$ given by $I^{n+2} \le I^{n+1}$; and two proofs, that each transition is a thickening (a surjective closed immersion) and that the tower is adic: the ideal sheaf of $V(I^{n+1})$ in $V(I^{n+2})$ is the $(n+1)$-st power of that of $V(I)$.

Stacks, Lemma 87.14.2 and Definition 87.14.3, form the completion $X_{/V(I)}$ as the colimit of the $V(I^{n+1})$, a formal scheme; the Lean object retains the levels and inclusions as data in place of that colimit, as its docstring says.

## What it says
A subgroup $\Lambda$ of a group $G$ has relative property (T) when every unitary representation of $G$ with almost invariant vectors has a nonzero vector fixed by $\Lambda$.

- `{G : Type v} [Group G]`: a group without topology, the discrete case.
- `(Λ : Subgroup G)`: a subgroup.
- The value is the proposition: for every `H : Type u` with `[NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]`, a complex Hilbert space in universe `u`, and every `ρ : ContRepresentation ℂ G H`, a homomorphism from $G$ to the bounded operators on $H$, if `ρ.IsUnitary` (each $\rho(g)$ preserves the inner product) and `ρ.HasAlmostInvariantVectors` (for every finite $F \subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ some unit vector $v$ has $\|\rho(g)v - v\| < \varepsilon$ for all $g \in F$), then some $v \ne 0$ lies in `(ρ.restrict Λ.subtype).invariants`: $\rho(g)v = v$ for all $g \in \Lambda$.

This is Definition 14.1.1 of Anantharaman–Popa for discrete groups, and Section 1.4 of Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette read for discrete $G$, where every unitary representation is continuous. Property (T) of $G$ is the case $\Lambda = G$.

- A `ContRepresentation` is a monoid homomorphism into continuous linear maps: continuity of each operator, nothing about $g \mapsto \rho(g)$, so $G$ needs no topology.

- $H = 0$ has no unit vector, so `HasAlmostInvariantVectors` fails there; for $\Lambda = \bot$ every vector is fixed, and almost invariant vectors force $H \ne 0$.

## What it says
The primitive central idempotent $e_\rho$ of an irreducible representation $\rho$ acts on any representation $\sigma$ as a projection whose image is the $\rho$-isotypic component of $\sigma$.

- `{k : Type u_1} [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k]`: an algebraically closed field.
- `{G : Type u_2} [Group G] [Fintype G] [Invertible (Nat.card G : k)]`: a finite group whose order is invertible in $k$.
- `{V : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup V] [Module k V] [FiniteDimensional k V]`, `(ρ : Representation k G V) [ρ.IsIrreducible]`: a finite-dimensional irreducible representation.
- `{W : Type u_4} [AddCommGroup W] [Module k W]`, `(σ : Representation k G W)`: any representation, with no finiteness.
- The conclusion: `LinearMap.range (σ.asAlgebraHom (primitiveCentralIdempotent ρ))`, the image of $\sigma(e_\rho)$ for $e_\rho = (\chi(1)/|G|) \sum_g \chi(g^{-1})\, g$ and `asAlgebraHom` the extension of $\sigma$ to $k[G]$, equals `isotypicComponent k[G] σ.asModule ρ.asModule`, the sum of the $k[G]$-submodules of $W$ isomorphic to $\rho$, read as a $k$-subspace of $W$ by `restrictScalars k` and `comap σ.asModuleEquiv.symm`.

This is Serre, §2.6, Theorem 8: $p_i = (n_i/g)\sum_t \chi_i(t)^* \rho_t$ projects $V$ onto $V_i$. Serre works over $\mathbb{C}$ with $V$ finite-dimensional; here $k$ is any algebraically closed field of good characteristic, $W$ is arbitrary, and $\chi(g^{-1})$ replaces $\overline{\chi(g)}$.

## What it says
For $\Gamma \le \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with a compact convex fundamental polygon $P$, the area of $\Gamma \backslash \mathbb{H}$ is $2\pi\bigl(-\chi + \sum_e (1 - 1/m_e)\bigr)$ over the elliptic orbits $e$ with stabiliser orders $m_e$.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n] {P : CompactConvexPolygon n}`: a convex hyperbolic polygon with $n \ge 3$ vertices in $\mathbb{H}$.
- `(σ : P.toConvexPolygon.SidePairing)`: an involution `pair` of the sides with maps `map i ∈ PSL(2, ℝ)` carrying side $i$ onto side `pair i`, `map (pair i) = (map i)⁻¹`.
- `{Γ : Subgroup PSL(2, ℝ)}`, `(hmap : ∀ i, σ.map i ∈ Γ)`: the pairing maps lie in $\Gamma$.
- `(hlf : LocallyFinite fun γ : Γ ↦ γ • P.carrier)`: the translates of $P$ are locally finite.
- `(hdisj : ∀ γ : Γ, γ ≠ 1 → Disjoint (γ • interior P.carrier) (interior P.carrier))`: translates have disjoint interiors.
- The conclusion: `covolume Γ ℍ`, the area of a fundamental domain, equals `ENNReal.ofReal` of $2\pi(-\chi + \sum_e (1 - 1/m_e))$, with $\chi$ the `eulerChar` of the orbit space `orbitRel.Quotient Γ ℍ`, whose finite CW type the statement supplies from the same hypotheses; `Γ.ellipticOrbits` are the orbits with nontrivial stabiliser, of order `cardStabilizerOnOrbit e`.

Beardon and Katok give the area of a cocompact Fuchsian group of signature $(g; m_1, \dots, m_r)$ as $2\pi(2g - 2 + \sum (1 - 1/m_i))$. Here $-\chi$ stands for $2g - 2$; the identification $\chi = 2 - 2g$ is not part of the statement, and cusps are excluded by the compactness of $P$, as the docstring says.

## What it says
On a σ-finite measure space, for conjugate exponents $1 < p, q < \infty$, integration against an $L^p$ function is an isometric isomorphism of $L^p$ onto the continuous dual of $L^q$.

- `{α : Type u_1} {mα : MeasurableSpace α} (μ : Measure α) [SigmaFinite μ]`: a σ-finite measure.
- `(𝕜 : Type u_2) [RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalars, $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `(p q : ℝ≥0∞) [Fact (1 ≤ p)] [Fact (1 ≤ q)] [p.HolderConjugate q]`: extended exponents at least $1$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.
- `(hq : 1 < q) (hq_top : q ≠ ∞)`: $q$ strictly between $1$ and $\infty$, hence so is $p$.
- The value, `Lp 𝕜 p μ ≃ₗᵢ[𝕜] StrongDual 𝕜 (Lp 𝕜 q μ)`, is a $\mathbb{k}$-linear isometric equivalence from $L^p(\mu)$ onto the continuous linear functionals on $L^q(\mu)$ with the operator norm, sending $g$ to $f \mapsto \int g f\, d\mu$: the isometric embedding `toDual` made an equivalence by `toDual_surjective`.

This is the $L^p$ duality theorem, Folland Theorem 6.15 and Rudin Theorem 6.16, stated there for σ-finite $\mu$ and $1 \le q < \infty$. Here $1 < q < \infty$ only, where σ-finiteness could be dropped; the Lean keeps it as the textbooks state it.

## What it says
Young's inequality for convolution with an integrable function: $\|f \ast g\|_p \le \|L\|\,\|f\|_1\,\|g\|_p$ for $1 \le p \le \infty$.

- `{𝕜} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]`, `{E E' F}` normed spaces over $\mathbb{k}$, with `[NormedSpace ℝ F]` so that $F$-valued integrals make sense.
- `(L : E →L[𝕜] E' →L[𝕜] F)`: a continuous bilinear map, the product in the convolution.
- `{f : G → E} {g : G → E'}`: the two functions.
- `[AddGroup G] [MeasurableSpace G] [MeasurableAdd₂ G] [MeasurableNeg G]`: a measurable additive group.
- `{μ : Measure G} [SigmaFinite μ] [μ.IsAddRightInvariant]`: a σ-finite measure with $\mu(s + t) = \mu(s)$.
- `(hf : AEStronglyMeasurable f μ) (hg : AEStronglyMeasurable g μ)`: measurability only, no integrability.
- `{p : ℝ≥0∞} (hp : 1 ≤ p)`: the exponent, $\infty$ allowed.
- The conclusion: `eLpNorm (f ⋆[L, μ] g) p μ`, the $L^p$ norm in $[0,\infty]$ of $x \mapsto \int L(f(t))(g(x - t))\, d\mu(t)$, is at most $\|L\|_e\,\|f\|_1\,\|g\|_p$, with `‖L‖ₑ` the operator norm of $L$ in $[0,\infty]$.

Folland, Proposition 8.7, states this for scalar functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $f \in L^1$, $g \in L^p$. The Lean form holds on any measurable group with a σ-finite right-invariant measure, vector-valued through $L$, and in $[0,\infty]$, so without integrability. It is the case $q = 1$, $r = p$ of the general Young inequality $1/p + 1/q = 1 + 1/r$ (Lieb–Loss, Theorem 4.2), as the docstring's "with an integrable function" says.

## Lean subtleties
- All three norms are in $[0,\infty]$: when $f \notin L^1$ or $g \notin L^p$ the right side is $\infty$ and the inequality says nothing.
- The Bochner integral defining the convolution is $0$ where the integrand is not integrable; the pointwise bound still holds, so the inequality is true as stated.
- `eLpNorm f 1 μ` is $\int \|f\|_e\, d\mu$; at $p = \infty$ the norm is the essential supremum.
- The measure is right-invariant, matching the variable $x - t$; on a commutative group this is left-invariance.

## What it says
Over a complex Hopf star algebra with a nonzero positive right invariant integral, every comodule with a finite basis has a basis whose coefficient matrix is unitary: finite corepresentations are unitarizable.

- `{A : Type u_1} [Ring A] [StarRing A] [HopfAlgebra ℂ A] [StarModule ℂ A] [StarCoalgebra ℂ A]`: a complex Hopf algebra with a conjugate-linear involution $a \mapsto a^*$ with $\Delta(a^*) = \Delta(a)^*$.
- `{M : Type u_2} [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℂ M] [Comodule ℂ A M]`: a comodule over $A$ with coaction $\delta$.
- `{ι : Type u_3} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]`: a finite index type.
- `{h : A →ₗ[ℂ] ℂ} (hh : h.IsRightInvariantIntegral)`: a linear functional with $(h \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta(a) = h(a)\,1$.
- `(h0 : h ≠ 0) (hpos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ h (star a * a))`: nonzero and positive.
- `(b : Basis ι ℂ M)`: a basis of $M$.
- The conclusion: a basis `c` indexed by the same `ι` whose `coefficientMatrix` $u \in M_\iota(A)$, with $\delta(c_j) = \sum_i c_i \otimes u_{ij}$, lies in `unitary (Matrix ι ι A)`: $u^* u = 1 = u u^*$ for the conjugate transpose $u^*$.

This is the algebraic unitarization of Timmermann, Proposition 2.2.4 and §3.2, and Klimyk–Schmüdgen §11.1: over a Hopf $*$-algebra with a positive Haar functional every finite-dimensional corepresentation is equivalent to a unitary one.

- No norm or completion of $A$ enters.
- For `ι` empty, $M = 0$ and the empty matrix is unitary.
- The new basis comes from `Matrix.inv`, whose junk value for singular matrices is not reached, $P$ being invertible.

## What it says
The pro-category of a category $C$, realised as the opposite of the ind-category of $C^{\mathrm{op}}$.

- `(C : Type u) [Category.{v} C]`: a category with objects in universe `u` and morphisms in universe `v`.
- The value: `(Ind Cᵒᵖ)ᵒᵖ`, a category in `Type (max 0 u (v + 1))`. Mathlib's `Ind D` is the category of ind-objects of $D$: presheaves on $D$ that are filtered colimits of representables, with morphisms shrunk to universe `v`. For $D = C^{\mathrm{op}}$ these are the functors $C \to \mathrm{Type}$ that are filtered colimits of corepresentables $\mathrm{Hom}(c, -)$, that is, formal cofiltered limits $``\lim" Y_i$ of objects of $C$; reversing the arrows gives $\mathrm{Hom}(``\lim" Y_i, ``\lim" Z_j) = \lim_j \operatorname{colim}_i \mathrm{Hom}(Y_i, Z_j)$.

This is the definition of Kashiwara–Schapira, Chapter 6, where $\mathrm{Pro}(C) = \mathrm{Ind}(C^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}$ by duality, and the pro-category of Scholze's Proposition 7.10. The double-limit formula for morphisms is not among the recorded declarations.

## References and tests
- M. Kashiwara and P. Schapira, *Categories and Sheaves*, Chapter 6, by duality.
- P. Scholze, *Étale cohomology of diamonds*, §7, Proposition 7.10.
- Roadmap: [AdicSpacesPartII, pro-categories](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/AdicSpacesPartII/README.md#L7795), target `pro-mk`.
- `TauCeti.Pro.const` — the fully faithful embedding of $C$ as constant pro-objects (`TauCeti.Pro.const.fullyFaithful`).
- `TauCeti.Pro.mk` — the pro-object of a small cofiltered diagram $I \to C$.
- `TauCeti.Pro.mkConeIsLimit` — its stage projections make it the limit of the constant objects of the stages.
- `TauCeti.Pro.mkConstIso` — a constant diagram presents the constant pro-object.
- Check *Pro_two_to_three_hom_card*, `TauCeti/Examples/CategoryTheory/Pro.lean:25` — passes, as an untagged `example`: nine maps between the constant two- and three-element sets.
- Check *Pro_empty_to_point_unique*, `TauCeti/Examples/CategoryTheory/Pro.lean:32` — passes, untagged: one map from the constant empty set to the point.
- Check *Pro_point_to_empty_no_map*, `TauCeti/Examples/CategoryTheory/Pro.lean:37` — passes, untagged: no map the other way.
- Check *s0_13_pro_flatten_projection*, `TauCeti/Examples/CategoryTheory/Pro.lean:62` — passes, untagged: on the constant Boolean tower, negation induces a map other than the identity.

## Lean subtleties
- `Pro C` is an `abbrev`: Lean unfolds it to `(Ind Cᵒᵖ)ᵒᵖ`, so a morphism of pro-objects is the `op` of a morphism of ind-objects of $C^{\mathrm{op}}$, with composition reversed.
- Objects are not diagrams: a diagram gives an object through `Pro.mk`.
- Indexing categories must be small (`I : Type v`) and cofiltered; `C` itself may be large. `Type (max 0 u (v + 1))` is one universe above the morphisms of $C$.
- No choice is involved; the category structure on `Ind` is noncomputable.

## What it says
The Sard–Smale theorem at Smale's sharp regularity, in index at most two: the critical values of such a Fredholm map between Banach manifolds are meagre.

- `{n : ℕ∞ω}`: the regularity: a natural number, $\infty$ or $\omega$.
- `{E} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E]`, `{I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H} [I.Boundaryless]`: a real Banach model without boundary; `E'`, `J` likewise.
- `{M} [ChartedSpace H M] [IsManifold I 1 M] [HereditarilyLindelofSpace M]`: a $C^1$ manifold all of whose subspaces are Lindelöf, as for second-countable ones; `N` a $C^1$ manifold.
- `{f : M → N}`, `(hf : ContMDiff I J n f)`: $f$ is $C^n$.
- `(hFred : ∀ x, (mfderiv I J f x).IsFredholm)`: the derivative is Fredholm at every point: closed range, finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel.
- `(hindex : ∀ x, (mfderiv I J f x).index ≤ 2)`: the index $\dim\ker - \dim\operatorname{coker}$ is at most $2$.
- `(hn : ∀ x, ((mfderiv I J f x).index.toNat + 1 : ℕ) ≤ n)`: $n > \max(\mathrm{index}, 0)$ at every point.
- The conclusion: `IsMeagre (f '' {x | ¬ IsRegularPoint I J f x})`: the image of the points with non-surjective derivative is meagre.

Smale's Theorem 1.3 states this for a $C^q$ Fredholm map on a second-countable manifold with $q > \max(\mathrm{index}, 0)$ and no bound on the index. The Lean statement adds `index ≤ 2`, which its name and docstring carry, and lets the index vary with the point; hereditarily Lindelöf is weaker than second countable.

## References and tests
- S. Smale, *An infinite dimensional version of Sard's theorem*, Amer. J. Math. 87 (1965), Theorem 1.3.
- D. McDuff and D. Salamon, *J-holomorphic Curves and Symplectic Topology*, 2nd ed., Appendix A.5.
- Roadmap: [HeegaardFloer §2.2 (F0.0)](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/HeegaardFloer/README.md#L1388), target `sharp_sardSmale`.
- `ContMDiff.mem_residual_setOf_isRegularValue_of_index_le_two` — the equivalent form: the regular values are residual.
- `TauCeti.isMeagre_image_of_not_isRegularPoint_of_index_le_two` — the local form on a Lindelöf set.

The README's three Checks (the identity of $\mathbb{R}$, $t \mapsto (t, 0)$ of index $-1$, the zero map $\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ at $k = 3$) carry no tags; no `example` carrying them was found at this commit.

## Lean subtleties
- `index.toNat` sends a negative index to $0$, so for negative index `hn` asks only $n \ge 1$.
- `IsRegularPoint` is surjectivity of `mfderiv`, which is $0$ where $f$ is not differentiable; `hn` forces $n \ge 1$, so that does not occur.
- `IsMeagre s` means the complement of $s$ is residual in $N$; $N$ is not assumed Baire, so meagre sets are small only when it is.

## What it says
A continuous self-map of a nonempty closed convex set in a real normed space, whose image is relatively compact, has a fixed point.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {C : Set E}` (section variables): a real normed space $E$, not assumed complete, and a subset $C$.
- `(hC : IsClosed C) (hconv : Convex ℝ C) (hne : C.Nonempty)`: $C$ is closed, convex and nonempty.
- `{f : E → E} (hf : ContinuousOn f C) (hfC : MapsTo f C C)`: a function on all of $E$, continuous at the points of $C$ relative to $C$, with $f(C) \subseteq C$.
- `(hK : IsCompact (closure (f '' C)))`: the closure of the image $f(C)$ is compact.
- Conclusion `∃ x ∈ C, IsFixedPt f x`: some $x \in C$ has $f(x) = x$.

This is Schauder's theorem as in Corollary 11.2 of Gilbarg–Trudinger, which is stated for a closed convex set in a Banach space with precompact image. Here $E$ need not be complete: the compactness of $\overline{f(C)}$ is assumed outright, which is what completeness is used for in the book. The roadmap target asks in addition that $C$ be bounded; neither the book's corollary nor this statement needs that. Their Theorem 11.1, for compact convex $C$, is the specialisation below.

## References and tests
- J. Schauder, *Der Fixpunktsatz in Funktionalräumen*, Studia Math. 2 (1930), 171–180.
- D. Gilbarg and N. S. Trudinger, *Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order*, Theorem 11.1 and Corollary 11.2.
- Roadmap: [BanachAlgebras, §8.2 "Schauder and Lomonosov"](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/eaf17b10d9267c0e3cdd3b62dd5e8983e47c690d/TauCetiRoadmap/BanachAlgebras/README.md#L1964), target `schauder_fixedPoint`, stated there for a closed bounded convex set in a real Banach space.
- `TauCeti.schauderFixedPoint_compactConvex` — the compact-convex specialisation, in any dimension.
- `TauCeti.schauderFixedPoint_closedConvex` — the same for a bundled map `C(C, C)`, by extending the map by the identity off $C$.
- `TauCeti.leraySchauderFixedPoint_closedBall` — the Leray–Schauder form on a ball, by applying this theorem to $T$ followed by the radial retraction.

The roadmap's Checks ($C = \{0\}$, $f = 0$ gives the fixed point $0$; $C = \emptyset$ shows nonemptiness cannot be dropped) have no `example` carrying them.

## Lean subtleties
- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]` are typeclass hypotheses; no `CompleteSpace E` is assumed.
- `f` is a total function `E → E` and only its values on $C$ matter; `f '' C` is the image $f(C)$.
- `IsFixedPt f x` unfolds to `f x = x`; `Convex ℝ C` is convexity for real scalars.
- The zero space is allowed: then $C = \{0\}$ and $0$ is the fixed point.

## What it says
Equality in the isodiametric inequality, almost-everywhere form: a bounded null-measurable set has the measure of a closed ball of radius half its diameter exactly when it agrees almost everywhere with such a ball.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]` (section variables): a finite-dimensional real inner product space with its Borel σ-algebra.
- `(μ : Measure E) [μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]`: an additive Haar measure on $E$, such as Lebesgue measure; it is explicit.
- `{s : Set E} (hs : Bornology.IsBounded s)`: a bounded set, so that `diam s` is its diameter.
- `(hsm : NullMeasurableSet s μ)`: $s$ differs from a measurable set by a $\mu$-null set.
- `(x : E)`: any centre; the measure of a closed ball does not depend on it.
- Conclusion: $\mu(s) = \mu\bigl(\overline{B}(x, \operatorname{diam}(s)/2)\bigr)$ if and only if there is $c$ with $s =^{\mu\text{-a.e.}} \overline{B}(c, \operatorname{diam}(s)/2)$, that is, the symmetric difference is null.

The isodiametric inequality, `addHaar_le_addHaar_closedBall_diam_div_two` in the same file, says $\mu(s)$ is at most this ball measure for every bounded $s$; this is its equality case. The literature states equality for compact sets, as the closed-set form in the same file does; the a.e. form is the measure-theoretic version, with the radius tied to the diameter of $s$ itself, since a null modification can enlarge the diameter without changing the measure.

## References and tests
- R. J. Gardner, *The Brunn–Minkowski inequality*, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. **39** (2002), 355–405, for the difference-body argument from Brunn–Minkowski.
- R. Schneider, *Convex Bodies: The Brunn–Minkowski Theory*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 2014, Theorem 7.1.1, for the equality case of Brunn–Minkowski for convex bodies, which the forward direction uses.
- `MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_eq_addHaar_closedBall_diam_div_two_iff_exists_eq` — the closed-set form: for a nonempty closed bounded $s$, equality holds exactly when $s$ is a closed ball of radius $\operatorname{diam}(s)/2$.
- `MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_subset_closedBall_diam_div_two_of_addHaar_ge` — the containment behind the forward direction: a bounded set with at least the ball's measure lies in a closed ball of radius half its diameter.
- `MeasureTheory.Measure.addHaar_le_addHaar_closedBall_diam_div_two` — the inequality this is the equality case of.

No roadmap Checks are recorded for this declaration.

## Lean subtleties
- `Metric.diam s` is $0$ for an unbounded set; `hs` rules that out. For $s = \emptyset$ the diameter is $0$ and the ball is a point, null in positive dimension, so both sides hold; in dimension $0$ the point is the whole space and both sides fail.
- `s =ᵐ[μ] t` is `ae_eq_set`: the two symmetric differences are $\mu$-null; it is weaker than equality, which the closed-set form recovers.
- `IsAddHaarMeasure` is a typeclass hypothesis: $\mu$ is translation invariant, finite on compacts and positive on opens, so `addHaar_closedBall_center` makes the centre irrelevant.
- Null measurability of $s$ is needed only for the forward direction, through `ae_eq_closedBall_of_subset_of_measure_eq`; the inequality itself needs none.

## What it says
Let $X$ be a topological space with a measurable structure, $\mu$ a measure on $X$ and $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ a function that is $\mu$-a.e. measurable and $\mu$-a.e. nonzero. Then the measure $f\,d\mu$ has the same topological support as $\mu$, i.e. the set of points all of whose neighbourhoods have positive measure is unchanged by the weight. This is the standard fact that $f\,d\mu$ and $\mu$ are mutually absolutely continuous when $f>0$ a.e., together with the monotonicity of the support under absolute continuity.

## References and tests
- Mutual absolute continuity of $\mu$ and $f\,d\mu$ for a.e. positive $f$ is given by Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.withDensity_absolutelyContinuous` and `MeasureTheory.withDensity_absolutelyContinuous'`.
- No named test declaration; the closure-type support lemmas of the same file are consequences for explicit densities.

## Lean subtleties
`Measure.support` is the topological support. $\infty$ is allowed as a value of $f$ and counts as nonzero. The a.e. measurability hypothesis is exactly what Mathlib needs to make $\mu \ll f\,d\mu$ (for non-measurable $f$ the weighted measure is built from lower integrals and the statement is not claimed). No further hypothesis on $\mu$ or the topology is needed; for $\mu=0$ both supports are empty.

## What it says
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space and $w:\alpha\to\mathbb R$ a function that is $\mu$-almost everywhere measurable and $\mu$-almost everywhere strictly positive. Write $\mu_w$ for the measure with density $\max(w,0)$ with respect to $\mu$, that is $\mu_w(A)=\int_A \max(w,0)\,d\mu$. Then $\mu\ll\mu_w$: every set that $\mu_w$ gives measure zero already has $\mu$-measure zero. The converse $\mu_w\ll\mu$ always holds for a weighted measure, so the two measures are mutually absolutely continuous. The reason is that the weight vanishes only on a $\mu$-null set, so weighting destroys no null sets. This is the standard fact that a density positive almost everywhere gives an equivalent measure.

## References and tests
- The proof is Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.withDensity_absolutelyContinuous'` (the case of an a.e. nonzero extended-real density), applied to the density $\mathrm{ofReal}\circ w$.
- No named test declaration of the library records this statement; it is used as a building block by the weighted $L^2$ isometry and Gaussian, Chebyshev and Gamma-type density files.

## Lean subtleties
`ENNReal.ofReal` truncates negative reals to $0$; this is harmless here because positivity of $w$ almost everywhere is a hypothesis, and positivity is what makes `ofReal (w x)` nonzero almost everywhere. The density takes values in $[0,\infty)$, never $\infty$. No finiteness or $\sigma$-finiteness of $\mu$ is needed. Measurability of $w$ is only required almost everywhere (`AEMeasurable`).

## What it says
Over a semiring `R`, let `S ⊆ R` and let `U` be an additive submonoid of `R` such that `r x ∈ U` for every `x ∈ S` and every `r ∈ R`. Then the left ideal generated by `S` is contained in `U`. This is true because the left ideal is the additive closure of the left multiples of the generators.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Submodule.span_eq_closure` (the span as an additive closure of scalar multiples) is used.

## Lean subtleties
In Lean, `Ideal R` over a possibly noncommutative semiring means a left ideal, `span` is the left ideal generated, and the product of ideals is the span of the pairwise products; `[I.IsTwoSided]` is the assumption that `I` is also a right ideal (automatic over a commutative ring).

## What it says
Let `I` be a two-sided ideal of a semiring and `J` a left ideal with `I J = (1)`. Then `I = (1)`. Indeed `I J ⊆ I` because `I` is a right ideal, so `(1) ⊆ I`.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Ideal.mul_le_left` (`I * J ≤ I` for two-sided `I`) gives the inclusion used.

## Lean subtleties
In Lean, `Ideal R` over a possibly noncommutative semiring means a left ideal, `span` is the left ideal generated, and the product of ideals is the span of the pairwise products; `[I.IsTwoSided]` is the assumption that `I` is also a right ideal (automatic over a commutative ring). The unit ideal `1` is `⊤` (`Ideal.one_eq_top`).

## What it says
In a semiring `A`, the left ideal generated by a set `s` of central elements is two-sided. Indeed for central `z` one has `z b = b z`, so right multiples of generators are left multiples.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Semigroup.mem_center_iff` (centrality) and `Submodule.span_induction` are used.

## Lean subtleties
The conclusion is a typeclass-valued property `(span s).IsTwoSided`, which is a `Prop` field: right multiples of members stay in the ideal. `Set.center A` is the multiplicative center.

## What it says
The sum `I + J` of two two-sided ideals of a semiring is two-sided. It provides the typeclass instance (at low priority) so that `IsTwoSided` is inferred for sums.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
In Lean, `Ideal R` over a possibly noncommutative semiring means a left ideal, `span` is the left ideal generated, and the product of ideals is the span of the pairwise products; `[I.IsTwoSided]` is the assumption that `I` is also a right ideal (automatic over a commutative ring).

## What it says
In a commutative semiring, an element `f` lies in the square of the ideal `(u, v)` iff `f = a u² + b u v + c v²` for some `a, b, c`: the square is spanned by the three monomials `u², u v, v²`, which is the standard description of the square of a two-generated ideal.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Ideal.span_pair_mul_span_pair` (product of two pair ideals is spanned by the four products) is used.

## Lean subtleties
`^ 2` is the ideal power, i.e. `I * I`, not the set of squares.

## What it says
In a commutative semiring, for a pair `(v₀, v₁)` the square of the ideal they generate consists exactly of the elements `a v₀² + b v₀ v₁ + c v₁²`. This is the standard description of the square of a two-generated ideal.

## References and tests
- Mathlib's `Ideal.span_pair_mul_span_pair` and `Submodule.mem_span_triple` are used.

## Lean subtleties
The generators are given as a function `Fin 2 → R`; `^ 2` is the ideal power `I * I`, not the set of squares.

## What it says
Over a commutative semiring `R`, for ideals `I`, `J`, regard `I` as an `R`-module. Then the submodule `J • I` of the module `I` is the preimage, under the inclusion `I → R`, of the product ideal `I J`; that is, an element of `I` lies in `J • I` iff it lies in `I J`.

## References and tests

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- The inverse is a total function in Lean; outside the target its value is the junk value of `e.symm`, but the stated equality holds for every $v \in E$ since both sides are defined by the same formula.

## What it says
For a maximal-atlas chart $e$ with boundaryless model, the target of `e.toPartialDiffeomorphOfMemMaximalAtlas he` is the set of $v \in E$ with $I^{-1}(v)$ in the target of $e$, that is $(I^{-1})^{-1}(e.\mathrm{target})$.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- `I.symm` is the inverse of the model embedding, a total function on $E$ (the model is boundaryless, so $I$ is onto $E$); the preimage is the genuine one.

## What it says
If $\Phi : M \to N'$ is a $C^n$ partial diffeomorphism and $e$ is a chart of the $C^n$ maximal atlas of $N'$, then the composite $e \circ \Phi$ is a chart of the $C^n$ maximal atlas of $M$.

- `[IsManifold I n M]`: $M$ is a $C^n$ manifold.
- `Φ`: a partial diffeomorphism with $C^n$ forward and inverse maps on open source and target.
- `he`: $e$ belongs to the maximal atlas of $N'$.
- The conclusion: `Φ.toOpenPartialHomeomorph.trans e` belongs to the maximal atlas of $M$.

The composite is smooth in both directions by chain rule on open subsets.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- The composite chart has source $\{x \in \Phi.\mathrm{source} : \Phi(x) \in e.\mathrm{source}\}$.
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic.

## What it says
Given an open partial homeomorphism $\Theta$ from the vector space $E$ to the vector space $F$ (over $\mathbb{K}$) such that $\Theta$ is $C^n$ on its source and $\Theta^{-1}$ is $C^n$ on its target, this is $\Theta$ regarded as a partial diffeomorphism between the manifolds $E$ and $F$ with their canonical model with corners.

- `Θ : OpenPartialHomeomorph E F`: a homeomorphism between open subsets of $E$ and $F$.
- `hΘ`, `hΘsymm`: $C^n$ in the usual (Fréchet) sense on the source, respectively the target.
- The value: the same partial equivalence, with manifold smoothness (`ContMDiffOn`) proved from `ContDiffOn`.

## References and tests
None. The underlying partial equivalence is `TauCeti.PartialDiffeomorph.ofOpenPartialHomeomorph_toPartialEquiv`.

## Lean subtleties
- The spaces $E$ and $F$ are regarded as manifolds modelled on themselves via `𝓘(𝕂, E)`, so manifold and Fréchet smoothness agree (`contMDiffOn_iff_contDiffOn`).
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic.

## What it says
The partial equivalence underlying `PartialDiffeomorph.ofOpenPartialHomeomorph Θ hΘ hΘsymm` is the one of $\Theta$.

## References and tests
None. It is used for the definition `TauCeti.PartialDiffeomorph.ofOpenPartialHomeomorph`.

## Lean subtleties
- None; this is the defining equation.

## What it says
For a bijective local diffeomorphism $f : M \to N$ ($C^n$, with models with corners $I, J$), the diffeomorphism that Mathlib builds from it by `IsLocalDiffeomorph.diffeomorphOfBijective` has forward map $f$.

- `hf`: $f$ is a $C^n$ local diffeomorphism (every point has a $C^n$ partial diffeomorphism agreeing with $f$ nearby).
- `hf'`: $f$ is bijective.
- The conclusion: the coercion of the resulting diffeomorphism to a function is $f$.

This says that the constructor only chooses an inverse, which is unique as $f$ is bijective.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- `hf` and `hf'` are implicit arguments: they are proofs, found by unification. `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic.

## What it says
The forward map of `extChartPartialDiffeomorph I n x` is the extended chart `extChartAt I x`, as a function on all of $M$.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- Partial maps are total functions in Lean; the equality is of these total functions, so it also includes values outside the source.

## What it says
For a $C^n$ manifold $M$ with model with corners $I$ and a point $x \in M$, the extended chart $\varphi_x = I \circ e_x$ at $x$, restricted to the points whose coordinates lie in the interior of the chart's target, as a partial diffeomorphism from $M$ to the model vector space $E$ (a $C^n$ diffeomorphism between open subsets, in both directions).

- `(I : ModelWithCorners 𝕂 E H)`, `(n : WithTop ℕ∞)`, `[IsManifold I n M]`: the model and the smoothness class, with $M$ a $C^n$ manifold.
- `(x : M)`: the base point of the chart.
- The value: the partial equivalence `extChartAt I x` cut down to the preimage of the interior of its target, so that source and target are open.

At a boundary point the restriction does not contain $x$; see `TauCeti.mem_extChartPartialDiffeomorph_source`. For a boundaryless model it is the whole extended chart.

## References and tests
None. Its source, target, forward map and inverse are computed by `TauCeti.extChartPartialDiffeomorph_source`, `TauCeti.extChartPartialDiffeomorph_target`, `TauCeti.coe_extChartPartialDiffeomorph` and `TauCeti.extChartPartialDiffeomorph_symm_apply`.

## Lean subtleties
- The interior is the topological interior in $E$ of the chart target, which is needed since a manifold with boundary has a non-open extended chart target.
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic.

## What it says
The source of `extChartPartialDiffeomorph I n x` is the set of points of the extended chart's source whose chart value lies in the interior of the chart's target: $\{y \in \mathrm{source}_x : \varphi_x(y) \in \mathrm{int}(\mathrm{target}_x)\}$.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- None specific; the statement is a set equality, with no junk values.

## What it says
For $y \in E$, the inverse of `extChartPartialDiffeomorph I n x` at $y$ equals the inverse of the extended chart `extChartAt I x` at $y$.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- The inverse is a total function; the equality is for every $y \in E$, including those outside the target where the value is Lean's arbitrary extension (the same on both sides).

## What it says
The target of `extChartPartialDiffeomorph I n x` is the interior of the target of the extended chart at $x$.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- The interior is taken in the model vector space $E$.

## What it says
For a map $f : M \to N$ which is $C^n$ ($n \ge 1$) on an open set $s$ containing an interior point $x$, $f$ is a $C^n$ local diffeomorphism at $x$ if and only if its differential $Df(x) : T_xM \to T_{f(x)}N$ is a continuous linear isomorphism, that is, equals the underlying map of some continuous linear equivalence $e$.

- `[RCLike 𝕂]`, `[CompleteSpace E]`: scalars $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and a Banach source model space.
- `[IsManifold I n M] [IsManifold J n N]`, `hf`, `hs`, `hx`, `hIx`, `hn`: as in `TauCeti.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_mfderiv_eq`.
- The conclusion: `IsLocalDiffeomorphAt I J n f x ↔ ∃ e, ↑e = mfderiv I J f x`.

The forward direction is Mathlib's `IsLocalDiffeomorphAt.mfderivToContinuousLinearEquiv`; the converse is the inverse function theorem.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_mfderiv_eq` — the converse direction, the inverse function theorem for manifolds.
- `TauCeti.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_pow` — the power map $w \mapsto w^k$ is a local diffeomorphism away from $0$, since its derivative is multiplication by a unit.

## Lean subtleties
- `TangentSpace I x` is $E$ itself, so $e$ identifies $E$ with $F$.
- `mfderiv` is $0$ where $f$ is not differentiable, a junk value; here $f$ is $C^n$ with $n \ge 1$ near $x$, so $Df(x)$ is the true differential.
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic; `1 ≤ n` excludes $n = 0$.

## What it says
If $\Phi : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ partial diffeomorphism, $x$ lies in its source and $f$ agrees with $\Phi$ on the whole source, then $f$ is a $C^n$ local diffeomorphism at $x$.

- `hx : x ∈ Φ.source`: the point is in the source.
- `hf : EqOn f Φ Φ.source`: $f(y) = \Phi(y)$ for every $y$ in the source.
- The conclusion: `IsLocalDiffeomorphAt I J n f x`, whose definition asks exactly for such a $\Phi$.

The lemma is the definition, packaged for use.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- `f` is only compared with $\Phi$ on the source; outside it nothing is claimed.
Approves the standard review `c68ca440ab32537f`.

## What it says
Global inverse function theorem: a $C^n$ map $f : M \to N$ ($n \ge 1$) from a manifold without boundary, all of whose differentials $Df(y) : T_yM \to T_{f(y)}N$ are continuous linear isomorphisms, is a $C^n$ local diffeomorphism, that is, a local diffeomorphism at every point.

- `[RCLike 𝕂]`, `[CompleteSpace E]`, `[IsManifold I n M] [IsManifold J n N]`, `[BoundarylessManifold I M]`: Banach source, $C^n$ manifolds, and $M$ has empty boundary.
- `hf : ContMDiff I J n f`: $f$ is $C^n$ everywhere.
- `hn : 1 ≤ n`.
- `he`: at every point $y$ the differential is the underlying map of a continuous linear equivalence.
- The conclusion: `IsLocalDiffeomorph I J n f`.

The target model $J$ may have boundary; invertibility of the differential forces image points to be interior.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_mfderiv_eq` — the pointwise form, used here at every point with $s$ the whole space.
- `TauCeti.isLocalDiffeomorph_of_deriv_ne_zero` — the one-variable case: a $C^n$ function $\mathbb{K} \to \mathbb{K}$ with nowhere zero derivative is a local diffeomorphism.

## Lean subtleties
- `TangentSpace I y` is $E$ itself.
- `mfderiv` is $0$ at non-differentiable points, but $f$ is $C^n$ with $n \ge 1$ everywhere, so these are true differentials.
- `n : WithTop ℕ∞` includes $\infty$ and analytic.

## What it says
The base point $x$ lies in the source of `extChartPartialDiffeomorph I n x` exactly when $x$ is an interior point of the manifold (its extended chart value lies in the interior of the model range).

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- Interior point is meant in the sense of manifolds with boundary, `I.IsInteriorPoint x`; for a boundaryless model every point is interior and the restricted chart is centred at $x$.
