## What it says
The map `Ring.inverse : ℤ_p → ℤ_p` (inverse of units, `0` on nonunits) is continuous. The reason is that the set of nonunits `pℤ_p` is open, so the map is the continuous inverse on the open set of units and the constant `0` on the open set of nonunits.

## References and tests
- The criterion `NormedRing.continuous_inverse_of_isOpen_nonunits` (in Tau Ceti's `TauCeti/Analysis/Normed/Ring/Units.lean`, not Mathlib): `Ring.inverse` is continuous on a complete normed ring whose nonunits form an open set. `ℤ_p` is a local ring whose maximal ideal `pℤ_p`, the set of nonunits, is open (`IsLocalRing.isOpen_maximalIdeal`).

## Lean subtleties
The value at nonunits is the junk value `0`, so it is *not* an inverse there. Continuity relies on the nonunits being clopen in `ℤ_p`.

## What it says
For probability measures `μ`, `ν` on `ℝ`, the cdf of the convolution (the law of `X + Y` for independent `X ∼ μ`, `Y ∼ ν`) at `x` is `∫ cdf ν (x - y) dμ(y)`, that is `P(X + Y ≤ x) = E[F_Y(x - X)]`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The integrand is bounded and measurable, so the Bochner integral is the genuine integral and no junk value of the integral arises.

## What it says
If almost every sample of the probability measure `ν` is at most `x`, then `F(x) = 1`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
For a probability measure the cdf is the genuine distribution function; no junk value is involved in this statement.

## What it says
If almost every sample of the probability measure `ν` exceeds `x`, then `F(x) = 0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
For a probability measure the cdf is the genuine distribution function; no junk value is involved in this statement.

## What it says
If a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ` gives zero mass to `(-∞, c)`, then `F(x) = 0` for every `x < c`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
For a probability measure the cdf is the genuine distribution function; no junk value is involved in this statement.

## What it says
If an atomless probability measure gives zero mass to `(-∞, c)`, then `F(c) = 0`, because the mass of `(-∞, c]` equals that of `(-∞, c)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The atomless hypothesis (`NullSingletonClass`) is a typeclass; it is the reason the endpoint `c` has no mass.

## What it says
If a probability law on `ℝ` is almost surely in the open interval `(a, b)` and has support exactly `[a, b]`, then `F(x) < 1` iff `x < b`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The almost-sure condition in the open interval excludes atoms at the endpoints, which is why `F(b) = 1` only at `x ≥ b`.

## What it says
If `y` is in the support of a probability measure `μ` on `ℝ` and `x < y`, then `F(x) < 1`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Measure.support` is the topological support.

## What it says
If the cdf of a real measure `ν` is strictly increasing on `[c, ∞)`, then `F(x) < 1` at every `x`, because a strictly increasing function bounded by `1` cannot attain the limit.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
No probability hypothesis is stated; Mathlib's cdf is bounded by `1` for every measure, so the statement is a fact about the Mathlib function.

## What it says
If `μ` is a probability measure, `label` is a.e. measurable, then the cdf of the pushforward law at `x` is the probability that `label ≤ x`: `μ{label ≤ x}`. This is the definition of the distribution function of a random variable.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
A pushforward along a map that is not a.e. measurable is a Dirac mass in Mathlib, not zero, so the a.e. measurability hypothesis is a genuine hypothesis of the statement. `μ.real` is the real-valued measure (`toReal` of the extended measure), harmless for probability measures.

## What it says
For a symmetric probability law `μ` on `ℝ` and `x ≥ 0`, the cdf of `|X|` at `x` is `2F(x) - 1`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Symmetry makes the mass strictly below `-x` equal to `1 - F(x)`, with any atom at `x` handled consistently on both sides. No junk values are involved.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℝ` and `x < 0`, the cdf of `|X|` at `x` is `0`, since `|X| ≥ 0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
For a probability measure the cdf is the genuine distribution function; no junk value is involved in this statement.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℝ` and `x ≥ 0`, the cdf of `|X|` at `x` is `F(x) - P(X < -x)`, the mass of `[-x, x]`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`|·|` is continuous, hence measurable, so the pushforward is the genuine law of `|X|`. `μ.real (Iio (-x))` is the left limit of `F` at `-x`, excluding any atom at `-x`.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℝ` and `s > 0`, the law of `s√Y` has cdf `0` for `x < 0` and `F((x/s)²)` for `x ≥ 0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Real.sqrt` is `0` on negative arguments, so negative values of `Y` are sent to `0` and the stated formula counts them in the mass below `(x/s)²`; this is part of the formula, and for a law carried by `[0, ∞)` it is the usual one.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℤ` viewed on `ℝ` by the cast, the cdf at a real `x` is the mass `μ(-∞, ⌊x⌋]` of the integers up to the floor of `x`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`⌊x⌋` is the integer floor, which is correct at negative `x` (unlike the natural floor, which is `0` there).

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℕ` viewed on `ℝ` by the cast and `x ≥ 0`, the cdf at `x` is `μ{0, …, ⌊x⌋}`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`⌊x⌋₊` is the natural floor; it is `0` for negative `x`, which is why the hypothesis `0 ≤ x` is required, and negative `x` is handled by `cdf_map_natCast_of_neg`.

## What it says
For a probability law on `ℕ` viewed on `ℝ`, the cdf is `0` at every negative point, since no mass lies below `0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
For a probability measure the cdf is the genuine distribution function; no junk value is involved in this statement.

## What it says
If `μ` is a probability law on `ℝ` with no atom at `-x`, the cdf of the reflected law `-X` at `x` is `1 - F(-x)`: `P(-X ≤ x) = P(X ≥ -x) = 1 - P(X < -x) = 1 - F(-x)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`μ.neg` is the pushforward under negation, a measurable map, so no Dirac junk arises. The no-atom hypothesis is needed because `P(X < -x)` and `P(X ≤ -x)` differ by the atom at `-x`.

## What it says
If a probability law on `ℝ` is almost surely in the open interval `(a, b)` and has support exactly `[a, b]`, then `F(x) > 0` iff `x > a`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The almost-sure condition in the open interval excludes atoms at the endpoints, which is why `F(a) = 0`; support equal to the closed interval alone would allow an atom at `a`.

## What it says
If `y` is in the support of a probability measure `μ` on `ℝ` and `y < x`, then `F(x) > 0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Measure.support` is the topological support.

## What it says
For an atomless probability measure `ν` on `ℝ` and a level `y < 1`, the sublevel set `{x : F(x) ≤ y}` has measure `ofReal y`, the extended-real measure `max y 0` (so `0` for `y ≤ 0`). This is the core of the probability integral transform: `F(X)` is uniform for atomless `ν`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The right side is `ENNReal.ofReal y`, which truncates negative `y` to `0`; this agrees with the sublevel set being empty for `y < 0`. The atomless hypothesis is a typeclass (`NullSingletonClass`). The set `{F ≤ y}` is a closed ray `(-∞, q]` because `F` is continuous.

## What it says
For a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ`, its cdf is continuous at `x` exactly when `ν{x} = 0`, that is when `x` is not an atom. The jump of a cdf at `x` is the mass of `{x}`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`ν {x} = 0` is stated in the extended-real measure, where equality with `0` is the usual one.

## What it says
If a probability measure on `ℝ` has no atoms (`NullSingletonClass`), its cdf is continuous.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`NullSingletonClass ν` is the typeclass hypothesis that every singleton is `ν`-null, the Lean form of atomless on `ℝ`.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℕ` and any level `u < 1`, some initial segment `{0, …, k}` has mass at least `u`. This is the existence of a witness for the smallest `k` in a discrete quantile.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Uses the real-valued measure `μ.real`. No junk values arise.

## What it says
For a probability law `μ` on `ℕ` and any `u < 1`, some initial segment `{0, …, n}` has mass strictly greater than `u`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Uses the real-valued measure `μ.real`. No junk values arise.

## What it says
For a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ`, the left limit of `F` at `x`, `F(x-)`, equals `ν(-∞, x)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`leftLim` is Mathlib's one-sided limit from below; for a monotone function it exists, and `μ.real` is the real-valued measure.

## What it says
For a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ`, `ν(-∞, x) ≤ t` iff `F(y) ≤ t` for all `y < x`. This reflects `F(x-) = sup_{y<x} F(y)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The left-hand side uses the real-valued measure `μ.real`. No junk values arise.

## What it says
If `μ` is a symmetric probability law on `ℝ` (invariant under `x ↦ -x`), the mass of `(-∞, -x)` equals `1 - F(x)`, the mass of `(x, ∞)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`μ.real` is the real-valued measure. The open ray `(-∞, -x)` is used, so atoms at `-x` are not counted; for a symmetric law this is consistent with `1 - F(x)`, which excludes an atom at `x` by symmetry.

## What it says
For a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ` and `a ≤ b`, `ν(a, b] = F(b) - F(a)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Real subtraction on `ℝ`, so no truncation. The hypothesis `a ≤ b` is needed because otherwise the interval is empty and the right side is negative.

## What it says
For a probability measure `ν` on `ℝ`, the interval `(a, b]` has positive mass iff `F(a) < F(b)`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
The mass `ν(Ioc a b)` is the extended-real measure, so positivity is the honest statement; when `b ≤ a` both sides are false.

## What it says
For a finite measure `μ` on any measurable space, an a.e. measurable `f : α → ℝ` and any real measure `ν`, the function `x ↦ cdf ν (f x)` lies in `Lᵖ(μ)` for every exponent `p ∈ [0, ∞]`. The reason is that cdf values lie in `[0,1]` and `μ` is finite.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`MemLp` for `p = 0` is only a.e. strong measurability, and `p = ∞` means essentially bounded. No hypothesis on `ν` is needed because Mathlib's cdf is bounded by `0` and `1` for every measure.

## What it says
For every level `t < 1` there is a point `x` with `t ≤ cdf μ x`. This holds because the cdf tends to `1` at `+∞`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Holds for every real measure in Mathlib's formalisation, since the cdf tends to `1` at `+∞` for every measure (it is a junk step cdf for non-probability measures); for probability measures it is the textbook fact.

## What it says
If `s` is an order-connected set (an interval) contained in the support of a probability measure on `ℝ`, then the cdf is strictly increasing on `s`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Set.OrdConnected` means that `s` contains every point between two of its points, so `s` is an interval of any kind, possibly empty or a point.

## What it says
If the cdf of a probability measure on `ℝ` is strictly increasing, then the topological support of the measure is all of `ℝ`: every nonempty open interval has positive mass.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Measure.support` is Mathlib's topological support, the set of points all of whose neighbourhoods have positive mass.

## What it says
For every real `x`, the cdf of the zero measure on `ℝ` at `x` is `1` if `0 ≤ x` and `0` otherwise, that is, the cdf of a point mass at `0`. The zero measure is not a probability measure, so this is a statement about Mathlib's chosen value, not a distribution function in the textbook sense.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Mathlib defines `cdf` through a conditional cdf that falls back to a default step function at zero when no genuine cdf exists; this lemma records that junk value for the zero measure. It is a convention of the formalisation, not mathematics.

## What it says
If a probability law is almost surely in an interval `s`, and a point `q` has `μ(-∞, q) ≤ t ≤ F(q)` with `0 < t < 1`, then `q ∈ s`. Otherwise `s` lies entirely on one side of `q`, forcing the left mass to be `1` or the cdf at `q` to be `0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`Set.OrdConnected s` means `s` is an interval of any kind; `μ.real` is the real-valued measure.

## What it says
If an atomless probability law gives zero mass to `(-∞, 0)`, its survival function `1 - F` equals `1` at `0`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
`NullSingletonClass` makes the point `0` null; without it an atom at `0` would give survival `< 1`.

## What it says
If a probability law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and gives zero mass to `(-∞, 0)`, its survival function at `0` equals `1`.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
Absolute continuity implies atomless since Lebesgue measure gives singletons mass zero.

## What it says

In the same setting, if $x_3 \in H_i(X_3)$ has connecting image equal to the class of a cycle $z_1$ of $X_1$ in degree $j$, then some $x_2 \in X_{2,i}$ has $d x_2$ equal to the image of $z_1$ exactly (not only up to boundaries) and maps onto a cycle of $X_3$ representing $x_3$. This is a converse to `moduleCat_δ_homologyπ`.

The statement is the standard elementwise form of the corresponding fact about homology of complexes of modules; no hypothesis beyond those stated is used.

## References and tests

Then the function equal to $c$ on $t$ and $0$ elsewhere is locally integrable on $s$. The proof replaces $t$ by a measurable set equal to it almost everywhere (for the restricted measure), where the indicator of a constant is locally integrable, and transfers back along the almost-everywhere equality.

## References and tests

- Mathlib, `MeasureTheory.locallyIntegrable_const`, local integrability of a constant function for a locally finite measure.
- Mathlib, `MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrable.indicator`, the measurable-set case of the indicator.

No test or roadmap Check is recorded for this declaration.


## Lean subtleties

Throughout, `LocallyIntegrableOn f s μ` is Mathlib's notion: every point $x\in s$ has a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ relative to $s$ (a set containing $s\cap V$ for some open $V\ni x$) such that $f$ is integrable on $U$ with respect to $\mu$. Integrability in Lean includes almost-everywhere strong measurability. Null-measurability of `t` is only required for the measure restricted to `s`, which is weaker than null-measurability for $\mu$ and than measurability; the indicator is the Lean function `Set.indicator t (fun _ => c)`, taking the value $0$ off `t`. No relation between the topology and the $\sigma$-algebra on `X` is assumed.

## What it says
For real Banach spaces $E$, $F$ (complete normed real vector spaces), a measure $\mu$ on a measurable space $X$, an additive map $T : E \to F$ that is continuous and an integrable $f : X \to E$, the Bochner integral commutes with $T$: $\int T(f(x))\,d\mu = T\left(\int f\,d\mu\right)$.

This is the familiar fact that a bounded operator passes under the integral sign; here only additivity and continuity of $T$ are assumed, and additive continuous maps between real normed spaces are automatically $\mathbb{R}$-linear, so it is the standard statement.

## What it says
Let $\psi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nonnegative with $\int \psi\,d\mu = 1$ for a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, vanishing outside $[-\varepsilon, 0]$, and let $F$ be antitone (non-increasing) on $[t, t+\varepsilon]$. Then the average
$$\int \psi(s)\,F(t-s)\,d\mu(s)$$
lies in the interval $[F(t+\varepsilon),\,F(t)]$.

Since $s \in [-\varepsilon, 0]$ on the support of $\psi$, the point $t - s$ lies in $[t, t+\varepsilon]$, where $F$ is between $F(t+\varepsilon)$ and $F(t)$; averaging against a probability density keeps it there. This bounds a mollification of a monotone function by two of its values.

## What it says
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a normed field with a measurable space structure, $\rho$ a measure on $\mathbb{K}$ and $p \in \mathbb{K}[X]$ a nonzero polynomial. If $w \mapsto \|p(w)\|^2$ is integrable for $\rho$ and $\int \|p(w)\|^2\,d\rho = 0$, then the complement of the finite set of roots of $p$ is $\rho$-null: $\rho(\mathbb{K}\setminus Z(p)) = 0$. In other words $\rho$ is carried by the roots of $p$.

A nonnegative integrable function with integral zero vanishes almost everywhere, and $\|p(w)\|^2 = 0$ exactly at the roots.

## What it says
Let $F, G, N : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable with $0 \le F \le N$ and $F + G \le N$ almost everywhere. Then
$$\max\Big(\int F,0\Big) + \max\Big(\int G,0\Big) \le \max\Big(\int N, 0\Big),$$
as extended nonnegative reals.

If $\int G \ge 0$ this is $\int F + \int G = \int (F+G) \le \int N$. If $\int G < 0$ the second term is $0$ and the claim is $\int F \le \int N$.

## What it says
Let $g, h : X \to F$ take values in a seminormed group $F$, $\mu$ a measure on $X$ and $s \subseteq X$ a set. If $\|g\|^2$ and $\|h\|^2$ are integrable on $s$, then
$$\int_s \|g+h\|^2\,d\mu \le 2\int_s \|g\|^2\,d\mu + 2\int_s \|h\|^2\,d\mu.$$

This integrates the pointwise inequality $\|a+b\|^2 \le 2\|a\|^2 + 2\|b\|^2$, which follows from the triangle inequality and $(x+y)^2 \le 2x^2 + 2y^2$.

## What it says
Let $s \subseteq S$ be sets, $f, K : X \to F$ with values in a seminormed commutative group, $b, k, c \in F$, and constants $D \ge 0$, $0 \le q \le 1$. Assume $\|f-c\|^2$ and $\|f-K\|^2$ are integrable on $S$ and $\|K-k\|^2$ on $s$; that $b$ is at least as good a constant as $k$ for approximating $f$ on $s$,
$\int_s\|f-b\|^2 \le \int_s\|f-k\|^2$; and that $K$ has the decay $\int_s\|K-k\|^2 \le Dq\int_S\|K-c\|^2$. Then
$$\int_s\|f-b\|^2 \le 4Dq\int_S\|f-c\|^2 + (4D+2)\int_S\|f-K\|^2.$$

This is the comparison step of Campanato's method: the decay of $K$ (a harmonic replacement of $f$) is inherited by $f$ up to the $L^2$ distance between them. It follows from $\|u+v\|^2 \le 2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2$ applied on $s$ and on $S$, monotonicity in the set, and $q \le 1$.

## What it says

$$\Big(\int_S f\,d\mu\Big)^2 \le \mu(S)\int_S f^2\,d\mu,$$
where $\mu(S)$ is read as a real number.

This is the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for $f \cdot 1$ on $S$, or equivalently Jensen's inequality for the convex function $x \mapsto x^2$ on the normalised measure $\mu|_S/\mu(S)$.

## What it says
An isomorphism of Lie algebras $e : L \to L'$ over a commutative ring $R$ carries the centralizer of an element $x$ onto the centralizer of $e(x)$, so the two centralizers have the same rank.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring (any characteristic; not necessarily a field).
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra R L]`, `[LieRing L'] [LieAlgebra R L']`: $L$ and $L'$ are Lie algebras over $R$.
- `(e : L ≃ₗ⁅R⁆ L')`: an isomorphism of Lie algebras: an $R$-linear bijection with $e([y, z]) = [e(y), e(z)]$.
- `(x : L)`: an element $x$ of $L$.
- The conclusion: $\operatorname{rank}_R \ker(\operatorname{ad} e(x)) = \operatorname{rank}_R \ker(\operatorname{ad} x)$, the rank taken by `Module.finrank` as a natural number. Here `LieAlgebra.ad R L x` is the linear map $\operatorname{ad} x : L \to L$, $z \mapsto [x, z]$, and its kernel `LinearMap.ker` is the centralizer $\{z \in L : [x, z] = 0\}$ of $x$; likewise in $L'$ for $e(x)$.

Since $e([x, z]) = [e(x), e(z)]$ and $e$ is injective, $[x, z] = 0$ exactly when $[e(x), e(z)] = 0$, so $e$ maps the centralizer of $x$ bijectively and linearly onto that of $e(x)$. This is the standard invariance of centralizer dimension under isomorphism; over a field it is the dimension.

- `Module.finrank` is the rank as a natural number, and it is $0$ when the module is not finitely generated (and over a general ring it may be $0$ for other modules). No finiteness is assumed, and none is needed: isomorphic modules have equal `finrank`, so when one side is $0$ for such a reason so is the other.
- `e x` is the isomorphism $e$ applied to $x$, seen as a function.
- `↥(LinearMap.ker …)` is the kernel, a submodule, seen as a module in its own right.
- The lemma is tagged `@[simp]`, so Lean's simplifier rewrites the left side to the right by itself.

## What it says
An isomorphism of Lie algebras $e : L \to L'$ over a commutative ring $R$ carries the centralizer of an element $x$ onto the centralizer of $e(x)$, so the two centralizers have the same rank, as cardinal numbers, in any size.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring (any characteristic; not necessarily a field).
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra R L]`, `[LieRing L'] [LieAlgebra R L']`: $L$ and $L'$ are Lie algebras over $R$.
- `(e : L ≃ₗ⁅R⁆ L')`: an isomorphism of Lie algebras: an $R$-linear bijection with $e([y, z]) = [e(y), e(z)]$.
- `(x : L)`: an element $x$ of $L$.
- The conclusion: $\operatorname{rank}_R \ker(\operatorname{ad} e(x)) = \operatorname{rank}_R \ker(\operatorname{ad} x)$, the ranks taken by `Module.rank` as cardinal numbers and both moved by `Cardinal.lift` into a common universe. Here `LieAlgebra.ad R L x` is the linear map $\operatorname{ad} x : L \to L$, $z \mapsto [x, z]$, and its kernel `LinearMap.ker` is the centralizer $\{z \in L : [x, z] = 0\}$ of $x$; likewise in $L'$ for $e(x)$.

Since $e([x, z]) = [e(x), e(z)]$ and $e$ is a bijection, $e$ maps the centralizer of $x$ linearly and bijectively onto that of $e(x)$, and isomorphic modules have the same rank. This is the standard invariance of centralizer dimension under isomorphism, without finiteness; over a field it is the dimension.

name: The duality of Lᵖ spaces
text: on a σ-finite measure space, for 1 < q < ∞ and 1/p + 1/q = 1, every continuous linear functional on Lᵠ is integration against a unique Lᵖ function, and this pairing is an isometric isomorphism Lᵖ ≅ (Lᵠ)* (Folland, *Real Analysis*, Thm 6.15).

name: Schauder's fixed-point theorem
text: a continuous self-map of a nonempty closed convex subset of a real normed space whose image is relatively compact has a fixed point (Gilbarg–Trudinger, *Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order*, Thm 11.1).

name: Schaefer's fixed-point theorem
text: a continuous map T of a real normed space into itself that sends bounded sets to relatively compact sets has a fixed point whenever the solutions of u = θ·T(u), 0 < θ < 1, form a bounded set (Gilbarg–Trudinger, Thm 11.3).

name: Harnack's inequality with the sharp constant
text: a nonnegative harmonic function on a ball B(c, R) ⊆ ℝⁿ satisfies u(x) ≤ ((R + r)/(R − r))ⁿ u(y) for x, y in the concentric closed ball of radius r < R, sharpening the qualitative form announced earlier (Gilbarg–Trudinger, Thm 2.5).

name: Totally reflexive modules are exactly the Gorenstein-projective modules
text: over a two-sided Noetherian ring A, a finitely generated module M has a complete resolution by finitely generated projectives exactly when it is reflexive and Extⁱ(M, A) = 0 = Extⁱ(M*, A) for i > 0 (Avramov–Martsinkovsky, Proc. LMS 85 (2002), Thm 3.1; Auslander–Bridger, *Stable Module Theory*, Prop. 3.8).

name: Harnack's principle
text: a monotone family of harmonic functions on a connected open subset of ℝⁿ either converges locally uniformly to a harmonic function or tends to +∞ uniformly on compact sets; the bounded half was announced earlier, now the dichotomy in full (Gilbarg–Trudinger, Thm 2.9).

name: The Modulus Lemma
text: for a computably enumerable set Z, a total function ℕ → ℕ is computable in Z exactly when it has a computable approximation whose modulus of convergence is computable in Z (Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Lemma III.3.2).

name: Meyers' example
text: for every p > 2 there is a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation on ℝ² with an H¹ weak solution whose gradient is not in Lᵖ, so bounded measurable coefficients admit no gradient Lᵖ estimate for every p (Meyers, Ann. Sc. Norm. Sup. Pisa 17 (1963), §5).

name: Relative property (T)
text: a subgroup Λ of a discrete group G has relative property (T) when every unitary representation of G with almost-invariant vectors has a nonzero Λ-fixed vector; finite subgroups have it, and it passes to subgroups and quotients (Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, *Kazhdan's Property (T)*, Def. 1.4.3).

## What it says

## What it says
**The Galois characterization of the quantile.** For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ and a level $0<t<1$, the quantile is at most a point $x$ exactly when the cdf at $x$ reaches $t$: $q_\mu(t)\le x \iff t\le F_\mu(x)$.

This is the standard defining property of the generalized inverse of a right-continuous nondecreasing function (Embrechts and Hofert, *A note on generalized inverses*, cited in the file's module docstring). The two hypotheses on $t$ are the range where the infimum is attained and the junk-free range.

## What it says

- `(hδ : 0 < δ) (hcompact : IsCompact (f ⁻¹' Icc (c - δ) (c + δ)))`: the band $f^{-1}[c-\delta, c+\delta]$ is compact.
- Conclusion, in order: a width $0 < \varepsilon \le \delta$; for each critical point $p$ on the level (the subtype `criticalPoints I f ∩ f ⁻¹' {c}`) a smooth chart `ψ p` to $\mathbb{R}^m =$ `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)`, with pairwise disjoint domains, centred at $p$, whose image contains the closed ball of radius $\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$, in which $f = c - \sum_{i < \lambda} y_i^2 + \sum_{i \ge \lambda} y_i^2$ with $\lambda =$ `manifoldMorseIndex I f p`; handles `H p ⊆ (ψ p).source`; homeomorphisms `e p` from `H p` onto $D^\lambda \times D^{m-\lambda}$, the closed unit balls of the coordinates $i < \lambda$ and $i \ge \lambda$; and a diffeomorphism `Φ : M ≃ₘ⟮I, I⟯ M`, such that a point of `H p` lies in $\{f \le c - \varepsilon\}$ iff its first component has norm $1$ (the handle meets the lower sublevel in $\partial D^\lambda \times D^{m-\lambda}$); its second component is $0$ iff its coordinates $i \ge \lambda$ vanish (the core $D^\lambda \times 0$); $\Phi(x) \in \{f \le c-\varepsilon\} \cup \bigcup_p H_p$ iff $f(x) \le c + \varepsilon$ ($\Phi$ carries the upper sublevel onto the lower one with the handles attached); and $f(x) = c + \varepsilon$ iff $\Phi(x)$ has second component of norm $1$ in every handle containing it and lies on $f^{-1}(c - \varepsilon)$ if in none (the level goes to the free boundary).

Context: a real vector bundle `V` with fibre type $F$ over a manifold $M$ modelled on a finite-dimensional space $E$ with model with corners $I$, `[IsManifold I 2 M]`, `[FiniteDimensional ℝ F]`, `[ContMDiffVectorBundle 2 F V I]` (a $C^2$ bundle); `cov : CovariantDerivative I F V`, a connection $\nabla$, written `cov σ x v` for $\nabla_v \sigma$ at $x$; `hs : IsLocalFrameOn I F 2 s u`, sections $s_i$, $i$ in a finite type `ι` (`[Fintype ι]`), $C^2$ on $u$ and a basis of each fibre over $u$; `hu : IsOpen u`; `[ContMDiffCovariantDerivativeOn F 1 cov.toFun u]`, the connection is $C^1$ on $u$.

- `(hx : x ∈ u)`: the point.
- `{X Y : Π y, TangentSpace I y} (hX : CMDiff[u] 1 (T% X)) (hY : …)`: two vector fields, $C^1$ on $u$ as sections of the tangent bundle.
- `(j l : ι)`: a frame index and a coefficient index.
- Conclusion: `hs.coeff l x (cov.curvatureOperator X Y (s j) x)`, the $l$-th frame coefficient at $x$ of $R(X, Y)s_j$, where $R(X, Y)\sigma = \nabla_X\nabla_Y\sigma - \nabla_Y\nabla_X\sigma - \nabla_{[X, Y]}\sigma$ (Lee's sign), equals `mextDeriv (hs.connectionForm cov j l) x ![X x, Y x]`, the exterior derivative of the one-form $A^l{}_j$ at $x$ on $(X_x, Y_x)$, plus $\sum_m (A^l{}_m \wedge A^m{}_j)_x(X_x, Y_x)$. Here `connectionForm cov j l` is the scalar one-form $A^l{}_j(v) =$ coefficient $l$ of $\nabla_v s_j$.

This is the structure equation $F = dA + A \wedge A$ of Lee's Chapter 7, with section coefficients as columns so that the wedge is in matrix-multiplication order, stated entrywise and evaluated on values of $C^1$ vector fields (every tangent vector is such a value). It holds for a $C^1$ connection and a $C^2$ frame, with no metric and with boundary allowed.

## Lean subtleties
- `wedge` is normalised so that $(\alpha \wedge \beta)(v, w) = \alpha(v)\beta(w) - \alpha(w)\beta(v)$ for one-forms, with no factor $\tfrac12$; with this normalisation the equation has no extra constant.
- `RoughForm I M ℝ 1` is a one-form with no regularity, a covector at each point; `mextDeriv` is total, with junk values where the form is not differentiable. `contMDiffAt_connectionForm` shows $A^l{}_j$ is $C^1$ on $u$, so the value here is the actual exterior derivative.
- `hs.coeff l x` is $0$ outside $u$ (junk); `hx` keeps $x$ in $u$.
- `connectionForm cov j l` takes the input index $j$ first and the output index $l$ second, as the Christoffel-symbol API does; it is $A^l{}_j$ in matrix notation.
- `![X x, Y x]` is the pair as a function on `Fin 2`.

## What it says
For a finite simple graph $G$, the block–cut graph of $G$ is a tree exactly when $G$ is connected.

- `{V : Type u}`: the type of vertices; `{G : SimpleGraph V}`: a simple graph on it, without loops or multiple edges.
- `[Finite V]`: the vertex set is finite, a hypothesis carried as a typeclass.
- `G.blockCutGraph`: the block–cut incidence graph. Its vertices are the blocks of $G$ (`G.BlockVertex`: the vertex sets $B$ with `G.IsBlock B`, the maximal sets inducing a connected subgraph without a cut vertex) and the cut vertices of $G$ (`G.CutVertex`: the vertices whose deletion separates two vertices that were connected). A block and a cut vertex are adjacent exactly when the vertex lies in the block; there are no other edges.
- The conclusion: `IsTree`, "connected and acyclic", of the block–cut graph holds if and only if `G.Connected`.

This is the block–cut tree of Diestel's Lemma 3.1.4: the block graph of a connected graph is a tree. The converse comes from the bijection `blockCutComponentEquiv` between the connected components of the two graphs, so for a disconnected finite graph the block–cut graph is a forest with one component per component of $G$. Acyclicity alone, `blockCutGraph_isAcyclic`, needs no finiteness. Blocks are maximal connected induced subgraphs without a cut vertex, as in Diestel: a bridge with its ends and an isolated vertex are blocks.

- Mathlib's `Connected`, hence `IsTree`, includes that the vertex type is nonempty. For the empty graph both sides are false: blocks are nonempty, so the block–cut graph has no vertices. A one-vertex graph is one block with no cut vertex; both sides are true.

## What it says
For a morphism of schemes $f : X \to Y$, a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules $M$ and $q \ge 0$, the abelian sheaf underlying the higher direct image $R^q f_* M$ is isomorphic to the sheafification of the presheaf $V \mapsto H^q(f^{-1}V, M)$ on $Y$.

- `{X Y : Scheme.{u}} (f : X ⟶ Y)`: two schemes in the universe `u` and a morphism between them.
- `(M : X.Modules)`: a sheaf of modules over the structure sheaf of $X$.
- `(q : ℕ)`: the degree.
- The value is an isomorphism `≅` of sheaves of abelian groups on $Y$ (`AddCommGrpCat`, for the topology of open covers `Opens.grothendieckTopology Y`). On the left, `f.higherDirectImage q` is the $q$-th right derived functor of the pushforward of module sheaves, computed by injective resolutions among $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules, and `toSheaf Y` forgets the module structure. On the right, `cohomologyPresheaf q` of the abelian sheaf underlying $M$ is Mathlib's presheaf $U \mapsto H^q(U, M)$; composing with `(Opens.map f.base).op` sends an open $V \subseteq Y$ to $H^q(f^{-1}V, M)$, and `presheafToSheaf` sheafifies.

This is Hartshorne's Proposition III.8.1, stated there for a continuous map and a sheaf of abelian groups, with $R^q f_*$ derived among abelian sheaves. Here $R^q f_*$ is derived among $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules; the comparison uses that injective $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules are flasque, through the site-level `sheafPushforwardContinuousHomologyIsoSheafify` for acyclic resolutions. It holds for every morphism, module sheaf and $q$.

## What it says
For real numbers $\sigma > 0$ and $y > 0$,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^{-(\sigma + it)}\, \Gamma(\sigma + it)\, dt = 2\pi e^{-y}.$$

- `{σ : ℝ} (hσ : 0 < σ)`: a positive real, the abscissa of the vertical line.
- `{y : ℝ} (hy : 0 < y)`: a positive real number.
- The conclusion: the integral over $t \in \mathbb{R}$ of `(y : ℂ) ^ (-(σ + t * I)) * Gamma (σ + t * I)`, the complex power of $y$ times the complex Gamma function at $s = \sigma + it$, equals `2 * π * Real.exp (-y)`, read in $\mathbb{C}$.

With $s = \sigma + it$ and $ds = i\,dt$ this is $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\operatorname{Re} s = \sigma} \Gamma(s)\, y^{-s}\, ds = e^{-y}$: the Mellin inversion of $\Gamma$, the Mellin transform of $t \mapsto e^{-t}$, on any vertical line in the right half-plane (the Cahen–Mellin integral). The normalised form `Complex.mellinInv_Gamma`, `mellinInv σ Gamma y = Real.exp (-y)`, is the same statement with Mathlib's factor $1/2\pi$. The literature states it for complex $y$ with $\operatorname{Re} y > 0$; here $y$ is real and positive.

## Lean subtleties
- `∫ t : ℝ, …` is the Bochner integral for Lebesgue measure, and is $0$ by convention when the integrand is not integrable. Integrability holds here: `Complex.verticalIntegrable_Gamma` proves $\Gamma$ integrable on every vertical line avoiding its poles, from the decay $\|\Gamma(\sigma + it)\| \le C(1 + t^2)^{-m}$.
- `(y : ℂ) ^ z` is the principal complex power $\exp(z \log y)$; for real $y > 0$ the logarithm is the real one, so $y^{-s}$ is unambiguous.
- `Complex.Gamma` takes a junk value at its poles; the line $\operatorname{Re} s = \sigma > 0$ contains none, so the convention does not enter.
- `π` is `Real.pi` and `Real.exp (-y)` a real number; both are coerced to $\mathbb{C}$.
- `0 < σ` is what makes $\Gamma$ the Mellin transform of $e^{-t}$ on the line; nothing is asserted for $\sigma \le 0$.

## What it says
For $n \ge 1$, the antipodal map $x \mapsto -x$ of the unit sphere $S^n$ has degree $(-1)^{n+1}$, for every orientation of $S^n$ and at every point.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]`: a real inner product space.
- `{n : ℕ} [Fact (finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]`: $E$ has dimension $n + 1$, carried as a typeclass fact, so `sphere (0 : E) 1` is $S^n$.
- `[NeZero n]`: $n \ne 0$, that is $n \ge 1$.
- `(o : Manifold.Orientation (𝓡 n) (sphere (0 : E) 1) (Fin n))`: an orientation of $S^n$ as a smooth manifold modelled on `𝓡 n`, the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, its tangent spaces indexed by `Fin n`.
- `(y : sphere (0 : E) 1)`: a point of $S^n$.
- The conclusion: `degreeAtRegularValue o o (fun x ↦ -x) y = (-1) ^ (n + 1)` in $\mathbb{Z}$: the sum over the fibre $\{x : -x = y\}$ of `orientationSign o o f x`, which is $1$ where the derivative preserves the orientation, $-1$ where it reverses it, $0$ where it is not invertible, with the same orientation $o$ on source and target.

This is the computation of Milnor's §5 and Lee's degree theory, in the smooth form: a signed count of preimages at a value. The fibre is the single point $-y$, where the sign is $(-1)^{n+1}$ (`orientationSign_neg_sphere`). For $n \ge 1$ the sphere is connected and has two orientations, $o$ and $-o$, and the sign is the same for both, since reversing source and target cancels.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a semiring and $M$ an $R$-module that is a generator. Write $\Gamma = \operatorname{End}_R(M)$, acting on $M$ by evaluation. Then the map $R \to \operatorname{End}_\Gamma(M)$, $r \mapsto (x \mapsto rx)$, is bijective: $R$ is exactly the ring of $\Gamma$-linear endomorphisms of $M$.

- `(R : Type*) [Semiring R]`: a semiring, not assumed commutative.
- `(M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: an additive commutative monoid with an $R$-action.
- `[IsGenerator R M]`: finitely many linear forms $\varphi_i : M \to R$ and vectors $m_i \in M$ satisfy $\sum_i \varphi_i(m_i) = 1$; equivalently the trace ideal of $M$ is $R$, or $R$ is a quotient of some $M^n$.
- The conclusion: `Function.Bijective (Module.toModuleEnd (Module.End R M) M (S := R))`. `Module.End R M` is $\Gamma$, and `Module.toModuleEnd Γ M : R →+* Module.End Γ M` is the ring homomorphism sending $r$ to multiplication by $r$, which is $\Gamma$-linear because $R$-linear maps commute with scalars.

This is the double centralizer property of a generator, Theorem 17.8 of Anderson–Fuller: a generator is balanced, and is finitely generated projective over its endomorphism ring (here the instances `IsGenerator.finite_end` and `IsGenerator.projective_end`). Anderson–Fuller work with rings and right modules; here $R$ is any semiring and $M$ a left module, with no finiteness or semisimplicity assumed. The isomorphism is packaged as `ringEquivEndEndOfIsGenerator`.

## Lean subtleties

## What it says
`HasLDP l ε μ I` says that the family of measures $\mu_i$, indexed along the filter $l$, satisfies a large deviation principle with speed $\varepsilon$ and rate function $I$.

- `{ι X : Type*}`, `[TopologicalSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X]`: an index type and a space with a topology and a σ-algebra, not assumed compatible.
- `(l : Filter ι)`: the direction of the limit, such as $n \to \infty$; `(ε : ι → ℝ≥0)`: the speeds, nonnegative reals such as $1/n$.
- `(μ : ι → Measure X)`: the measures; `(I : X → ℝ≥0∞)`: the rate function, with values in $[0, \infty]$.
- Fields: `lowerSemicontinuous`, that $I$ is lower semicontinuous; `lower_bound`, that for every open $G$, $-\inf_G I \le \liminf_{l} \varepsilon_i \log \mu_i(G)$; `upper_bound`, that for every closed $F$, $\limsup_{l} \varepsilon_i \log \mu_i(F) \le -\inf_F I$. The infima are taken in $[0,\infty]$ and negated in the extended reals `EReal`, where the logarithms `ENNReal.log` also live.

This is the definition of Dembo–Zeitouni §1.2, in its equivalent form as an open-set lower bound and a closed-set upper bound, for a rate function with values in $[0, \infty]$. Differences: the measures are any measures, not only probability measures; the index set and filter are arbitrary; and the speeds are any nonnegative reals, with no condition $\varepsilon_i \to 0$ in the definition. Goodness of the rate function is the separate predicate `IsGoodRateFunction`.

## What it says
`C.KMethodSpace θ q` is the real interpolation space $(X_0, X_1)_{\theta, q}$ of the $K$-method, as a type.

- `{𝕜 : Type*} [NormedField 𝕜]`: the scalar field; `{X₀ X₁}` normed spaces over it; `{V}` an additive group with a $\mathbb{k}$-module structure, a topology and continuous addition.
- `(C : CompatibleCouple 𝕜 X₀ X₁ V)`: a compatible couple, continuous injective linear maps of $X_0$ and $X_1$ into the common space $V$.
- `(θ : ℝ) (q : ℝ≥0∞)`: the parameters; `ℝ≥0∞` is $[0, \infty]$, so $q = \infty$ is allowed.
- The value, a `Type _`: the subtype of the sum space `C.SumSpace`, which is $X_0 + X_1$ with norm $\inf\{\|x_0\| + \|x_1\| : u = x_0 + x_1\}$, of the $u$ with `C.kMethodENorm θ q u < ∞`, that is $\| t \mapsto t^{-\theta} K(t, u) \|_{L^q(dt/t)} < \infty$, where $K(t,u) = \inf\{\|x_0\| + t\|x_1\| : u = x_0 + x_1\}$ is Peetre's $K$-functional (`kFunctional`) and $dt/t$ is `multHaar` on $(0, \infty)$.
- Instances: for `[T1Space V]` and `[Fact (1 ≤ q)]`, a normed space with $\|u\| = \|t^{-\theta}K(t,u)\|_{L^q(dt/t)}$, complete when $X_0$ and $X_1$ are; continuous inclusions `toSum` into the sum and, for $0 < \theta < 1$, `ofInter` of the intersection; and `map`, the map induced by a map of couples, with norm at most $M_0^{1-\theta} M_1^{\theta}$ (`norm_map_le`).

This is the $K$-method of Bergh–Löfström §3.1 with the same normalisation; `norm_map_le` is their Theorem 3.1.2. The type is defined for every real $\theta$ and $q \in [0, \infty]$, where the book takes $0 < \theta < 1$ and $1 \le q \le \infty$, the range in which the intersection embeds and the norm is a norm. Banach couples are replaced by normed spaces over any normed field with a $T_1$ ambient space.

## What it says
`IsKrullSchmidt C` says that the category $C$ is Krull–Schmidt: every object is isomorphic to a finite biproduct of objects whose endomorphism rings are local.

- `{C : Type u} [Category.{v} C]`: a category, with objects in universe `u` and morphisms in `v`.
- `[Preadditive C]`: the Hom-sets are abelian groups and composition is bilinear.
- `[HasFiniteBiproducts C]`: finite direct sums (which are also products) exist, so $C$ is additive.
- The single field, `exists_iso_biproduct (X : C)`: for every object $X$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and objects $P_0, \dots, P_{n-1}$ (`P : Fin n → C`) such that each `End (P i)` is a local ring (`IsLocalRing`) and there is an isomorphism $X \cong \bigoplus_i P_i$ (`Nonempty (X ≅ ⨁ P)`).

This is Krause's definition in §4: an additive category is Krull–Schmidt when every object decomposes into a finite direct sum of objects having local endomorphism rings. The file proves the basic consequences: such a category is idempotent complete (`isIdempotentComplete_of_isKrullSchmidt`), an object is indecomposable exactly when its endomorphism ring is local (`IsKrullSchmidt.indecomposable_iff_isLocalRing_end`), and the property passes along equivalences of categories (`CategoryTheory.Equivalence.isKrullSchmidt`). The uniqueness of the decomposition up to permutation and isomorphism, the Krull–Schmidt theorem for such categories, is not among these declarations.

## Lean subtleties

## What it says
A family of smooth embeddings $i_a : S_a \to M$ *exhibits* $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ *as a Morse–Bott function*. From the section's variables: $M$ is a manifold modelled by `I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H`, so it may have boundary or corners; $\iota$ is an index type; each piece $S_a$ is a manifold with its own model `J a`, so pieces may differ in dimension; `n : ℕ∞ω` is a smoothness class; `SmoothEmbedding (J a) I n (S a) M` is a bundled $C^n$ immersion that is also a topological embedding. The structure is a proposition with eight fields:

- `contMDiff`: $f$ is $C^\infty$.
- `isNondegenerateCriticalSubmanifold`: each $i_a$ is a nondegenerate critical submanifold: $f$ is $C^2$ along the image, its points are critical, and at each $i_a(s)$ the kernel of the Hessian of $f$ lies in the tangent space of the image (the reverse inclusion is automatic, so the kernel is that tangent space: the normal Hessian is nondegenerate).
- `nonempty`, `boundarylessManifold`: each $S_a$ is nonempty and without boundary.
- `range_eq_connectedComponentIn`: the image of $i_a$ is the connected component of the critical set $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ through any of its points.
- `range_injective`: distinct indices give distinct images.
- `criticalPoints_subset_iUnion_range`: the images cover $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$.
- `locallyFinite_range`: every point of $M$ has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many images.

This is Bott's notion: the critical set is a disjoint union of nondegenerate critical manifolds. It is packaged as a predicate on an explicit family indexed by the components rather than as a property of $f$ alone, and local finiteness is an explicit axiom.

where `realCliffordWeight 1 3 μ` is $+1$ for $\mu = 0$ and $-1$ otherwise ($\eta = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$), `Pi.single μ 1` is the basis vector $e_\mu$ in time-first coordinates, `timeFirstToNative` is the fixed change $P(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3) = (x_3,-x_2,x_1,x_0)$ to the time-last coordinates of $\mathrm{Cl}(3,1)$, and `diracVector` is $C(v) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & X(v) \\ \operatorname{adj} X(v) & 0\end{pmatrix}$ with $X(v)$ the Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrix of $v$. `C : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ` is a candidate price $C(s, t)$ of spot $s$ and time $t$; `r σ K T A : ℝ` are the rate, volatility, strike, expiry and a growth constant.

- `(hσ : 0 < σ)`, `(hK : 0 < K)`; $r$ and $T$ are any reals.
- `(hC : ContinuousOn (Function.uncurry C) (Ioi 0 ×ˢ Icc 0 T))`: $(s, t) \mapsto C(s, t)$ is jointly continuous on $(0, \infty) \times [0, T]$.
- `(hcd : …)`: for $s > 0$, $0 < t < T$, $s \mapsto C(s, t)$ is $C^2$ near $s$ (`ContDiffAt ℝ 2`).
- `(hdiff : …)`: for such $s, t$, $t \mapsto C(s, t)$ is differentiable at $t$.
- `(hpde : …)`: for $s > 0$, $0 < t < T$, $\partial_t C + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 s^2 \partial_{ss} C + r (s\, \partial_s C - C) = 0$, the Black–Scholes equation, written with `deriv`.
- `(hgrowth : …)`: $|C(s, t)| \le A (1 + s)$ for $s > 0$, $t \in [0, T]$: linear growth.
- `(hterminal : …)`: $C(s, T) = (s - K)^+$ for $s > 0$, the call payoff.
- Conclusion: for $s > 0$ and $t \in [0, T]$, $C(s, t) = $ `callValue s r σ K (T - t)`, the Black–Scholes call price with remaining maturity $\tau = T - t$: the closed form `callPrice` for $s > 0$, $\tau > 0$, and $(s - K e^{-r\tau})^+$ otherwise.

This is uniqueness for the terminal-value problem of the Black–Scholes equation in a growth class, here linear growth; with the earlier `TauCeti.BlackScholes.callValue_pde`, which says the formula solves the equation, the formula is the only such solution. Nothing is assumed at $s = 0$ and no time derivative is asked at $t = 0$ or $t = T$. The proof applies the comparison principle `TauCeti.Finance.eq_of_pde_eq_of_terminal_eq` with constant coefficients.

- `Ioi 0`, `Icc 0 T`, `Ioo 0 T` are $(0, \infty)$, $[0, T]$, $(0, T)$; `×ˢ` is the product of sets; `Function.uncurry C` is $(s, t) \mapsto C(s, t)$; `⦃s⦄` are implicit arguments.
- If $T < 0$ then $[0, T]$ is empty and the conclusion says nothing; if $T = 0$ it reduces to the terminal condition, since `callValue` at maturity $0$ is $(s - K)^+$.
- `callValue` is defined on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by cases; only $s > 0$, $\tau \ge 0$ is used.

## What it says
`ι : Type*` with `[Fintype ι]` is a finite index set, so `ι → ℝ` is $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n = |\iota|$; `[Nonempty ι]` says $n \ge 1$. `A B : Set (ι → ℝ)` are subsets, `δ : ℝ≥0∞` an extended nonnegative real, `volume` Lebesgue measure. `dyadicCube k m`, for `k : ℤ`, `m : ι → ℤ`, is the half-open box $\prod_i [m_i 2^k, (m_i + 1) 2^k)$ of side $2^k$; its parent is the cube of level $k + 1$ containing it.

- `(hA : NullMeasurableSet A)`: $A$ differs from a Borel set by a null set; `(hA' : volume A ≠ ∞)`.
- `(hδ0 : δ ≠ 0)`, `(hδ1 : δ < 1)`: $0 < \delta < 1$.
- `(hB : …)`: for all $k, m, m'$ with `dyadicCube k m ⊆ dyadicCube (k + 1) m'` (the second is the parent $P$ of $Q = $ `dyadicCube k m`), if $\delta |Q| < |A \cap Q|$ then $P \subseteq B$.
- Conclusion: $|A| \le \delta |B|$.

This is the covering lemma of the Krylov–Safonov theory in the form of Caffarelli and Cabré: the local condition, that the parent of every cube in which $A$ has density above $\delta$ lies in $B$, gives $|A| \le \delta |B|$. The lemma of Caffarelli–Cabré and of Gilbarg–Trudinger is stated inside a cube $Q_0$ with $A \subseteq Q_0$ and $|A| \le \delta |Q_0|$; that is the file's `TauCeti.volume_le_mul_volume_of_subset_dyadicCube`, and this declaration is the version on $\mathbb{R}^n$, which asks instead that $|A|$ be finite. It is the cube-decomposition lemma of the theory, proved by the Calderón–Zygmund stopping-time argument, not the Harnack inequality itself.

## Lean subtleties
- Arithmetic is in `ℝ≥0∞`: if $|B| = \infty$ then $\delta |B| = \infty$ (as $\delta \ne 0$) and the conclusion is trivial.
- Both bounds on $\delta$ are needed, as the docstring records: for $\delta \ge 1$ the hypothesis holds with $B = \emptyset$, since $|A \cap Q| \le |Q| \le \delta |Q|$; for $\delta = 0$ it holds for a cube $A$ with $B = \mathbb{R}^n$, and $|A| \le 0$ fails.

## What it says
This is Mecke's identity for a Poisson number of independent locations: the finite-intensity case, forward direction, for the explicit sampling representation. `Ω X : Type*` are measurable spaces; `P : Measure Ω`, `Q : Measure X` are probability measures; `N : Ω → ℕ` is a random count, `Z : ℕ → Ω → X` a sequence of random locations, `r : ℝ≥0` a rate, `g : X × Measure X → ℝ≥0∞` a test function of a point and a measure, with `(hg : Measurable g)`.

- `(hNZ : IndepFun N (fun ω i ↦ Z i ω) P)`: $N$ is independent of the whole sequence $(Z_i)$.
- `(hind : iIndepFun Z P)`: the $Z_i$ are mutually independent.
- `(hZ : ∀ i, HasLaw (Z i) Q P)`: each $Z_i$ has law $Q$ (`HasLaw`: almost-everywhere measurable with image measure $Q$).
- `(hN : HasLaw N (poissonMeasure r) P)`: $N$ is Poisson with mean $r$.
- Conclusion, with $\eta(\omega) = \sum_{i < N(\omega)} \delta_{Z_i(\omega)}$ the empirical measure of the sample: $\mathbb{E} \int g(y, \eta)\, \eta(dy) = r \int_X \mathbb{E}\, g(y, \delta_y + \eta)\, Q(dy)$.

The Mecke equation for a Poisson process $\eta$ with intensity measure $\lambda$ reads $\mathbb{E} \int f(x, \eta)\, \eta(dx) = \int \mathbb{E} f(x, \eta + \delta_x)\, \lambda(dx)$. Here $\lambda = r Q$ is finite and $\eta$ is the mixed binomial sample, the finite-intensity case the textbook proof establishes first. The statement for an arbitrary Poisson process with $s$-finite intensity, and the converse, that the identity characterises Poisson processes, are not part of this declaration.

## What it says
`A B : Type*` carry `[CStarAlgebra A] [PartialOrder A] [StarOrderedRing A]` and the same for `B`: unital C*-algebras with the star order, in which $a \le b$ when $b - a$ lies in the closed cone generated by the $x^* x$, the usual positive cone. `(ι : B →⋆ₐ[ℂ] A)` is a unital $*$-algebra homomorphism, the inclusion of $B$ into $A$.

The structure `CStarConditionalExpectation ι` has the fields:

- `extends A →ₚ[ℂ] B`: a positive $\mathbb{C}$-linear map $E : A \to B$ (Mathlib's `PositiveLinearMap`: linear and order preserving, so $a \ge 0$ implies $E(a) \ge 0$);
- `map_one'`: $E(1) = 1$;
- `map_mul_left'`: $E(\iota(b)\, a) = b\, E(a)$ and `map_mul_right'`: $E(a\, \iota(b)) = E(a)\, b$, the $B$-bimodule identities.

Consequences in the file: $E(\iota(b)) = b$ (`map_inclusion`), so $\iota$ is injective and $\iota \circ E$ is an idempotent projection onto the image of $B$; the Schwarz inequality $E(a)^* E(a) \le E(a^* a)$ (`star_map_mul_map_le`); contractivity $\|E(a)\| \le \|a\|$; norm one when $B$ is nontrivial; positivity of the $B$-valued quadratic forms of the Gram matrices $E(a_i^* a_j)$.

This is the conditional expectation of operator algebras: a positive unital projection of $A$ onto a subalgebra $B$ with the bimodule property. Two points of presentation differ: the subalgebra is given through a homomorphism $\iota$ rather than as a subset, with $E \circ \iota = \mathrm{id}$ derived from the fields; and both bimodule identities are fields. Complete positivity is not part of the definition, and the theorems of Tomiyama and Umegaki are not in this file.

## What it says
This is the Yoneda $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ of an exact category as a pointed set with its two functorialities; the Baer sum, which makes it a group, is not in this file. `C : Type u` with `[Category.{v} C] [Preadditive C] [HasZeroObject C] [HasBinaryBiproducts C]` is an additive category with a zero object and direct sums `X ⊞ Z`. `E : ExactStructure C` is an exact structure in the sense of Quillen and Bühler: a class of conflations, kernel–cokernel pairs $X \xrightarrow{f} Y \xrightarrow{g} Z$, satisfying Quillen's axioms.

`Ext1 (Z X : C) : Type (max u v)` is the quotient of `E.Extension Z X` by Yoneda equivalence. An `E.Extension Z X` is a conflation of $E$ with end terms $X$ and $Z$: a middle object `obj`, maps `f : X ⟶ obj`, `g : obj ⟶ Z`, `zero : f ≫ g = 0`, and the proof that it is a conflation. Two extensions are Yoneda equivalent (`Extension.Rel`) when some morphism of middle terms is compatible with the inflations and deflations; by the short five lemma it is an isomorphism.

The file gives `Ext1` a base point `0`, the class of the split conflation $X \to X \oplus Z \to Z$ (`mk_eq_zero_iff_isSplitEpi`: a class is $0$ exactly when its deflation has a section); `Ext1.pullback` along $u : Z' \to Z$, contravariant in $Z$, and `Ext1.pushout` along $v : X \to X'$, covariant in $X$, which commute; and the first exactness statements of the $\mathrm{Hom}$–$\mathrm{Ext}$ sequences.

This is Yoneda's description of $\mathrm{Ext}^1(Z, X)$ by extensions of $Z$ by $X$, as in Mac Lane for modules, inside an exact category, with no ambient abelian category and no projectives or injectives. The order `Ext1 Z X` matches $\mathrm{Ext}(C, A)$ for $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$. The comparison with derived-functor Ext is not made.

## What it says
`Ω` is a measurable space (`[mΩ : MeasurableSpace Ω]`) with a probability measure `μ`; `ℱ : Filtration ℕ mΩ` is a filtration, an increasing sequence of sub-σ-algebras $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1 \subseteq \dots$; `Y : ℕ → Ω → ℝ` is a sequence of real random variables and `b : ℕ → ℝ≥0` a sequence of nonnegative bounds.

- `(h_adapted : StronglyAdapted ℱ Y)`: each $Y_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable (strongly measurable, which for real functions is measurability).
- `(n : ℕ)`: the number of terms.
- `(hbound : ∀ i < n, ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, |Y i ω| ≤ b i)`: $|Y_i| \le b_i$ almost surely for $i < n$.
- `(hmean0 : ∫ ω, Y 0 ω ∂μ = 0)`: $Y_0$ has mean $0$.
- `(hmean : ∀ i < n - 1, μ[Y (i + 1) | ℱ i] =ᵐ[μ] 0)`: the conditional expectation of $Y_{i+1}$ given $\mathcal{F}_i$ vanishes almost surely, for $i + 1 < n$.
- `(hε : 0 ≤ ε)`.
- Conclusion: $\mu\{\varepsilon \le \sum_{i < n} Y_i\} \le \exp\!\big(-\varepsilon^2 / (2 \sum_{i < n} b_i^2)\big)$, with `μ.real` the probability as a real number.

This is the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality, one-sided upper tail: for a martingale $S_k = \sum_{i < k} Y_i$ with increments bounded by $b_i$, $\mathbb{P}(S_n \ge \varepsilon) \le \exp(-\varepsilon^2 / 2\sum b_i^2)$. The hypotheses are the martingale-difference form: $Y_0$ is the first increment, with mean $0$, and each later increment is conditionally centred given the past. The file's interval version `measureReal_sum_range_ge_le_of_mem_Icc_martingale_differences`, with $Y_i \in [a_i, b_i]$ and constant $((b_i - a_i)/2)^2$, is the sharper form of which this is the symmetric case; the `abs` versions are the two-sided bounds with the factor $2$. It is stated on an arbitrary probability space, with no standard Borel assumption.

- `n - 1` is truncated subtraction on `ℕ`: for $n = 0$ or $n = 1$ the hypothesis `hmean` is empty, which is the intended reading, there being no later increment.
- Division by zero is $0$ in Lean: when $\sum_{i < n} b_i^2 = 0$ (all $b_i = 0$ for $i < n$, or $n = 0$) the exponent is $0$ and the bound is $1$, which holds trivially; likewise for $\varepsilon = 0$.
- `μ[f | m]` is Mathlib's conditional expectation, $0$ when $f$ is not integrable; here $Y_{i+1}$ is bounded, hence integrable, so it is the usual one. `=ᵐ[μ]` is equality almost everywhere and `∀ᵐ ω ∂μ` is "almost surely".

## What it says
Every element of a compact connected real Lie group lies in a maximal torus.

- `{E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, the model space.
- `{H : Type u_2} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)`: a model with corners $I$ on $E$; the charts of the group take values in $H$.
- `{G : Type u_3} [TopologicalSpace G] [ChartedSpace H G] [Group G] [LieGroup I ∞ G]`: a group $G$ with a $C^\infty$ manifold structure modelled on $I$, in which multiplication and inversion are smooth: a Lie group. The smoothness parameter `∞`, which the docs print as `↑⊤`, is the top element of `ℕ∞` coerced into `WithTop ℕ∞`, and means $C^\infty$.
- `[CompactSpace G] [ConnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is compact and connected.
- `(g : G)`: an element.
- Conclusion: `∃ T : Subgroup G, IsMaximalTorus T ∧ g ∈ T`, some maximal torus contains $g$. `IsTorus T` means the subgroup $T$ is compact, connected and commutative (`IsMulCommutative T`); `IsMaximalTorus T` means $T$ is maximal under inclusion among such subgroups (`Maximal IsTorus T`).

This is the maximal torus theorem. With the conjugacy of maximal tori, `IsMaximalTorus.exists_map_conj_eq`, every element is conjugate into any fixed maximal torus; that corollary is `IsMaximalTorus.iUnion_map_conj_eq_univ` in the same file. In a compact Lie group a compact connected abelian subgroup is a closed Lie subgroup isomorphic to $(S^1)^r$, so `IsTorus` is the usual notion. No Hausdorff hypothesis and no Riemannian metric are assumed: the proof derives the Hausdorff property from the Lie group structure, and uses surjectivity of the exponential map on a compact connected group rather than Knapp's induction.

- Bröcker and tom Dieck, *Representations of Compact Lie Groups*, Theorem IV.1.6 (the comparison made for Voyager's announcement).

- `∞` is not `⊤ : WithTop ℕ∞`: in Mathlib the latter means analytic ($C^\omega$), while `∞ = ↑(⊤ : ℕ∞)` means $C^\infty$. The hypothesis asks smoothness only, not analyticity.
- Lie groups in Mathlib are modelled on a `ModelWithCorners`; a Lie group is automatically boundaryless, so corners in the model do not change the result.
- `IsConnected (T : Set G)` includes nonemptiness; a subgroup contains $1$, so this is no extra condition.

## What it says
- `Γ : Type v`, `[Group Γ]`: a group with no topology, so a discrete group; `Λ : Subgroup Γ` a subgroup.
- Left side, `Λ.RelativePropertyT.{max u v}`: for every complex Hilbert space $H$ in universe `max u v` (`[NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]`) and every unitary representation $\rho$ of $\Gamma$ on $H$ (`ContRepresentation ℂ Γ H` is a homomorphism to bounded operators; `IsUnitary` says each $\rho(g)$ preserves the inner product), if $\rho$ has almost invariant vectors (for every finite $F \subseteq \Gamma$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ some unit vector $\xi$ has $\|\rho(g)\xi - \xi\| < \varepsilon$ for all $g \in F$), then $\rho$ has a nonzero vector fixed by $\Lambda$ (`(ρ.restrict Λ.subtype).invariants`).
- Right side: there are a finite set `F : Finset Γ` and a real $\delta > 0$ with `Λ.IsKazhdanPair.{max u v} F δ`: every unitary representation on such a Hilbert space with a unit vector $\xi$ satisfying $\|\rho(g)\xi - \xi\| < \delta$ for all $g \in F$ has a nonzero $\Lambda$-fixed vector.

So a subgroup of a discrete group has relative property (T) exactly when it has a Kazhdan pair $(F, \delta)$ with $\delta > 0$. This is the standard characterisation; for a discrete group the compact Kazhdan sets of the general theory are the finite sets, and $\Lambda = \Gamma$ gives Kazhdan's property (T) itself. The direction from a Kazhdan pair to relative property (T) is immediate, since an $(F, \delta)$-invariant unit vector is an almost invariant vector. The direction from relative property (T) to a Kazhdan pair is the one with content: if no pair $(F, 1/(n+1))$ works, one takes the Hilbert direct sum of chosen counterexamples, one for each $(F, n)$; it has almost invariant vectors, so a nonzero $\Lambda$-fixed vector, whose coordinates are $\Lambda$-fixed and hence all zero.

## References and tests
- C. Anantharaman and S. Popa, *An Introduction to II₁ Factors*, Proposition 14.1.2.
- B. Bekka, P. de la Harpe and A. Valette, *Kazhdan's Property (T)*, Chapter 1.
- Roadmap: `FactorRigidity`, Layer 3, §3.1, per the PR description.

- Both sides quantify over Hilbert spaces in the universe `max u v`, `v` being the universe of $\Gamma$; the direct sum in the proof is indexed by `Finset Γ × ℕ`, which forces this level. It is bookkeeping, not a mathematical restriction.
- For $\delta \le 0$ the condition $\|\rho(g)\xi - \xi\| < \delta$ never holds, so $(F, \delta)$ is a Kazhdan pair vacuously; hence the right side demands $0 < \delta$.
- For $F = \emptyset$ a Kazhdan pair means every unitary representation on a nonzero Hilbert space has a nonzero $\Lambda$-fixed vector; the unit vector $\xi$ rules out $H = 0$.
- No continuity in $g$ is required, since $\Gamma$ carries no topology; `ContRepresentation` only asks that each $\rho(g)$ be a bounded operator.
