name: Cobham’s theorem
text: for multiplicatively independent bases k, l ≥ 2, a sequence that is both k-automatic and l-automatic is eventually periodic, and conversely every eventually periodic sequence is automatic in both bases (Allouche–Shallit, *Automatic Sequences*, Thm 11.2.2).

name: The maximal torus theorem
text: every element of a compact connected Lie group lies in a maximal torus, so the conjugates of any one maximal torus cover the group; with the conjugacy of maximal tori announced earlier, the theorem is now in full (Knapp, *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction*, Thm 4.36).

name: Milnor’s handle attachment theorem
text: across a critical level of a Morse function with compact band, a diffeomorphism carries the upper sublevel set onto the lower one with a handle Dᵏ × Dᵐ⁻ᵏ attached at each index-k critical point, sharpening the homotopy form announced earlier (Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Remark 3.3).

name: Compatible almost complex structures exist on symplectic manifolds
text: every nondegenerate smooth two-form on a σ-compact Hausdorff manifold, in particular every symplectic form, admits a compatible almost complex structure, the manifold version of the linear statement announced earlier, with contractibility of the space of such structures not claimed (McDuff–Salamon, *Introduction to Symplectic Topology*, §4.1).

name: The contraction principle
text: if a family of measures satisfies a large deviation principle with good rate function I and f is continuous, the pushforwards under f satisfy a large deviation principle with the good rate function y ↦ inf{I(x) : f(x) = y} (Dembo–Zeitouni, *Large Deviations Techniques and Applications*, Thm 4.2.1).

name: The weak maximum principle for parabolic equations
text: a subsolution of ∂ₜu ≤ Σ aⁱʲ∂ᵢ∂ⱼu + b·∇u + cu with a ≥ 0 and c ≤ 0 is at most the maximum of u⁺ on the parabolic boundary, extending the heat-equation case announced earlier to variable coefficients (Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, §7.1.4).

name: Auslander’s theorem on global dimension
text: the global dimension of a semiprimary ring A, in particular of any Artinian ring or Artin algebra, equals the projective dimension of the single module A/J, where J is the Jacobson radical (Auslander, Nagoya Math. J. 9 (1955)).

name: Cartan’s second structure equation
text: for a connection on a vector bundle, the curvature matrix in a local frame is dA + A ∧ A, where A is the matrix of connection one-forms of the frame (Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, Ch. 7).

name: The block–cut tree
text: the incidence graph of the blocks and cut vertices of a graph is a forest, and for a finite graph it is a tree exactly when the graph is connected (Diestel, *Graph Theory*, Lemma 3.1.4).

name: Higher direct images are sheafified cohomology presheaves
text: for a morphism of schemes f : X → Y and a sheaf of 𝒪_X-modules M, the abelian sheaf underlying Rᵠf_*M is the sheafification of V ↦ Hᵠ(f⁻¹V, M), for every q (Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*, III.8.1).

name: The Cahen–Mellin integral
text: for real y > 0 and σ > 0, (1/2πi)∫_{Re s = σ} Γ(s) y⁻ˢ ds = e⁻ʸ, the Mellin inversion of Γ as the transform of e⁻ᵗ, with Γ integrable on every such vertical line (Titchmarsh, *The Theory of Functions*, §9.5).

name: The degree of the antipodal map
text: for n ≥ 1 and any orientation of Sⁿ, the antipodal map x ↦ −x has degree (−1)ⁿ⁺¹, computed as the signed count of preimages of a regular value (Milnor, *Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint*, §5).

name: Generators are balanced
text: if M is a generator of the category of R-modules, the action map from R to the endomorphisms of M over Γ = End_R(M) is bijective, and M is finitely generated projective over Γ (Anderson–Fuller, *Rings and Categories of Modules*, Thm 17.8).

name: Large deviation principles and good rate functions
text: a family of measures satisfies a large deviation principle with speed ε and rate function I when the open-set lower and closed-set upper bounds hold, and a rate function is good when its finite sublevel sets are compact (Dembo–Zeitouni, §1.2).

name: The real interpolation spaces (X₀, X₁)_θ,q
text: the K-method spaces of a compatible couple, Banach when the endpoints are, with the exact interpolation theorem: an operator bounded by M₀ and M₁ on the endpoints is bounded by M₀¹⁻ᶿM₁ᶿ between the interpolation spaces (Bergh–Löfström, *Interpolation Spaces*, Thm 3.1.2).

name: Krull–Schmidt categories
text: a preadditive category with finite biproducts in which every object is a finite biproduct of objects with local endomorphism rings; such a category is idempotent complete, and an object is indecomposable exactly when its endomorphism ring is local (Krause, Expo. Math. 33 (2015), §4).

name: Morse–Bott functions
text: a smooth function whose critical set is a locally finite disjoint union of nondegenerate critical submanifolds, given as a family of embeddings exhibiting its components, with Morse functions as the zero-dimensional case (Bott, Ann. of Math. 60 (1954)).

name: The Dirac gamma matrices in the Weyl representation
text: the chiral representation of the Clifford algebra Cl(3,1) on ℂ² ⊕ ℂ², with the anticommutation relations {Γᵘ, Γᵛ} = 2ηᵘᵛ, the chirality matrix Γ⁵ = diag(1, −1) and covariance under Spin(3,1) ≅ SL₂(ℂ) (Peskin–Schroeder, *An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory*, §3.2).

## What it says
For a field $k$, a commutative $k$-algebra $K$ and a formal power series $f \in K[[X]]$, the series is D-finite over $k$ exactly when its coefficient sequence is P-recursive over $k$.

- `{k K : Type*} [Field k] [CommRing K] [Algebra k K]`: the field $k$ and the commutative ring $K$ with its $k$-algebra structure, all implicit.
- `{f : K⟦X⟧}`: the power series, implicit.
- The left side, `IsDFinite k f`: $f$ satisfies a linear differential equation $\sum_{i \le n} p_i f^{(i)} = 0$ with coefficients $p_i \in k[X]$ and $p_n \neq 0$, where $k[X]$ acts on $K[[X]]$ by multiplication.
- The right side: there are $r$ and polynomials $q_0, \dots, q_r \in k[X]$ with $q_r \neq 0$ such that $\sum_{i=0}^{r} q_i(n)\, a_{n+i} = 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $a_m$ is the coefficient of $X^m$ in $f$ and $q_i(n)$ is $q_i$ evaluated at the image of $n$ in $k$.

This is the equivalence between D-finite (holonomic) generating functions and P-recursive sequences, in the form of Stanley's *Enumerative Combinatorics*, volume 2, §6.4, with the recurrence normalised to have a nonzero top coefficient. The book works in characteristic zero; the formal statement holds over every field.

## References and tests
- R. P. Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics*, volume 2, §6.4 (D-finite generating functions), the equivalence of D-finiteness and P-recursiveness.
- Roadmap: DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence, §5.1 "D-finite series and minimal equations", API item `isDFinite_iff_pRecursive`.

No test declaration is recorded; the geometric series in the same file is proved D-finite from its recurrence.

## Lean subtleties
- The sum on the right runs over `Fin (r + 1)`, so the recurrence has $r + 1$ terms $q_0(n) a_n, \dots, q_r(n) a_{n+r}$ and must hold for every $n \ge 0$, not only for large $n$.
- `(q i).eval (n : k)` casts the natural number $n$ into $k$. In characteristic $p$ this cast is periodic, and both sides of the equivalence become degenerate (for instance $q_0 = X^p - X$ annihilates every sequence); the statement is still true there, but its content lies in characteristic zero.
- `IsDFinite k f` asks for a nonzero leading coefficient $p_n \neq 0$, not merely a nonzero equation; the two are equivalent, as a nonzero equation can be shortened.
- `[Field k]` and `[Algebra k K]` are typeclass hypotheses, found by Lean.

## What it says
Over an Iwanaga–Gorenstein ring $A$, a module $M$ is Gorenstein-projective exactly when it is finitely generated and $\operatorname{Ext}^{i}_A(M, A) = 0$ for every $i \ge 1$.

- `{A : Type u} [Ring A]`: an associative unital ring, not necessarily commutative.
- `[IsIwanagaGorenstein A]`: $A$ is left and right noetherian and has finite injective dimension as a left module and as a right module over itself.
- `(M : ModuleCat.{u} A)`: a left $A$-module in universe `u`.
- `IsGorensteinProjective A M`: $M$ is isomorphic to the degree-zero cycles of a totally acyclic complex of finitely generated projective modules, a complete resolution.
- The right side: `Module.Finite A M`, $M$ is finitely generated, and every element of `Ext M (ModuleCat.of A A) (n + 1)` is zero for every natural $n$, that is $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}(M, A) = 0$.

This is the classical description of Gorenstein-projective (maximal Cohen–Macaulay, totally reflexive) modules over a Gorenstein ring as the finitely generated modules Ext-orthogonal to the ring, in the two-sided noetherian generality of Iwanaga–Gorenstein rings. The forward direction holds over any ring; the converse is the content, proved through the Auslander–Bridger transpose.

## References and tests
- M. Auslander and M. Bridger, *Stable module theory*, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 94 (1969), Theorem (2.17) and Proposition (3.8), the inputs named by the module.
- Roadmap: StablePeriodicCurved, Layer 2 (self-injective modules, total acyclicity and singularities), target `isGorensteinProjective_iff_ext_eq_zero`.

No declaration testing this theorem is recorded. The forward direction, `IsGorensteinProjective.ext_eq_zero`, and the finiteness `IsGorensteinProjective.finite` are separate declarations of the library used in the proof.

## Lean subtleties
- `Ext` is Mathlib's `CategoryTheory.Abelian.Ext` in the abelian category `ModuleCat.{u} A`; the vanishing is stated as "every element is zero" rather than as an isomorphism with a zero object.
- The index is written `n + 1` with `n : ℕ`, so it covers exactly the positive degrees; $\operatorname{Ext}^0(M, A) = \operatorname{Hom}(M, A)$ is not constrained.
- `IsGorensteinProjective` is a complete resolution by finitely generated projectives, so finite generation is built into the left side; the right side states it explicitly.
- `[IsIwanagaGorenstein A]` is a typeclass hypothesis and does not fix the injective dimension; the proof uses the right injective dimension $d$ of $A$ as the syzygy depth.
- Over the zero ring every module is zero and both sides hold.

## What it says
The Monsky–Washnitzer weak completion of a finitely generated algebra over the valuation ring of a complete non-archimedean field is a noetherian ring, provided that valuation ring is noetherian.

- `{K : Type*} [NormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]`: a complete field with a non-archimedean absolute value.
- `O`, the local notation for `Subring.unitClosedBall K`: the closed unit ball $K^\circ = \{x : |x| \le 1\}$, the valuation ring of $K$.
- `{S : Type*} [CommRing S] [Algebra O S] [Algebra.FiniteType O S]`: a commutative $K^\circ$-algebra of finite type.
- `[IsNoetherianRing O]`: the valuation ring is noetherian, which for a nontrivially valued $K$ means $K$ is discretely valued.
- `{π : O} (hπ : π ≠ 0) (hπ1 : ‖(π : K)‖ < 1)`: a nonzero topologically nilpotent element of $K^\circ$, the parameter of the completion.
- Conclusion: `IsNoetherianRing (weakCompletion π S)`, where `weakCompletion π S` is the $K^\circ$-subalgebra $S^\dagger$ of the $\pi$-adic completion of $S$ cut out by the degree-growth condition on a finite generating family.

This is Fulton's theorem that weakly complete finitely generated algebras in the sense of Monsky and Washnitzer are noetherian, in the setting of a noetherian valuation ring; the proof presents $S^\dagger$ as a quotient of the integral Monsky–Washnitzer algebra $K^\circ\langle X_1, \dots, X_n\rangle^\dagger$, whose noetherianity is already in the library.

## References and tests
- W. Fulton, *A note on weakly complete algebras*, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 75 (1969), 591–593.
- P. Monsky and G. Washnitzer, *Formal cohomology: I*, Ann. of Math. 88 (1968), §2, as cited by the module.
- M. van der Put, *The cohomology of Monsky and Washnitzer*, §2, (2.1)–(2.2), the presentation used in the proof.
- Roadmap: AdicSpacesPartIV, milestone F1.5 (weak completions and algebras of Monsky–Washnitzer type), target `weak-completion-noetherian`.

No declaration testing this theorem is recorded on the site.

## Lean subtleties
- `weakCompletion π S` is defined through a chosen finite generating family (classical choice inside the definition); the library proves the result is independent of the family.
- If the absolute value of $K$ is trivial then $K^\circ = K$ and no $\pi$ with $|\pi| < 1$ exists, so the hypotheses are empty there; the theorem has content only for nontrivially valued $K$.
- Neither flatness nor $\pi$-adic separatedness of $S$ is assumed; $S$ may have $\pi$-torsion.
- `IsNoetherianRing` for a commutative ring is the ascending chain condition on ideals, as usual.

## What it says
The BMO seminorm of a function $f$ on a pseudometric measure space: the supremum over all open balls $B$ of the mean oscillation of $f$ on $B$.

- `{X F : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]`: a pseudometric space with a σ-algebra, and a real normed space of values.
- `(f : X → F) (μ : Measure X)`: the function and the measure.
- Value: $\|f\|_{BMO} = \sup_{c \in X,\, r \in \mathbb{R}} ⨍^-_{B(c,r)} \|f - f_{B(c,r)}\|\, d\mu$ in $[0, \infty]$, where $f_B = ⨍_B f\, d\mu$ is the (Bochner) average of $f$ on $B$ and $⨍^-$ is the lower (Lebesgue) average of the extended norm.

This is the John–Nirenberg seminorm $\sup_B \frac{1}{|B|}\int_B |f - f_B|$, taken over balls rather than cubes; on $\mathbb{R}^n$ the two choices give comparable seminorms and the same space.

## References and tests
- F. John and L. Nirenberg, *On functions of bounded mean oscillation*, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 14 (1961), 415–426.
- L. Grafakos, *Modern Fourier Analysis*, 3rd ed., §3.1.
- Roadmap: PDE, §2.4 "Gehring, BMO and VMO (B11)", target `bmoseminorm`.

No test declaration is recorded. The library proves the expected properties: the seminorm is the supremum of the sharp maximal function, vanishes on constants and only on a.e. constant functions (on proper spaces with measures finite on compacts), is subadditive and homogeneous, is at most $2\|f\|_\infty$, and is invariant under translation and dilation on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Lean subtleties
- The value lies in `ℝ≥0∞`, so the seminorm is defined for every function, finite or not.
- Balls of radius $r \le 0$ are empty and contribute $0$. A ball of infinite measure also contributes $0$, since Lean's average over a set of infinite measure is $0$; in the standard setting all balls have finite measure.
- If $f$ is not integrable on a ball, Lean's average $f_B$ is $0$ there and the term becomes $⨍^-_B \|f\|$, which is consistent with $f$ failing to be BMO.
- The enorm `‖·‖ₑ` is the norm as an extended real, so the inner integral never fails for integrability reasons.

## What it says
A function has bounded mean oscillation when it is locally integrable and its BMO seminorm is finite.

- `{X F : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]`: the ambient pseudometric measure space and the real normed space of values.
- `(f : X → F) (μ : Measure X)`: the function and the measure.
- Value: `LocallyIntegrable f μ ∧ bmoSeminorm f μ < ∞`, that is $f$ is integrable on a neighbourhood of every point and $\sup_B ⨍_B \|f - f_B\| < \infty$.

This is the space $BMO$ of John and Nirenberg as a predicate on functions, in the generality of a pseudometric measure space; on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Lebesgue measure it is the usual space. The library proves that it is closed under sums (on second countable spaces), scalars, negation and a.e. modification, and that bounded functions belong to it with $\|f\|_{BMO} \le 2\|f\|_\infty$.

## References and tests
- F. John and L. Nirenberg, *On functions of bounded mean oscillation*, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 14 (1961), 415–426.
- L. Grafakos, *Modern Fourier Analysis*, 3rd ed., §3.1.
- Roadmap: PDE, §2.4 "Gehring, BMO and VMO (B11)", the carrier `BMO(ℝⁿ)`.

No test declaration is recorded. `MeasureTheory.MemLp.memBMO`, that every $L^\infty$ function (for a locally finite measure) has bounded mean oscillation, is the library's check that the space contains what it should.

## Lean subtleties
- Local integrability is part of the definition, not a consequence: a finite seminorm alone does not force $f_B$ to be a genuine average, since Lean sets the average of a non-integrable function to $0$.
- Local integrability in Mathlib means integrability on a neighbourhood of each point, which on a proper space is integrability on every ball, but on a general pseudometric space is weaker.
- The predicate is not a quotient by constants; two functions differing by a constant both satisfy it, with equal seminorm.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses found by Lean.

## What it says
The VMO modulus $\eta_f(r)$ of a function $f$: the supremum of its mean oscillations over the open balls of radius at most $r$.

- `{X F : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]`: the pseudometric measure space and the real normed space of values.
- `(f : X → F) (μ : Measure X) (r : ℝ)`: the function, the measure and the radius bound.
- Value: $\eta_f(r) = \sup_{c \in X,\ s \le r} ⨍^-_{B(c,s)} \|f - f_{B(c,s)}\|\,d\mu$ in $[0, \infty]$.

This is Sarason's modulus for vanishing mean oscillation, with the smallness of a ball measured by its radius rather than by its measure; on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Lebesgue measure the two agree up to $|B(c,r)| = \omega_n r^n$. The library proves it monotone in $r$, bounded by the BMO seminorm, and with supremum over all $r$ equal to the BMO seminorm.

## References and tests
- D. Sarason, *Functions of vanishing mean oscillation*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 207 (1975), 391–405.
- Roadmap: PDE, §2.4 "Gehring, BMO and VMO (B11)", the modulus `η(r)`.

No test declaration is recorded. `TauCeti.iSup_vmoModulus`, $\sup_r \eta_f(r) = \|f\|_{BMO}$, and `TauCeti.monotone_vmoModulus` are the library's consistency checks.

## Lean subtleties
- For $r \le 0$ every ball in the supremum is empty, so $\eta_f(r) = 0$.
- The supremum is over all radii $s \le r$ including negative ones, which contribute $0$.
- Values are in `ℝ≥0∞`; the Bochner average $f_B$ is $0$ when $f$ is not integrable on $B$, as for the BMO seminorm.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses found by Lean.

## What it says
A function has vanishing mean oscillation when it has bounded mean oscillation and its VMO modulus tends to zero with the radius.

- `{X F : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]`: the pseudometric measure space and the real normed space of values.
- `(f : X → F) (μ : Measure X)`: the function and the measure.
- Value: `MemBMO f μ ∧ Tendsto (vmoModulus f μ) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 0)`, that is $f \in BMO$ and $\eta_f(r) \to 0$ as $r \to 0^+$.

This is Sarason's space $VMO$, the functions whose mean oscillation over small balls is uniformly small. The library proves that $VMO$ is a subspace of $BMO$ closed for the BMO seminorm, that uniformly continuous $BMO$ functions and continuous compactly supported functions belong to it, which is the easy half of Sarason's description of $VMO$ as the $BMO$-closure of the uniformly continuous functions.

## References and tests
- D. Sarason, *Functions of vanishing mean oscillation*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 207 (1975), 391–405.
- Roadmap: PDE, §2.4 "Gehring, BMO and VMO (B11)", the carrier `VMO(ℝⁿ)`.

No test declaration is recorded. `Continuous.memVMO_of_hasCompactSupport` and `UniformContinuous.memVMO` are the library's checks that the space contains the expected functions.

## Lean subtleties
- `𝓝[>] 0` is the filter of right neighbourhoods of $0$: the limit is taken along radii $r > 0$, where the modulus is meaningful; for $r \le 0$ it is $0$.
- Smallness of a ball is measured by its radius, not its measure, as the docstring notes; on $\mathbb{R}^n$ the two are equivalent.
- The predicate includes `MemBMO`, hence local integrability, as part of its meaning.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses found by Lean.

## What it says
Over a commutative ring of characteristic two, the strands algebra with its crossing-resolution differential is an ungraded differential algebra: the differential satisfies the Leibniz rule and squares to zero.

- `{R : Type*} [CommRing R] [CharP R 2]`: a commutative ring with $2 = 0$, such as $\mathbb{F}_2$.
- `{α : Type*} [LinearOrder α] [Fintype α]`: a finite linear order, the set of positions $\{1, \dots, n\}$ in the case `Fin n`.
- Conclusion: `IsUngradedDGAlgebra (differential R α)`, where `differential R α` is the $R$-linear endomorphism of `StrandsAlgebra R α` sending a strand diagram to the sum of its resolutions at crossings whose resolution has exactly one crossing fewer; the predicate asks for $d(xy) = (dx)y + x(dy)$ and $d \circ d = 0$.

For $R = \mathbb{F}_2$ and $\alpha = \{1,\dots,n\}$ this is the statement that the strands algebra $\mathcal{A}(n)$ of Lipshitz, Ozsváth and Thurston is a differential algebra, as in §3.1 of their monograph: there the differential is defined by resolving one crossing at a time and keeping the terms where the number of crossings drops by exactly one, and $d^2 = 0$ and the Leibniz rule are verified over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The grading by the noncommutative grading group and the subalgebra $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z})$ of a pointed matched circle are not part of this statement.

## References and tests
- R. Lipshitz, P. Ozsváth and D. Thurston, *Bordered Heegaard Floer homology*, arXiv:0810.0687, §3.1, Definition 3.2.
- Roadmap: HeegaardFloer, Layer 7, §7.4 "The bordered algebra and finite tensor interface (F5.4)", target `strands-algebra-differential`.

No test declaration is recorded on the site. The component identities `TauCeti.StrandsAlgebra.differential_mul` (Leibniz) and `TauCeti.StrandsAlgebra.differential_differential` ($d^2 = 0$) are the two fields of the conclusion.

## Lean subtleties
- Characteristic two is a typeclass hypothesis; without it the Leibniz rule would need signs, which the differential does not carry. The algebra itself is defined over any commutative semiring.
- "Ungraded" means no grading enters the Leibniz rule; the algebra is not given a $\mathbb{Z}$-grading here.
- Resolutions that lower the crossing number by more than one, or that produce a double crossing, are omitted, as in the source.

## What it says
A pseudodifferential operator of order $m$ with symbol of compact spatial support extends to a bounded operator $H^s \to H^{s-m}$ between Bessel-potential Sobolev spaces, for every real $s$.

- `{n : ℕ} {m : ℝ}`: the dimension and the order.
- `{V W : Type*}` with `[NormedAddCommGroup] [NormedSpace ℂ] [CompleteSpace] [FiniteDimensional ℂ]` for each: finite-dimensional complex normed spaces of values, whose norms need not come from inner products.
- `(a : Symbol n V W m)`: a smooth function $a(x,\xi)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n$ with values in operators $V \to W$ satisfying the local symbol estimates $\|\partial_x^\alpha \partial_\xi^\beta a\| \le C \langle\xi\rangle^{m - |\beta|}$ uniformly for $x$ in compact sets.
- `(ha : a.HasCompactSpatialSupport)`: $a(x, \xi) = 0$ for $x$ outside a compact set, for all $\xi$.
- `(s : ℝ)`: the Sobolev index.
- Conclusion: there is a bounded linear operator $T : H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^n; V) \to H^{s-m}(\mathbb{R}^n; W)$ such that for every Schwartz $u$, $T u$ is the tempered distribution $\varphi \mapsto \int \varphi(x)\, (\mathrm{Op}(a)u)(x)\,dx$, where $\mathrm{Op}(a)u$ is the left quantization on Schwartz functions.

This is the Sobolev mapping property of pseudodifferential operators, $\mathrm{Op}(a) : H^s \to H^{s-m}$, in the compactly $x$-supported case treated in Taylor's MSRI lectures; the general theorem for uniform symbols (Hörmander, Theorem 18.1.13) is not covered.

## References and tests
- M. E. Taylor, *Pseudodifferential Operators: Four Lectures at MSRI*, Lecture I, (3.31).
- L. Hörmander, *The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators III*, Theorem 18.1.13, the uniform-symbol statement this specialises.
- Roadmap: PseudodifferentialOperators, Layer 5, §5.1 "Hilbert-scale mapping estimates" (P5.1), target `exists_quantizeSobolev`.

No test declaration is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- The statement is existential: the operator is characterised by its values on Schwartz functions, which are dense in $H^s$ for $p = 2$, so it is unique (`BesselPotentialSpace.continuousLinearMap_ext`).
- `H^{s}(CoordinateSpace n, V)` is Mathlib's Bessel-potential space at $p = 2$; `toDistr` is its inclusion into tempered distributions.
- The symbol class is the local one (bounds uniform on compact $x$-sets), which under compact spatial support is the same as the uniform class.
- `[FiniteDimensional ℂ V]` is a typeclass hypothesis; the Hilbert-space case is `TauCeti.Symbol.quantizeSobolev`.

## What it says
For $n \ge 1$, the evaluation map $SO(1+n) \to S^n$, $A \mapsto A e_0$, is a Serre fibration.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n]`: a natural number $n \ne 0$.
- The map: `specialOrthogonalSphereMap n`, sending a special orthogonal $(1+n) \times (1+n)$ real matrix $A$ to its first column $A e_0$, a unit vector of $\mathbb{R}^{1+n}$, packaged with its continuity as a morphism of `TopCat`.
- Conclusion: this morphism belongs to `TopCat.serreFibrations`, the class of maps with the homotopy lifting property for finite CW complexes (equivalently for cubes).

This is the classical fibre bundle $SO(n) \to SO(n+1) \to S^n$ of Steenrod and Hatcher, used to compute homotopy groups of the rotation groups; the proof exhibits local trivialisations over the complement of each point, from the rotation taking a unit vector $b$ to $y \ne -b$ given by two reflections, so the map is a locally trivial bundle with fibre the block subgroup $\mathrm{diag}(1, SO(n))$, hence a Serre fibration.

## What it says

## What it says
The LKJ law of positive shape on correlation matrices is a probability measure.

## What it says
The mean of the LKJ law of positive shape is the identity matrix.

- `{p : ℕ} {η : ℝ}`: the matrix size and the shape parameter.
- `(hη : 0 < η)`: positive shape.
- Conclusion: the Bochner integral $\int R \, d(\mathrm{LKJ}_{p,\eta})(R)$ over the real symmetric $p \times p$ matrices equals the identity matrix $1$, as an element of the self-adjoint matrices.

This is the expectation of an LKJ-distributed correlation matrix: the diagonal is $1$ almost surely, and sign symmetry (the law is invariant under $R \mapsto DRD$ for diagonal $D$ with entries $\pm 1$) forces every off-diagonal entry to have mean zero. Integrability is proved separately (`TauCeti.Probability.integrable_id_lkjMeasure`), since the matrices are bounded on the support.

name: D-finite power series are exactly those with P-recursive coefficients
text: a power series over a field satisfies a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients exactly when its coefficients satisfy a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients and nonzero leading coefficient (Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics* vol. 2, §6.4).

name: Gorenstein-projective modules over an Iwanaga–Gorenstein ring
text: over a two-sided noetherian ring of finite self-injective dimension on both sides, a module is Gorenstein-projective exactly when it is finitely generated with Extⁱ(M, A) = 0 for all i > 0 (Buchweitz, *Maximal Cohen–Macaulay Modules and Tate Cohomology*, 1986).

name: Weak completions of finitely generated algebras are noetherian
text: the Monsky–Washnitzer weak completion of a finitely generated algebra over the valuation ring of a complete non-archimedean field is noetherian whenever that valuation ring is (Fulton, *Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.* 75 (1969)).

name: The multicolour Szemerédi regularity lemma
text: a colouring of the pairs of a finite vertex set with finitely many colours admits an equipartition into at least l and at most M(ε, l) parts whose colour-irregular pairs of parts cover at most ε|V|² pairs, extending Mathlib's one-graph case (Komlós–Simonovits 1996, Thm 1.18).

name: The fibration SO(n) → SO(n+1) → Sⁿ
text: for n ≥ 1, evaluating a rotation of ℝⁿ⁺¹ on a fixed unit vector is a locally trivial bundle over the sphere with fibre SO(n), hence a Serre fibration (Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §4.2).

name: Functions of bounded and of vanishing mean oscillation
text: on a metric measure space, the BMO seminorm sup_B ⨍_B ‖f − f_B‖ and the spaces BMO and VMO, with L^∞ ⊆ BMO, ‖f‖_BMO = 0 exactly for a.e. constants, and VMO closed in BMO containing the uniformly continuous BMO functions (Grafakos, *Modern Fourier Analysis*, §3.1).

## What it says
A cochain complex is bounded exactly when its terms vanish outside a finite set of degrees.

- `(C : Type u)`, `[Category C]`, `[HasZeroMorphisms C]`: a category with zero morphisms.
- `(K : CochainComplex C ℤ)`: a cochain complex over $C$ indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$.
- The conclusion: `CochainComplex.bounded C K` (there are $a$, $b$ with $K^n$ zero for $n < a$ and for $n > b$) holds if and only if there is a finite set $s \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ (a `Finset ℤ`) such that $K^n$ is a zero object for every $n \notin s$.

This is the "finitely many nonzero terms" description of a bounded complex, the form used for alternating sums over the degrees of a complex. The equivalence is elementary: the interval $[a, b]$ is finite, and a finite set of integers has a least and a greatest element.

## What it says

## What it says
On $\operatorname{Proj} A$ the sections $r/1$ are multiplicative: for homogeneous $r$ of degree $m$ and $r'$ of degree $n$, the product of $r/1 \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal O(m))$ and $r'/1 \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal O(n))$ is $rr'/1 \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal O(m+n))$.

- `[CommRing A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring.
- `[SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: σ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: 𝒜, a family of such subgroups indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, is a grading of $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d \mathcal A_d$ with $\mathcal A_i \mathcal A_j \subseteq \mathcal A_{i+j}$.
- `(hi : ↑i = m)`: the natural number $i$, viewed as an integer, equals the integer $m$.
- `(hj : ↑j = n)`: likewise the natural number $j$ equals the integer $n$.
- `(U : (Proj 𝒜).Opens)`: an open set $U$ of $\operatorname{Proj} A$.
- `(r : ↥(𝒜 i))`: a homogeneous element $r$ of $A$ of degree $i$.
- `(r' : ↥(𝒜 j))`: a homogeneous element $r'$ of degree $j$.
- The conclusion: `twistingSheaf.mul`, the product $\Gamma(U, \mathcal O(m)) \times \Gamma(U, \mathcal O(n)) \to \Gamma(U, \mathcal O(m+n))$, takes the sections $r/1$ and $r'/1$ given by `toTwistingSheaf` to the section $rr'/1$, where $rr'$ is the product in $A$, of degree $i + j$.

Classically $r \mapsto r/1$ maps $A_d$ to $\Gamma(X, \mathcal O(d))$, and these maps together form a homomorphism of graded rings $\bigoplus_d A_d \to \bigoplus_d \Gamma(X, \mathcal O(d))$. This lemma is its multiplicativity, over each open $U$.

- Stacks, Section 27.10, display (27.10.1.3) — the map of graded rings $S \to \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X(n))$ for $X = \operatorname{Proj} S$, sending $r \in S_d$ to $r/1$; this lemma is its multiplicativity, over every open set $U$ and not only over $X$.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- The `⋯` in the signature are proofs that the docs elide: that $rr'$ lies in $\mathcal A_{i+j}$, and that $i + j$, viewed as an integer, equals $m + n$. They do not affect what is stated.

## What it says
The map $r \mapsto r/1$ from the homogeneous elements of degree $j$ of a graded ring $A$ to the sections of the twisting sheaf $\mathcal O(n)$ on $\operatorname{Proj} A$, for $j = n$, as a homomorphism of additive groups.

- `[CommRing A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring.
- `[SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: σ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `(𝒜 : ℕ → σ)`: the family 𝒜 of subgroups $\mathcal A_d$ of $A$, one for each degree $d \in \mathbb{N}$.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: 𝒜 is a grading of $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d \mathcal A_d$ with $\mathcal A_i \mathcal A_j \subseteq \mathcal A_{i+j}$.
- `(h : ↑j = n)`: the degree $j$, a natural number viewed as an integer, equals the twist $n$.
- `(U : (Proj 𝒜).Opens)`: an open set $U$ of $\operatorname{Proj} A$.
- The type: an additive map from $\mathcal A_j$ to $\Gamma(U, \mathcal O(n))$.

Its value sends $r \in \mathcal A_j$ to the section $r/1$: the function that gives each point $x$ of $U$ the fraction $r/1$ in the localization $A_x$. It is built with `twistingSheaf.const`, the section $r/s$ for homogeneous $r$ and $s$ with $\deg r = \deg s + n$, taking $s = 1$ of degree $0$; since $1$ vanishes nowhere, this works on every open set. It preserves $0$ and sums, since $0/1 = 0$ and $r/1 + r'/1 = (r + r')/1$. Over $U = \operatorname{Proj} A$ these maps are the components of the natural graded map $A \to \bigoplus_n \Gamma(\operatorname{Proj} A, \mathcal O(n))$, as the docstring says.

## References and tests
- Hartshorne II.5 — the natural graded map from $A$ to $\bigoplus_n \Gamma(\operatorname{Proj} A, \mathcal O(n))$, whose components these maps are over all of $\operatorname{Proj} A$.
- Stacks, Section 27.10, display (27.10.1.3) — the map of graded rings $S \to \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X(n))$ for $X = \operatorname{Proj} S$; over $U = \operatorname{Proj} A$ this map sends $r \in A_n$ to the section $r/1$.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- Degrees of elements are natural numbers, since the grading is by $\mathbb{N}$, while twists are integers; `h` ties the degree $j$ to the twist $n$. For $n < 0$ no such $j$ exists, so the map is only available for twists $\geq 0$, as an $\mathbb{N}$-graded ring has no elements of negative degree.
- `→+` is a homomorphism of additive groups: it preserves $0$ and $+$, and nothing more is claimed.
- `↥(𝒜 j)` is the subgroup $\mathcal A_j$ made into a type.
- Sections of $\mathcal O(n)$ here are functions into the full localizations $A_x$ that are locally fractions of degree $n$; $r/1$ is such a fraction everywhere.
- `(twistingSheaf 𝒜 n).presheaf.obj (Opposite.op U)` is $\Gamma(U, \mathcal O(n))$; `Opposite.op` appears because a presheaf is a contravariant functor.
- The square-bracket hypotheses are typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself.

## What it says
For an open set $U$ of $\operatorname{Proj} A$ and integers $m$ and $n$, `mul 𝒜 U m n` is the multiplication of sections $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m)) \times \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(n)) \to \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m+n))$, bilinear over the ring $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Proj} A})$.

- `[CommRing A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$.
- `[SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: each element of the type `σ` stands for an additive subgroup of $A$.
- `(𝒜 : ℕ → σ)`: a family `𝒜` of such subgroups, $A_d$ = `𝒜 d` for $d \in \mathbb{N}$.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: the family grades $A$: $A = \bigoplus_{d \ge 0} A_d$ with $A_d A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$.
- `(U : (Proj 𝒜).Opens)`: an open set `U` of the scheme $\operatorname{Proj} A$.
- `(m n : ℤ)`: two twists `m` and `n`.
- The type: a map from the sections of `twistingSheaf 𝒜 m` over $U$ to the linear maps from the sections of `twistingSheaf 𝒜 n` to those of `twistingSheaf 𝒜 (m + n)`, linear over the ring of sections of the structure sheaf over $U$; that is, a bilinear map in curried form.

Its value is built by `LinearMap.mk₂` from the map sending sections $s$ and $t$ to the function $x \mapsto s(x)\,t(x)$, the product taken in the localization $A_{\mathfrak p_x}$ of $A$ at the prime of $x$, with the proof (`isLocallyFraction_mul`) that it is a local fraction of degree $m + n$: a product $(r/g)(r'/g') = rr'/(gg')$ of fractions of degrees $m$ and $n$ has degree $m + n$. Bilinearity comes from distributivity, associativity and commutativity in each $A_{\mathfrak p_x}$.

This is the standard multiplication of sections of twisting sheaves, the one underlying the map $\mathcal{O}(m) \otimes \mathcal{O}(n) \to \mathcal{O}(m+n)$.

## References and tests
- Hartshorne II.5 — the twisting sheaves on $\operatorname{Proj}$ and the map $\mathcal{O}(m) \otimes \mathcal{O}(n) \to \mathcal{O}(m+n)$, which this multiplication gives on sections.
- Stacks, Section 27.10, display (27.10.1.1) — the canonical maps $\mathcal{O}_X(n) \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(m) \to \mathcal{O}_X(n+m)$, which come from $S(n) \otimes_S S(m) = S(n+m)$ and are not isomorphisms in general; on sections over $U$ they are given by this bilinear map.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `[CommRing A]`, `[SetLike σ A]`, `[AddSubgroupClass σ A]` and `[GradedRing 𝒜]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds these structures by itself. The grading is by `ℕ`; the twists are in `ℤ`.
- The sections of every twist are functions into the same rings, the whole localizations $A_{\mathfrak p_x}$ (`Localizations`), so the product of a section of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ and one of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ is their pointwise product there.
- `M →ₗ[R] N →ₗ[R] P` is a map linear over the ring $R$ into maps linear over $R$: a bilinear map $M \times N \to P$. Here $R$ is `(Proj 𝒜).presheaf.obj (Opposite.op U)`, the ring of sections of the structure sheaf over $U$.
- The `↑` turns these objects of categories of groups and rings into their sets of elements; `Opposite.op U` is $U$ in the opposite category, as presheaves are contravariant.
- `Type u` and `Type u_1` are universe levels, which do not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
On $X = \operatorname{Proj} A$, the product of sections of twisting sheaves is additive in its second factor: for a section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ and sections $t, t'$ of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ over the same open set $U$, $s\,(t + t') = s\,t + s\,t'$ as sections of $\mathcal{O}(m+n)$ over $U$.

- `[CommRing A] [SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$, and $\sigma$ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: the implicit family `𝒜 : ℕ → σ`, $d \mapsto A_d$, grades $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d A_d$ and $A_d A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$. The implicit `m n : ℤ` are the two twists, and `U` is an open set of the scheme $X$.
- `(s : ↑Γ(Proj.twistingSheaf 𝒜 m, U))`: a section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ over $U$.
- `(t t' : ↑Γ(Proj.twistingSheaf 𝒜 n, U))`: two sections $t, t'$ of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ over $U$.
- The conclusion: with `mul 𝒜 U m n` the multiplication $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m)) \times \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(n)) \to \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m+n))$, applied first to $s$ and then to the second factor, the product of $s$ with $t + t'$ is the sum of the products of $s$ with $t$ and with $t'$.

The sections of every twist are functions into the localizations $A_x$ of $A$ at the points $x$ of $U$, multiplied and added pointwise, so this is the distributive law $s(x)\,(t(x) + t'(x)) = s(x)\,t(x) + s(x)\,t'(x)$ in each ring $A_x$. It is the additivity in the second variable of the bilinear map through which the product $\mathcal{O}(m) \otimes \mathcal{O}(n) \to \mathcal{O}(m+n)$ is given on sections.

## What it says
On $X = \operatorname{Proj} A$, the product of sections of twisting sheaves is linear in its second factor over the sections of the structure sheaf: for a section $r$ of $\mathcal{O}_X$, a section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ and a section $t$ of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ over the same open set $U$, $s\,(r \cdot t) = r \cdot (s\,t)$ as sections of $\mathcal{O}(m+n)$ over $U$.

- `[CommRing A] [SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$, and $\sigma$ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: the implicit family `𝒜 : ℕ → σ`, $d \mapsto A_d$, grades $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d A_d$ and $A_d A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$. The implicit `m n : ℤ` are the two twists, and `U` is an open set of the scheme $X$.
- `(r : ↑Γ(Proj 𝒜, U))`: a section $r$ of the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$ over $U$, a function whose value at each point $x$ lies in the homogeneous localization $A_{(x)}$.
- `(s : ↑Γ(Proj.twistingSheaf 𝒜 m, U))`: a section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ over $U$.
- `(t : ↑Γ(Proj.twistingSheaf 𝒜 n, U))`: a section $t$ of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ over $U$.
- The conclusion: with `mul 𝒜 U m n` the multiplication $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m)) \times \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(n)) \to \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m+n))$, the product of $s$ with $r \cdot t$ is $r$ times the product of $s$ with $t$, where $\cdot$ (Lean's `•`) is the action of $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_X)$ that makes each $\mathcal{O}(k)$ a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules.

Pointwise, the action multiplies by $r(x)$, viewed in the localization $A_x$ of $A$ at $x$, and the product of sections multiplies values in $A_x$; so this is $s(x)\,(r(x)\,t(x)) = r(x)\,(s(x)\,t(x))$ in each commutative ring $A_x$. It is the $\mathcal{O}_X$-linearity in the second variable of the bilinear map through which $\mathcal{O}(m) \otimes \mathcal{O}(n) \to \mathcal{O}(m+n)$ is given on sections.

## What it says
For a graded commutative ring $A = \bigoplus_{d \ge 0} A_d$, the twisting sheaf $\mathcal{O}(0)$ on $X = \operatorname{Proj} A$ is isomorphic, as a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules, to the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$ regarded as a module over itself. This definition is that isomorphism.

- `[CommRing A] [SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$, and $\sigma$ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `(𝒜 : ℕ → σ)`: the family $d \mapsto A_d$ of graded pieces, indexed by the natural numbers.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: this family grades $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d A_d$ and $A_d A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$.
- Its type, `SheafOfModules.unit (Proj 𝒜).ringCatSheaf ≅ twistingSheaf 𝒜 0`: an isomorphism of sheaves of modules over the structure sheaf of $\operatorname{Proj} A$, from the free module of rank one on it, $\mathcal{O}_X$ itself, to $\mathcal{O}(0)$.

Its value: over each open set $U$, a section of $\mathcal{O}_X$ is a function with values $a(x)$ in the homogeneous localizations $A_{(x)}$, and a section of $\mathcal{O}(0)$ is a function with values in the localizations $A_x$ that is locally a fraction of degree $0$. The inclusions $A_{(x)} \to A_x$ identify the two, as modules over the sections of $\mathcal{O}_X$ over $U$ (`sectionsLinearEquivTwistingSheafZero`). These isomorphisms commute with restriction, so they form an isomorphism of presheaves of modules (`PresheafOfModules.isoMk`). It is lifted to sheaves of modules, since the forgetful functor from sheaves to presheaves of modules is fully faithful (`SheafOfModules.fullyFaithfulForget`).

This is the standard identification of $\mathcal{O}(0)$ with the structure sheaf, made by the canonical comparison maps.

## References and tests
- Hartshorne II.5 — the twisting sheaves $\mathcal{O}(n)$ on $\operatorname{Proj}$, of which $\mathcal{O}(0)$ is the structure sheaf.
- Stacks, Definition 27.10.1 — for $X = \operatorname{Proj} S$ it defines $\mathcal{O}_X(n) = \widetilde{S(n)}$, which at $n = 0$ is $\widetilde{S}$; by Definition 27.8.3 the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$ is the sheaf of rings that agrees with $\widetilde{S}$ on the standard opens $D_+(f)$. Section 27.10 does not state $\mathcal{O}_X(0) = \mathcal{O}_X$ in so many words; it is these two definitions together.
- `AlgebraicGeometry.Proj.unitIsoTwistingSheafZero_hom_app_apply` — over each open set $U$ the isomorphism sends a section $a$ of $\mathcal{O}_X$ to `sectionsLinearEquivTwistingSheafZero 𝒜 U a`, the function $x \mapsto a(x)$ read in $A_x$.
- `AlgebraicGeometry.Proj.unitIsoTwistingSheafZero_inv_app_apply` — over each open set its inverse is the inverse of that comparison.

The two tests pin the isomorphism down: it is the canonical comparison through the inclusions $A_{(x)} \to A_x$, not merely some isomorphism between the two sheaves.

## Lean subtleties
- `SheafOfModules.unit` of a sheaf of rings is that sheaf viewed as a sheaf of modules over itself, the free one of rank one. `(Proj 𝒜).ringCatSheaf` is the structure sheaf of the scheme $\operatorname{Proj} A$ as a sheaf of rings (`RingCat`, forgetting commutativity), over which sheaves of modules are taken.
- `≅` is an isomorphism in a category: a morphism with a two-sided inverse. Here the category is that of sheaves of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules, so the isomorphism is $\mathcal{O}_X$-linear, not only an isomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups.
- $A_{(x)}$ consists of the fractions $f/g$ with $f$ and $g$ homogeneous of the same degree and $g \notin x$; $A_x$ holds fractions of every degree, and the sections of $\mathcal{O}(0)$ are those of its functions that are locally of degree $0$.
- It is a `def`, not a theorem: it gives one specific isomorphism, the canonical one, from which the bare fact that the two sheaves are isomorphic follows.
- The grading is indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, and the twist $0$ is the integer $0$ of the family $\mathcal{O}(n)$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.
- The square brackets carry hypotheses as typeclasses: Lean finds the ring structure and the grading by itself. `Type u` and `Type u_1` are universe levels, which do not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
The naive moduli problem $[\Gamma(N)]$ over `Ell/B`: to $E/S$ it assigns the homomorphisms $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(S)$ injective on every fibre.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme. `(N : ℕ)`: the level.
- The value: `naiveLevel B (Multiplicative (ZMod N × ZMod N))`. For $N \neq 0$ a structure is a pair $(P, Q) = (\varphi(1,0), \varphi(0,1))$ of sections of $E[N]$ such that no combination $aP + bQ$ with $(a, b) \neq 0$ meets the zero section (`gammaNaiveEquiv`).

Where $N$ is invertible on $S$, $E[N]$ is finite étale of rank $N^2$, and such a pair is a basis of the $N$-torsion of every geometric fibre (`EllipticCurveGeom.isFiberwiseInjective_iff_range_eq_ker`): an isomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2_S \cong E[N]$, the inverse of a level-$N$ structure of Deligne and Rapoport (IV 2.3). No Weil-pairing condition is imposed, as in theirs.

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 2.3: where $n$ is invertible on $S$, $E[n]$ is finite étale of rank $n^2$, and a level-$n$ structure is an isomorphism $\alpha : E[n] \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2_S$, with no condition on the Weil pairing; its inverse is a naive $[\Gamma(n)]$-structure here.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaIsoGammaNaive` — where $N$ is invertible on $B$, the naive problem $[\Gamma(N)]$ is isomorphic to the Drinfeld problem $[\Gamma(N)]$, so the naive definition gives the classical object there.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.exists_isFiberwiseInjective` — over a separably closed field in which $N \neq 0$, every elliptic curve has a homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(K)$ injective on fibres, so naive structures exist.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaNaiveThreeRepresentableBy` — the naive problem $[\Gamma(3)]$ is represented by the universal level-three curve.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.isRigid_gammaNaive` — rigidity for $N \ge 3$.

## Lean subtleties
- `Multiplicative (ZMod N)` is $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively, and `.ofAdd a` is its element $a$. `ZMod 0` is $\mathbb{Z}$, so for $N = 0$ the problem is about homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}^2$; level $0$ is not a level in the literature.
- `IsFiberwiseInjective` is tested at the points of the underlying space of $S$: for $a \neq 1$, the section $\varphi(a)$ and the zero section have different images at every point $s$. Two sections agree at $s$ exactly when they agree as $\kappa(s)$-points of the fibre, so this is injectivity on every fibre, and on every geometric fibre.
- The definition makes sense over every base, but it is the classical level structure only where $N$ is invertible: at a point whose residue field has characteristic $p \mid N$ the fibre has fewer than $N^2$ points killed by $N$, and over a general base the right notion is Drinfeld's.
- It is an `abbrev`, so lemmas about `naiveLevel` apply to it directly.

## What it says
The right action of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ on the naive moduli problem $[\Gamma(N)]$: a matrix $g$ sends a structure $\varphi : (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(S)$ to $\varphi \circ g$.

- `(B : Scheme)`, `(N : ℕ)`: a base scheme and a level.
- The value: a group homomorphism from the opposite group `(GL (Fin 2) (ZMod N))ᵐᵒᵖ` to the automorphisms of `gammaNaive B N`. It is `naiveLevelAction` composed with the identification of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ with the automorphisms of $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$.

In terms of the points, $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ sends $(P, Q)$ to $(P, Q)\,g = (aP + cQ, bP + dQ)$, the row vector $(P, Q)$ times $g$ (`gammaNaiveEquiv_gammaNaiveAction_hom_app_fst_torsionι`, `…_snd_…`).

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaNaiveEquiv_gammaNaiveAction_hom_app_fst_torsionι` — the first new point is $aP + cQ$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaNaiveEquiv_gammaNaiveAction_hom_app_snd_torsionι` — the second is $bP + dQ$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaNaiveAction_hom_comp_gammaNaiveToGammaOneNaive` — keeping $P$ is invariant under the matrices with first column $(1, 0)$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaNaiveAction_hom_comp_gammaNaiveToGamma` — the action agrees with the action on Drinfeld's $[\Gamma(N)]$ through the comparison map.

## What it says
For $N \neq 0$, a naive $[\Gamma(N)]$-structure on $E/S$ is the same as a pair of sections $(P, Q)$ of $E[N]$ whose nonzero combinations miss the zero section.

- `{B} {N : ℕ} [NeZero N]`: a base scheme and a level $N \neq 0$.
- `(X : EllObj B)`: an elliptic curve $E/S$.
- The value: a bijection from the naive $[\Gamma(N)]$-structures on $X$ to the subtype of pairs $(P, Q)$ of sections of $E[N]$ over $S$ such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ with $(a, b) \neq 0$ and every point $s$ of $S$, the section $aP + bQ$ (`(P ≫ torsionι N) ^ a.val * (Q ≫ torsionι N) ^ b.val`) does not meet the zero section at $s$. It sends $\varphi$ to $(\varphi(1,0), \varphi(0,1))$ (`gammaNaiveEquiv_apply_fst_torsionι`, `…_snd_…`), and its inverse sends $(P, Q)$ to $(a, b) \mapsto aP + bQ$.

Where $N$ is invertible on $S$, these pairs are the bases of the $N$-torsion of every geometric fibre (`EllipticCurveGeom.isFiberwiseInjective_iff_range_eq_ker`), the inverses of the level-$N$ structures of Deligne and Rapoport (IV 2.3).

## What it says
Relative representability of the naive problem $[\Gamma(N)]$: over $E/S$ it is represented by the open subscheme of $E[N] \times_S E[N]$ of pairs $(P, Q)$ none of whose nonzero combinations meets the zero section.

- `{B} {N : ℕ} [NeZero N]`: a base scheme and a level $N \neq 0$.
- The value: relative-representability data for `gammaNaive B N`. For each $X = (E/S)$ the representing scheme is `naiveLocusOver (X.curve.torsionPairHom N)`, the naive locus of the universal pair of points of $E[N]$ (the two projections of $E[N] \times_S E[N]$ followed by $E[N] \to E$); the representation is `naiveLevelRepresentableBy`, applied to the universality of $E[N] \times_S E[N]$ for homomorphisms from $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ (`EllipticCurveGeom.existsUnique_comp_torsionPairHom`).

This holds over every base. Where $N$ is invertible it is the scheme of level-$N$ structures, finite étale over $S$ (Deligne and Rapoport, IV 3.1).

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 3.1: for $n$ invertible on $S$ and an elliptic curve $E/S$, the functor sending an $S$-scheme $T$ to the level-$n$ structures on $E_T$ is represented by a finite étale cover of $S$, a principal homogeneous space under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})$.
- D. Loeffler, *Modular curves*, lecture notes, Proposition 3.8.2 and its proof: over a base on which $N$ is invertible, the full level-$N$ structures on the base changes of $E$ are represented by an étale $S$-scheme, an open subscheme of $E[N] \times_S E[N]$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.hasProperty_etale_gammaNaiveRelRepData` — étale where $N$ is invertible.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.hasProperty_isFinite_gammaNaiveRelRepData` — finite where $N$ is invertible.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.hasProperty_etale_gammaRelRepData` — étaleness of Drinfeld's $[\Gamma(N)]$ where $N$ is invertible, transported from this data through the isomorphism of the two problems.

## Lean subtleties
- `[NeZero N]` is the hypothesis $N \neq 0$, carried as a typeclass.
- `RelRepData` is data; its `rep` field is equal by definition to the naive locus (`gammaNaiveRelRepData_rep`), and the representation's inverse uses classical choice.

text:
## What it says
The naive moduli problem $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ over `Ell/B`: to $E/S$ it assigns the homomorphisms $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to E(S)$ injective on every fibre.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme. `(N : ℕ)`: the level.
- The value: `naiveLevel B (Multiplicative (ZMod N))`, the naive $A$-structures for $A = \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For $N \neq 0$ such a structure is a section $P = \varphi(1)$ of $E[N]$ none of whose multiples $P, 2P, \dots, (N-1)P$ meets the zero section at any point of $S$ (`gammaOneNaiveEquiv`): a point of exact order $N$ in every fibre.

Where $N$ is invertible on $S$ this is the classical notion: a point $P$ for which $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to E[N]$, $a \mapsto aP$, is an embedding, that is, a section of exact order $N$ everywhere (Deligne and Rapoport, IV 4.8).

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 4.7 and Construction 4.8: the level structures for the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})$ fixing $(1, 0)$, that is, for the map $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \to (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$, $x \mapsto (x, 0)$, are, where $n$ is invertible on $S$, the embeddings $\beta : \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow E[n]$, that is, the sections $\beta(1)$ of exact order $n$ everywhere.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaOneNaiveRepresentableBy` — for $N \ge 4$, over every base $B$, the naive problem $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ is represented by the universal curve over $Y_1(N)$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.isFiberwiseInjective_iff_isOfNaiveExactOrder` — a homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ is injective on fibres exactly when $\varphi(1)$ has naive exact order $N$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.isRigid_gammaOneNaive` — rigidity for $N \ge 4$, sharp at $N = 3$.

## Lean subtleties
- `Multiplicative (ZMod N)` is $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively, and `.ofAdd a` is its element $a$. `ZMod 0` is $\mathbb{Z}$, so for $N = 0$ the problem is about homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}^2$; level $0$ is not a level in the literature.
- `IsFiberwiseInjective` is tested at the points of the underlying space of $S$: for $a \neq 1$, the section $\varphi(a)$ and the zero section have different images at every point $s$. Two sections agree at $s$ exactly when they agree as $\kappa(s)$-points of the fibre, so this is injectivity on every fibre, and on every geometric fibre.
- The definition makes sense over every base, but it is the classical naive level structure only where $N$ is invertible: at a point whose residue field has characteristic $p \mid N$ the fibre has fewer than $N^2$ points killed by $N$, and over a general base the right notion is Drinfeld's.
- It is an `abbrev`, so lemmas about `naiveLevel` apply to it directly.

## What it says
Naive structures exist over geometric points: if $A$ embeds in $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ and $N$ is invertible on $B$, every relatively representable problem of naive $A$-structures is surjective over `Ell/B`.

- `{B} {A : Type} [Group A]`: a base scheme and a group.
- `(D : (naiveLevel B A).RelRepData)`: relative-representability data for naive $A$-structures, a scheme $\mathcal{P}_{E/S}$ over $S$ for every $E/S$ representing the structures on base changes of $E$.
- `{N : ℕ}`, `(hN : ∀ b : B, (N : B.residueField b) ≠ 0)`: $N$ is invertible on $B$.
- `{ψ : A →* Multiplicative (ZMod N × ZMod N)}`, `(hψ : Function.Injective ψ)`: an embedding of $A$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$.
- The conclusion: `D.HasProperty @Surjective`, every representing morphism $\mathcal{P}_{E/S} \to S$ is surjective.

Over an algebraic closure $\bar k$ of a residue field of $S$, $E[N](\bar k) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ since $N$ is invertible, so $A$ embeds in $E(\bar k)$, giving a structure over a point above each point of $S$.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.exists_isFiberwiseInjective` — over a separably closed field in which $N \neq 0$, every elliptic curve has a homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(K)$ injective on fibres, so naive structures exist.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.hasProperty_surjective_gammaOneNaiveRelRepData` — the case $A = \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.hasProperty_surjective_gammaNaiveRelRepData` — the case $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$.

- `RelRepData` is data, so the statement holds for any choice of representing schemes.
- Where $N$ is not invertible the conclusion can fail: a supersingular curve in characteristic $p \mid N$ has too few $N$-torsion points.

text:
## What it says
Full level-$N$ structures are rigid for $N \ge 3$: over any base, an automorphism of an elliptic curve $E/S$ that fixes a naive $[\Gamma(N)]$-structure on it is the identity.

- `(B : AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme)`: a base scheme $B$, with no hypothesis on it.
- `(N : ℕ)`: a natural number $N$, the level.
- `(hN : 3 ≤ N)`: the level is at least $3$.
- The conclusion: the moduli problem `gammaNaive B N` is rigid. That problem assigns to an elliptic curve $E$ over a $B$-scheme $S$ its naive $[\Gamma(N)]$-structures: group homomorphisms $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(S)$, that is pairs $(P, Q)$ of sections, such that $aP + bQ$ meets the zero section in no fibre for every $(a, b) \neq 0$. Rigid means that for every such $E/S$ the automorphism group of $E/S$ acts freely on these structures: an automorphism with $\sigma \circ P = P$ and $\sigma \circ Q = Q$ is the identity.

This is the classical rigidity of full level-$N$ structures for $N \ge 3$ (Deligne and Rapoport, IV 2.7). Where $N$ is invertible on $S$, a homomorphism injective on every fibre is a basis of $E[N]$ on every geometric fibre, the classical naive full level structure.

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 2.6 and Theorem 2.7 with its proof: for $n \ge 3$, an automorphism of an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic prime to $n$ which is trivial on $E[n]$ is the identity, so that, over every base on which $n$ is invertible, no nontrivial automorphism of an elliptic curve preserves a level-$n$ structure.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.exists_isFiberwiseInjective` — over a separably closed field in which $N \neq 0$, every elliptic curve carries such a fibrewise injective homomorphism.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.isFiberwiseInjective_zmod_three_prod_iff` — for $N = 3$, a pair $(P, Q)$ is a structure exactly when, at every point of $S$, $P \neq 0$, $Q \neq 0$, $Q \neq P$ and $Q \neq -P$.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.isRigid_gammaOneNaive` — the companion statement: the naive $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ problem is rigid for $N \ge 4$.

The first test shows that the structures exist, so the rigidity is not vacuous; the second spells out the condition at the smallest level, where the distinct points $0, P, -P, Q$ are what force an automorphism fixing $P$ and $Q$ to be trivial.

## Lean subtleties
- The base $B$ is any scheme, possibly nonreduced or non-affine, and $S$ any $B$-scheme.
- An automorphism of $E/S$ is an arrow of elliptic curves over $B$ from $E/S$ to itself lying over the identity of $S$; fixing a structure means that pulling it back along $\sigma$ returns it.
- At a point of $S$ whose residue field has characteristic dividing $N$, the fibre has fewer than $N^2$ points of order dividing $N$, so no naive structure exists over such an $S$: the statement has content over bases on which $N$ is invertible, as for the classical naive structures.
- The bound is the classical one: for $N = 2$, the automorphism $-1$ fixes every point of order $2$ and is not the identity.

text:
## What it says
The naive moduli problem $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ is rigid for $N \ge 4$: an automorphism of an elliptic curve $E/S$ fixing a point of exact order $N$ in every fibre is the identity.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme, with no hypothesis. `(N : ℕ)`: the level.
- `(hN : 4 ≤ N)`: the level is at least $4$.
- The conclusion: `(gammaOneNaive B N).IsRigid`. For every $E/S$ in `Ell/B`, an arrow $\sigma : E/S \to E/S$ over the identity of $S$ that fixes a naive $[\Gamma_1(N)]$-structure $P$ is the identity.

The automorphism fixes $P$, $2P$ and $-P$, which are nonzero and distinct in every fibre when $N \ge 4$. Only $[-1]$ among the nontrivial automorphisms fixes four points of a geometric fibre, and it fixes $P$ only if $2P = 0$. The bound is sharp, as the docstring notes: on $Y^2 + Y = X^3$ over a field with a primitive cube root of unity $\zeta$, the automorphism $(X, Y) \mapsto (\zeta X, Y)$ fixes the point $(0, 0)$ of order $3$.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.isRigid_gammaOne` — the Drinfeld problem $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ is rigid for $N \ge 4$ invertible on $B$, deduced from this theorem through the comparison map.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaOneNaiveRepresentableBy` — for $N \ge 4$, over every base $B$, the problem is represented by the universal curve over $Y_1(N)$, which also forces rigidity.

Representability by $Y_1(N)$ is the classical consequence of this rigidity, and the two agree.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsRigid` asks only about arrows over the identity of the base; fixing the structure means $\sigma \circ P = P$.
- The base is arbitrary. Where $N$ is not invertible the structures are naive in Lean's sense, injective on fibres, not the classical ones, which need $N$ invertible.
- At $N = 0$ (`ZMod 0 = ℤ`) the problem is also rigid, but the hypothesis $4 \le N$ excludes that case, which is no level in the literature.
- `Multiplicative (ZMod N)` is $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively, and `.ofAdd a` is its element $a$. `ZMod 0` is $\mathbb{Z}$, so for $N = 0$ the problem is about homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}^2$; level $0$ is not a level in the literature.

## What it says
Naive $A$-structures are rigid as soon as $A$ contains elements $a$ and $b$ with $a^2 \neq 1$, $b \neq 1$, $b \neq a$ and $b \neq a^{-1}$: an automorphism of $E/S$ fixing a naive $A$-structure is the identity.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme, with no hypothesis. `{A : Type} [Group A]`: a group.
- `{a b : A}`, `(ha : a * a ≠ 1)`, `(hb : b ≠ 1)`, `(hba : b ≠ a)`, `(hba' : b ≠ a⁻¹)`: the elements $a$ and $b$.
- The conclusion: `(naiveLevel B A).IsRigid`. For every object $E/S$ of `Ell/B`, an arrow $\sigma : E/S \to E/S$ over the identity of $S$ that fixes some naive $A$-structure is the identity.

An automorphism fixing $\varphi$ fixes the sections $\varphi(a)$, $\varphi(a)^{-1}$ and $\varphi(b)$. These are distinct and nonzero in every fibre, since $\varphi$ is injective there. On a geometric fibre, a nontrivial automorphism of an elliptic curve fixes at most four points, and exactly four only for $[-1]$, which fixes $\varphi(a)$ only if $a^2 = 1$. The proof uses `EllipticCurveGeom.IsFiberwiseInjective.eq_id_of_isPullback`. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary.

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 2.6 and Theorem 2.7 with its proof: for $n \ge 3$, an automorphism of an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic prime to $n$ which is trivial on $E[n]$ is the identity, so that, over every base on which $n$ is invertible, no nontrivial automorphism of an elliptic curve preserves a level-$n$ structure.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.isRigid_gammaNaive` — the case $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$, $N \ge 3$, with $a = (1, 0)$ and $b = (0, 1)$.

Where $N$ is invertible, that case is the classical rigidity of full level-$N$ structures above. None of the four conditions can be dropped, over a base such as $\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}$: in $A = \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ with $a = 1$, each of $b = 0, 1, 2$ fails exactly one of the three conditions on $b$, and $[\Gamma_1(3)]$ is not rigid (the automorphism $(X, Y) \mapsto (\zeta X, Y)$ of $Y^2 + Y = X^3$, $\zeta$ a primitive cube root of unity, fixes the point $(0, 0)$ of order $3$); in $A = (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$ with $a = (1, 0)$ and $b = (0, 1)$ only $a^2 \neq 1$ fails, and $[-1]$ fixes every point of order $2$.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsRigid` quantifies over all objects of `Ell/B` and asks only about arrows lying over the identity of the base, the automorphisms of $E/S$.
- Fixing a structure means that its pull-back along $\sigma$ is itself, that is, $\sigma \circ \varphi = \varphi$.
- No hypothesis on the base: it may be nonreduced or non-affine.
- The group $A$ lies in `Type`, the lowest universe, so that the structures, wrapped in `ULift`, lie in `Type (u + 1)` like the values of every moduli problem; this does not affect the mathematics.

text:
## What it says
The moduli problem of naive $A$-structures over `Ell/B`: to an elliptic curve $E/S$ it assigns the group homomorphisms $\varphi : A \to E(S)$ that are injective on every fibre of $E$ over $S$.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme, with no hypothesis.
- `(A : Type) [Group A]`: a group $A$.
- The value: a `ModuliProblem B`, that is, a contravariant functor from `Ell/B` to sets. An object $X = (E/S)$ of `Ell/B` (`EllObj B`) is a scheme $S$ over $B$ with an elliptic curve $E$ over $S$; an arrow $(E'/S') \to (E/S)$ is a cartesian square exhibiting $E'$ as the base change of $E$. On $X = (E/S)$ its value is the set of homomorphisms $\varphi : A \to E(S)$ such that for every $a \neq 1$ the section $\varphi(a)$ misses the zero section at every point of $S$ (`naiveLevelEquiv`). An arrow $(E'/S') \to (E/S)$ pulls $\varphi$ back by base change of sections (`naiveLevelEquiv_map`).

For $A = \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ these are the naive problems $[\Gamma_1(N)]$ and $[\Gamma(N)]$ (`gammaOneNaive`, `gammaNaive`). Where $N$ is invertible on $S$, the first are the embeddings $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow E[N]$, the sections of exact order $N$ everywhere, and the second the isomorphisms $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2_S \cong E[N]$: the classical level structures of Deligne and Rapoport (IV 4.8 and IV 2.3).

## References and tests
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 2.3: where $n$ is invertible on $S$, $E[n]$ is finite étale of rank $n^2$, and a level-$n$ structure is an isomorphism $\alpha : E[n] \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2_S$, with no condition on the Weil pairing; its inverse is a naive $[\Gamma(n)]$-structure here.
- P. Deligne and M. Rapoport, *Les schémas de modules de courbes elliptiques*, in *Modular Functions of One Variable II*, Lecture Notes in Math. 349 (1973), Chapter IV, 4.7 and Construction 4.8: the level structures for the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})$ fixing $(1, 0)$, that is, for the map $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \to (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$, $x \mapsto (x, 0)$, are, where $n$ is invertible on $S$, the embeddings $\beta : \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow E[n]$, that is, the sections $\beta(1)$ of exact order $n$ everywhere.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.gammaIsoGammaNaive` — where $N$ is invertible on $B$, the naive problem $[\Gamma(N)]$ is isomorphic to the Drinfeld problem $[\Gamma(N)]$, so the naive definition gives the classical object there.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.EllipticCurveGeom.exists_isFiberwiseInjective` — over a separably closed field in which $N \neq 0$, every elliptic curve has a homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2 \to E(K)$ injective on fibres, so naive structures exist.

## Lean subtleties
- $E(S)$ is written `𝟙_ (Over S) ⟶ Over.mk E.structureMap`: the sections of $E \to S$, with the group law written multiplicatively (`*`, `^`, and `1` for the zero section).
- `IsFiberwiseInjective` is tested at the points of the underlying space of $S$: for $a \neq 1$, the section $\varphi(a)$ and the zero section have different images at every point $s$. Two sections agree at $s$ exactly when they agree as $\kappa(s)$-points of the fibre, so this is injectivity on every fibre, and on every geometric fibre.
- Over the empty scheme every homomorphism is injective on every fibre, and $E(\emptyset)$ is trivial, so there is exactly one structure.
- The group $A$ lies in `Type`, the lowest universe, so that the structures, wrapped in `ULift`, lie in `Type (u + 1)` like the values of every moduli problem; this does not affect the mathematics.
- No hypothesis on the base is built in. Over a base where $N$ is not invertible, the structures for $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ are not the classical ones, which are defined only where $N$ is invertible; the module docstring points to Drinfeld's structures for a general base.

## What it says
The right action of the automorphism group of $A$ on the naive $A$-structures: an automorphism $\sigma$ of $A$ sends $\varphi$ to $\varphi \circ \sigma$.

- `(B : Scheme)`: a base scheme. `(A : Type) [Group A]`: a group.
- The value: a group homomorphism from `(MulAut A)ᵐᵒᵖ`, the opposite of the group of automorphisms of $A$, to `Aut (naiveLevel B A)`, the automorphisms of the moduli problem. The automorphism attached to $\sigma$ acts on every structure by $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \sigma$ (`naiveLevelEquiv_naiveLevelAction_hom_app`), and its inverse by $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \sigma^{-1}$.

Since $\varphi \circ (\sigma \tau) = (\varphi \circ \sigma) \circ \tau$, precomposition is a right action, which is why the source is the opposite group. For $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ it gives the action of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ on $[\Gamma(N)]$ (`gammaNaiveAction`).

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.eq_one_of_naiveLevelAction_hom_app_eq_self` — the action is free over a nonempty base.
- `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.ModuliProblem.naiveLevelEquiv_naiveLevelAction_hom_app` — the action is precomposition.

## Lean subtleties
- `Aut P` is the group of natural automorphisms of the functor $P$; `.asIso.hom.app (op X)` is the bijection the automorphism induces on the structures over $X$. `(MulAut A)ᵐᵒᵖ` is the opposite of the automorphism group of $A$: a homomorphism from it is a right action.
- That this is a homomorphism (the unit acts trivially, products act by composites) is checked by Lean.

## What it says
Naive $A$-structures are relatively representable once homomorphisms from $A$ are: they are represented by the naive locus of a universal homomorphism.

- `{B}`: a base scheme. `{X : EllObj B}`: an elliptic curve $E$ over a $B$-scheme $S$. `{A : Type} [Group A]`: a group.
- `{H : Over X.base}`, `(u : A →* (H ⟶ Over.mk X.curve.structureMap))`: a scheme $H$ over $S$ and a homomorphism $u : A \to E(H)$ to the points of $E$ with values in $H$.
- `[Finite A]`: $A$ is finite.
- `(hu : …)`: $u$ is universal: every homomorphism $\varphi : A \to E(T)$, for a scheme $T$ over $S$, is $a \mapsto x \circ u(a)$ for a unique morphism $x : T \to H$ over $S$. So $H$ represents $T \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(A, E(T))$.
- The value: a representation of the fibre of `naiveLevel B A` over $X$, the functor $T \mapsto$ {naive $A$-structures on $E_T$} on schemes $T$ over $S$, by the scheme `naiveLocusOver u`, the open subscheme of $H$ on which $u$ is injective on fibres.

For $A = \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$, $N \neq 0$, the scheme $H$ is $E[N]$ and $E[N] \times_S E[N]$ (`gammaOneNaiveRelRepData`, `gammaNaiveRelRepData`). Where $N$ is invertible, the case $A = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^2$ gives the relative representability of full level-$N$ structures by an étale scheme (Loeffler, Proposition 3.8.2; Deligne and Rapoport, IV 3.1); the statement here needs neither $N$ invertible nor any property of $H$.

## What it says
For a universal homomorphism $u$, the points of the naive locus of $u$ with values in $T$ are the naive $A$-structures on the base change $E_T$.

- `{B}`: a base scheme. `{X : EllObj B}`: an elliptic curve $E$ over a $B$-scheme $S$. `{A : Type} [Group A]`: a group.
- `{H : Over X.base}`, `(u : A →* (H ⟶ Over.mk X.curve.structureMap))`: a scheme $H$ over $S$ and a homomorphism $u : A \to E(H)$ to the points of $E$ with values in $H$.
- `[Finite A]`: $A$ is finite.
- `(hu : …)`: $u$ is universal: every homomorphism $\varphi : A \to E(T)$, for a scheme $T$ over $S$, is $a \mapsto x \circ u(a)$ for a unique morphism $x : T \to H$ over $S$. So $H$ represents $T \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(A, E(T))$.
- `(T : Over X.base)`: a scheme $T$ over $S$.
- The value: a bijection between the morphisms $T \to$ `naiveLocusOver u` over $S$ and the naive $A$-structures on $E_T$, a point $y$ going to the structure `naiveLocusHom u y` (`naiveLevelEquiv_naiveLocusEquiv`).

A homomorphism $A \to E_T(T)$ is a homomorphism $A \to E(T)$, hence by universality a morphism $x : T \to H$; it is injective on fibres exactly when $x$ lands in the naive locus. This is the open-locus argument behind the relative representability of naive level structures.

## What it says
For a morphism of finite bilinear modules, the function underlying its additive homomorphism is the function of the morphism itself.

- `{A : FiniteBilinearModule} {B : FiniteBilinearModule}`: two finite bilinear modules $A$ and $B$, implicit (Lean infers them from $f$).
- `(f : A.Hom B)`: a morphism `Hom A B`, that is, an additive homomorphism $f : A \to B$ with $b_B(f(x), f(y)) = b_A(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in A$.
- The conclusion: `⇑f.toAddMonoidHom = ⇑f`, an equality of functions $A \to B$: applying the stored additive homomorphism of $f$ to $x$ gives $f(x)$, for every $x \in A$.

This is bookkeeping: a morphism is an additive homomorphism with an extra property, and the two ways of reading it as a function agree.

## References and tests
None.

## Lean subtleties
- `⇑` is Lean's coercion of a bundled map to a plain function. A morphism `f` and its field `f.toAddMonoidHom` are different objects in Lean (one carries the pairing condition), and each has its own coercion to functions; the lemma says the two functions are equal.
- The lemma is tagged `@[simp]`, so Lean's simplifier rewrites the first form into the second, and statements about $f$ are kept in terms of $f$ itself.
- The modules may live in different universes (`FiniteBilinearModule.{u}`); universe levels do not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
The composite of two morphisms of finite bilinear modules.

- `{A B C : FiniteBilinearModule}`: three finite bilinear modules, implicit.
- `(g : B.Hom C)`: a morphism from $B$ to $C$.
- `(f : A.Hom B)`: a morphism from $A$ to $B$; here a morphism is an additive homomorphism preserving the pairings, $b_B(f(x), f(y)) = b_A(x, y)$.
- The value: a morphism `A.Hom C` whose underlying additive homomorphism is $g \circ f$; it preserves the pairing because $b_C(g(f(x)), g(f(y))) = b_B(f(x), f(y)) = b_A(x, y)$.

This is the usual composition of structure-preserving maps, in the usual order: `g.comp f` is $g \circ f$, apply $f$ first.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Hom.comp_apply` — its value at $x$ is $g(f(x))$.
- `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Hom.comp_assoc` — composition is associative.
- `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Hom.id_comp` — the identity morphism is a left unit for it.
- `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Hom.comp_id` — the identity morphism is a right unit for it.

These show it is composition of functions and satisfies the laws of a category.

## Lean subtleties
- The first explicit argument is the map applied second, as with $\circ$; by contrast `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Isometry.trans` composes isometries in diagrammatic order.
- The three modules may live in different universes; this does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A composite of morphisms of finite bilinear modules is evaluated by applying the two morphisms in turn.

- `{A B C : FiniteBilinearModule}`: three finite bilinear modules, implicit.
- `(g : B.Hom C)`, `(f : A.Hom B)`: morphisms, that is, additive homomorphisms preserving the pairings.
- `(x : A)`: an element of $A$.
- The conclusion: `(g.comp f) x = g (f x)`, that is $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$.

This says `TauCeti.FiniteBilinearModule.Hom.comp` is composition of maps, with $f$ applied first.

- The lemma is tagged `@[simp]`, so the simplifier evaluates composites pointwise.
- The three modules may live in different universes; this does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
Composition of morphisms of finite bilinear modules is associative.

- `{A B C D : FiniteBilinearModule}`: four finite bilinear modules, implicit.
- `(h : C.Hom D)`, `(g : B.Hom C)`, `(f : A.Hom B)`: three composable morphisms, each an additive homomorphism preserving the pairings.
- The conclusion: `(h.comp g).comp f = h.comp (g.comp f)`, that is $(h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)$ as morphisms $A \to D$.

This is the associativity law of a category for finite bilinear modules and their pairing-preserving homomorphisms; the file does not package the laws as a category instance.

## What it says
Composing a morphism of finite bilinear modules with the identity on the right gives the morphism back.

- `{A B : FiniteBilinearModule}`: two finite bilinear modules, implicit.
- `(f : A.Hom B)`: a morphism `Hom A B`, that is, an additive homomorphism $f : A \to B$ with $b_B(f(x), f(y)) = b_A(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in A$.
- The conclusion: `f.comp (id A) = f`, that is $f \circ \mathrm{id}_A = f$ as morphisms.

This is the right unit law of a category for finite bilinear modules and their pairing-preserving homomorphisms; the file does not package the laws as a category instance.
